1. 
PROPOSED TAX MILLAGE RATE – 2026 
 
 
 
 
Each year, the Gwinnett County Tax Assessor reviews the assessed value of taxable 
property in the County. When the total digest of taxable property is prepared, 
Georgia Law requires calculation of a "rollback" millage rate (RMR) that produces 
the same total revenue on the current year's new digest that last year's millage 
rate would have produced, had no reassessments occurred. 
 
The City of Duluth is considering maintaining the same millage rate as last year, 
which is 6.551 mills. For the 2026 digest, the current millage rate exceeded the 
rollback millage rate by 0.185 mills, or stated another way, as a percentage of the 
rollback millage rate, the current millage rate represents a 2.91% "increase." The 
reassessment revenue would add approximately $525,644. 
 
Georgia law requires that the City publish a "Notice of Property Tax Increase" in 
the legal organ when the tentative adopted millage rate exceeds the rollback 
millage rate. Attached for reference. 
 
This is the first of three public hearings as required by O.C.G.A 48-5-32.1. The 
second Public Hearing is scheduled Monday, August 10th at 6:00 p.m. in the 
Council Chambers and the third Public Hearing is scheduled for Monday, August 
24th at 5:30 p.m. in the City Hall Community Room. 
 
 
 
II. 
ADJOURNMENT

1. ORDINANCE TO AMEND DULUTH CODE – PARKING 
 
Council directed staff to prepare an amendment to Article III Stopping, Standing 
and Parking Section 8-68 subsection (14) of the Duluth Code of Ordinances. The 
proposed amendment modifies hours prohibiting overnight, on-street parking 
from 10 pm to 6 am to now prohibit from 12 am to 7 am. Approval of this item 
approves ordinance O2026-34 as presented.

2. ORDINANCE TO AMEND DULUTH CODE – NOISE 
 
 
Council directed staff to prepare an amendment to Article III Noise Section 9.64 of 
the Duluth Code of Ordinances. The proposed amendment modifies hours of use 
and limits noise levels for power tools, lawnmowers, leaf blowers, chain saws and 
other agricultural equipment. Approval of this item approves ordinance O2026-35 
as presented. 
 
3. ORDINANCE TO AMEND BUDGET-$46,500 – CAMERA SERVERS 
 
At the July 27th Work Session, Chief Carruth informed council that the three 
camera servers at Public Works, WP Jones, and Festival Center are at end of life 
and need to be replaced at a cost of $16,471. An additional server at City Hall will 
be at end of life in January 2027 and will be replaced at that time, costing $30,029. 
Total camera server replacement cost of$46,500 and will come from unallocated 
2023 SPLOST Public Safety Funds. Approval of this item approves budget 
amendment BA-FY27-05 to add $46,500 in 2023 SPLOST Public Safety Funds to 
Police Capital Projects - Police - Computers line item, including associated 
transfers. 
 
4. ORDINANCE TO AMEND BUDGET-$200,000 – RED CLAY 
 
 
Staff is seeking additional funds relating to the Red Clay renovation project. 
Specifically, additional carpet, security cameras/access control, electrical 
improvements and other items have been identified as needing to be upgraded 
during the renovation. Accordingly, staff is requesting a budget amendment in 
the amount of $200,000. Approval of this item approves budget amendment BA-
FY27-06 to add $200,000 in General Funds to Red Clay Theater - Special 
Recreational Facilities - Site Improvements line item, including associated 
transfers. 
 
5. ORDINANCE TO AMEND DULUTH CODE – STORMWATER 
 
 
Per ongoing and recent discussion by Mayor and Council, and decision at the 
annual strategic retreat held June 26, 2026, stormwater rates are to be increased 
by 3% per year starting with the 2026 property tax billing cycle. Approval of this 
item approves ordinance O2026-36 as presented. 
 
6. TRAFFIC CALMING POLICY/BUDGET AMENDMENT 
 
 
Per ongoing and recent discussion by Mayor and Council, and decision at the 
retreat of June 26, 2026, the City's traffic calming policy is to be approved to allow 
a formal path forward for residents to request service, and staff to investigate 
services requests related to traffic calming measures. Additionally, staff is 
requesting a budget amendment in the amount of $50,000 to cover initial studies 
related to the list of initial requests made over the years prior to this policy being 
adopted. Approval of this item approves the policy as presented, and budget 
amendment BA-FY27-04 to add $50,000 in unallocated 2017 SPLOST

7. RESOLUTION – DEPOSITORIES AND CHECK SIGNING 
 
 
In January of each year, staff brings before Council a Resolution regarding 
designating certain depositories for the City. Upon review, an error was found in 
the language identifying the depository for "Urban Redevelopment Agency" 
instead of the City of Duluth. Staff also at this time recommends narrowing down 
the list of banking institutions to only those banks the City currently hold funds in. 
Approval of this item approves resolution R2025-08 accordingly.

1. PROPOSED 2026 TAX MILLAGE RATE 
 
 
 
 
 
Each year, the Gwinnett County Tax Assessor reviews the assessed value of taxable 
property in the County. When the total digest of taxable property is prepared, 
Georgia Law requires calculation of a "rollback" millage rate (RMR) that produces 
the same total revenue on the current year's new digest that last year's millage 
rate would have produced, had no reassessments occurred. The City of Duluth is 
considering maintaining the same millage rate as last year, which is 6.551 mills. For 
the 2026 digest, the current millage rate exceeded the rollback millage rate by 
0.185 mills, or stated another way, as a percentage of the rollback millage rate, the 
current millage rate represents a 2.91% "increase." The reassessment revenue 
would add approximately $525,644. This is the second of three public hearings as 
required by O.C.G.A 48-5-32.1. 
 
Georgia law requires that the City publish a "Notice of Property Tax Increase" in 
the legal organ when the tentative adopted millage rate exceeds the rollback 
millage rate. Attached for reference. 
 
The third Public hearing is scheduled to be heard at 5:30 pm. August 24, 2026 in 
the Community Room, followed by adoption of an ordinance setting the 2026 
Millage Rate. 
 
 
 
VIII. NEW BUSINESS 
 
1. APPROVAL OF FRANCHISE AGREEMENT – GOOGLE FIBER 
 
Mayor and Council to consider approval of a proposed agreement with Google 
Fiber to allow for the expansion of Broadband Fiber in Duluth. Ryan Fender GMA 
Local Government and Jess George with Google Fiber will be on hand to answer 
questions. 
 

M&C Agenda 
August 10, 2026

5
The agreement includes paying the City a Franchise Fee equal to two percent (2%) 
of Gross Revenues for a calendar quarter. The payment will be accompanied by a 
report showing the basis for the computation and such other relevant facts as 
may be required by the City to determine the accuracy of the payment. 
The proposed agreement includes a franchise term of 10 years. The agreement 
has been reviewed by GMA's Legal Counsel as well as the City Attorney. The 
agreement and the Franchise are subject to the City's valid authority under State 
and local laws as they exist now or may be amended from time-to-time, and 
subject to the conditions set forth in the Agreement. Individual Permits Required 
and Performance Bond Required. Google Fiber will cooperate with the City in 
identifying ways to minimize the amount of construction in the Public ROW 
through joint trenching, sharing duct banks, and cost sharing with the City and 
third parties undertaking similar construction projects involving the installation of 
underground communications facilities. 
 
2. ADOPTION OF SIDEWALK AND TRAIL MAP 
 
 
 
Mayor and Council to consider readoption of the City of Duluth sidewalk and trail 
map. When applying for grants for specific sidewalk or trail projects, the City's 
current Sidewalk and Trail map must be included. The project for which the City is 
seeking funding must be depicted on the map (or in a plan). The City's map 
shows existing and future sidewalks, so it is interpreted as a map as well as a plan. 
 
Staff has added both the Chattahoochee River Trail and the McClure Bridge Road 
Trail (names of these projects may change, but the intent is the same) to the map 
so that applications for grant funding will be complete. 
 
3. RESOLUTION – GTIB GRANT MATCH – MCCLURE TRAIL 
 
The Mayor and Council to consider approval of resolution R2026-06. 
 
At the Mayor and Council Retreat of 2025, staff introduced several high level 
concepts for projects that will create a more comprehensive trail system within 
the City. Since that time, staff has been seeking out grant opportunities that align 
with these potential trail projects. The intent is to leverage these grants with 
locally funded matches such that the City's financial investment is reduced and 
the value of the trail project(s) is increased. 
 
One such grant is available for application at this time. The Georgia 
Transportation Infrastructure Bank (GTIB) has opened its call for projects for the 
2027 fiscal year. GTIB offers loans and grants for roadway, bike/pedestrian, and 
traffic operations projects. 
 
Staff believes the trail connection currently proposed between the Hudgens 
Property at Pleasant Hill Road and downtown Duluth would be a competitive 
application, and could help fund the preconstruction effort (design and right of 
way acquisition). An alternatives analysis is currently under way with public 
involvement meetings expected this fall.

Since a preferred alignment for this trail has not yet been determined, staff would 
feel more comfortable seeking funding in phases. 
 
The grant application requires a resolution from Council that commits a portion of 
the project cost which in this case could be derived from the City's SPLOST 
revenues for transportation. With information known to date, staff believes a 20% 
match is reasonable and customary. GTIB stipulates that grant requests over 
$2,000,000 require a 67% project sponsor match, where grant requests less than 
$2,000,000 do not have a minimum match requirement. Applications that 
include a local match are more competitive. 
 
Preliminary cost estimates show the design ($1,300,000) and right of way 
acquisition ($1,200,000) phases to cost about $2,500,000. The City sponsored 
match is therefore estimated at $500,000, with a total request from GTIB of 
$2,000,000. Staff is requesting Council adopt the resolution such that it can be 
included in the grant application.

1. ORDINANCE OF REZONING – CASE Z2026-004 – 3276 DELMA CT 
 
{C} 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Mayor Whitlock opened the public hearing to consider a rezoning request Oladeji to allow 
for the addition of a second duplex on a portion for 3276 Delma Court (Parcel ID R7264 
170) from R-75 (single family residential district) to RM (residential multifamily district) for 
the property that does not yet contain a structure, and make the existing duplex legal and 
conforming. 
 
Deputy Director of Planning and Engineering Aron Hall came forward to present. He 
outlined the surrounding property uses and existing conditions. 
 
The subject property is in the Established Neighborhood District. FORWARDuluth 
envisions this Character Area to continue to be the backbone of Duluth’s residential 
community. The Future Land Use Map (FLUM) envisions the uses to be low density 
residential (1-6 units an acre). 
 
The current property was platted in 1979, and the plat contemplated two duplexes when 
it was recorded. The current duplex was built in 1980; however, staff cannot locate when 
the duplex was rezoned to R-75 (Single-Family Residential District) from RM (Residential 
Multi-family). The property only became legal non-conforming in June of 2024 when 
duplexes were disallowed in RA-200, R-100 and R-75. 
 
The current owner purchased the property in August of 2015. There have been two code 
cases opened and subsequently closed on the property since the purchase: 
1. parking violation/outdoor storage and sanitary conditions (opened January 3, 2022, 
and closed January 22, 2022) 
2. Ground cover, outdoor storage, protective treatment, roof and drainage, unsafe 
structures and equipment, and vegetation (opened March 11, 2026, and closed April 
14, 2026). 
 
The Comprehensive Plan envisions low density residential (1-6 units an acre). Adding a 
duplex to this property would yield 10 units an acre, which is not in line with the 
Comprehensive Plan. It does, however, make the current duplex legal and conforming.

Mr. Hall described the General Conditions and concluded by reporting that the Planning 
Commission and staff recommended approval of this item 
 
Mayor Whitlock called for discussion from Council. 
 
Councilmember Thomas asked if it was on sewer, and owner-occupied or rented. 
 
Staff confirmed it was a rental. 
 
Councilmember Graeder noted that this request was only for the rezoning but not for the 
duplex approval itself. 
 
Mayor Whitlock called the applicant forward. 
 
Mr. Midia Jai of 810 Winderose Drive of Hoschton, Georgia came forward representing

Residential 
Traffic Calming Program 
Policy and Procedure 
City of Duluth 
Adopted: August 10, 2026 
 
 
 

 
Residential Traffic Calming Program 
1. 
Application and Intent 
 
The residential traffic calming program speciﬁcally applies to local city-owned 
roads in residential neighborhoods. This program does not apply to private roads, 
County or State-owned roads, or roads within non-residential areas. 
 
2. 
Deﬁnitions and Acronyms 
For the purposes of this policy, the following terms and phrases are defined. 
Unless the context clearly indicates otherwise, each term shall have the meaning 
assigned to it in this section. 
85th Percentile Speed: An index of traffic speeds for a road segment used by 
transportation professionals for traffic analysis purposes. The 85th percentile 
speed is the speed at which 85 percent of the total collected traffic volume are 
driving at or below in a typical 24-hour period. 
 
AASHTO: the American Association of State Highway and Transportation 
Officials. This non-proﬁt, non-partisan organization represents state 
departments of transportation in the U.S. and Puerto Rico, and set national 
guidelines for highway design, construction, and safety materials. 
 
ADT / Average Daily Traffic: Unit of measure used by transportation professionals 
for traffic volume analysis, in units of vehicles per day (vpd). ADT for the purpose 
of this policy refers to the traffic in both directions on a particular stretch of 
roadway within a typical 24-hour period. 
 
Affected Area / Service Area: The geographic portion of a neighborhood 
consisting of all property owners whose quality of life as a resident in the 
neighborhood, and not necessarily as a traveler through the neighborhood, is 
being directly impacted by the cut-through or speeding traffic problem being 
addressed. The affected area will include all lots from which residents must 
traverse all or a portion of the traffic calming measure. The affected area will also 
include all lots from which residents may have an alternate route without traffic 

calming measures, but whose lots have driveways that access the residential 
street for which traffic calming measures are sought. Non-fronting lots who have 
an alternate travel path may be considered part of the affected area based on 
proximity. 
 
Applicant: A real property owner who has initiated a request for traffic calming 
measures and/or has assumed a primary role in circulating the subsequent 
traffic-calming petition and undertakes to serve as the City's sole contact with 
respect to the progress of any subsequent traffic study and traffic-calming 
petition. 
 
City: City of Duluth, GA 
 
Department: The city’s Department of Community Development & Engineering. 
 
Director: Director of the Community Development & Engineering Department of 
the City of Duluth, unless otherwise noted. 
 
Eligible Petitioner: The person whose name is recorded as a property owner in 
the tax records maintained by the Gwinnett County tax commissioner and board 
of tax assessors for the address listed on the petition that falls within the affected 
area. 
 
GDOT: Georgia Department of Transportation 
 
HOA: Homeowners Association 
 
ITE: The Institute of Transportation Engineers. This member-driven educational 
association includes engineers and planners who work to improve mobility and 
safety for all road users. 
 
MUTCD: The Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, latest edition. This 
manual is published by the Federal Highway Administration, and is the national 
standard for all traffic signs, signals, and pavement markings in the U.S. 
 
Real Property Owners: Owners as indicated in the tax records maintained by the 
Gwinnett County tax commissioner and board of tax assessors. 
 

Residential Street: A street listed as “local” in the records of the City of Duluth 
Community Development and Engineering Department serving homes rather 
than businesses. This classiﬁcation is based on land use and is not considered a 
functional classiﬁcation. 
 
Traffic-Calming Measures: Those self-enforcing methods and processes, 
prescribed by "AASHTO" or other nationally recognized organizations, that the City 
may use in combination to reduce aggressive driving behavior that impair the 
quality of life of its citizens in any neighborhood in which the posted speed limit is 
no greater than thirty (30) miles per hour. A list of such potential measures is 
located later in this document. 
 
Traffic Study: The process by which data pertinent to the ﬂow, rate of speed and 
density of traffic, collected over a deﬁned period of time, is measured and 
analyzed to determine its impact on the safety of citizens within a neighborhood 
or affected area. 
 
3. 
Program Goals 
The City of Duluth supports traffic calming measures that are proven in the 
transportation industry to enhance public safety without delaying emergency 
response vehicles and personnel. The goals of the program include: 
• Reducing speeds such that 85% of vehicles travel within 5 mph of the 
posted speed limit. 
• Discouraging through traffic from using local residential streets while 
encouraging them to remain on arterials and collectors where possible. 
• Deterring heavy vehicles from using local roads where possible. 
• Maintaining emergency vehicle access and response time. 
• Maintaining or improving access (or future access) for bicycles and 
pedestrians. 
• Educating the neighborhood on traffic calming as projects move forward. 
 
4. 
Minimum Requirements 
• Only city-owned, local residential streets with a posted speed limit of 
30mph or less are eligible for the program. 
• Speed study (conducted by the City) must indicate the 85th percentile 
speed is greater than 10mph over the posted speed limit. Speed study to 

include a review of whether traffic calming techniques would be expected 
to cause a signiﬁcant impact on other local residential streets in or near 
the study area. 
• Length of the roadway segment is at least 500 feet. 
• Average daily traffic (ADT) exceeds the number of expected trips (based on 
ITE trip generation models) by 25% or more. For lower volume roads, 
average daily traffic must also exceed 400 vehicles per day. 
• Speeding issues must be officially reported to the City’s Department of 
Public Safety prior to requesting any traffic calming studies. 
5. 
Process 
1. An applicant or HOA must ﬁrst document the speeding issues by reporting 
them directly to the City of Duluth Public Safety Department. This will 
allow for enforcement opportunity and will allow engineers to understand 
whether the problem is ongoing or isolated. 
2. If a speeding problem exists, and if the City’s Public Safety Department 
conﬁrms it is an ongoing issue that should be further investigated for traffic 
calming measures, an applicant may request a traffic calming study. 
3. Traffic calming studies can be requested through the Department of 
Community Development and Engineering. 
4. Once the formal request has been received and conﬁrmed to be complete, 
staff will review the request, talk with Public Safety staff to conﬁrm 
speeding history, and visit the site for initial data collection. This would 
include conﬁrmation of road ownership, road length, adjacent land use, 
driveway locations, posted speed, geometry of exiting road, service area 
for future traffic calming enhancements, and logical location(s) for traffic 
counts. 
5. If criteria are met, staff will arrange for a speed study to determine 85th 
percentile speed within the service area. Traffic study will also determine 
whether traffic calming measures within the service area are expected to 
create a problem for adjacent services areas nearby. If criteria are not met, 
a denial letter will be sent to the applicant explaining the reason for denial. 
6. Based on the facts and the extent of the problem, the City may engage the 
neighborhood with an educational campaign related to speeding. 
7. If speed study criteria are met, the applicant will be required to circulate a 
petition within the service area. Staff will provide the form along with a 
map of the service area, and it will be the responsibility of the applicant to 
get the signatures. A minimum of 70% of the property owners within the 

service area must approve of adding traffic calming measures. Signatures 
must be from legal property owners of record, and only one signature per 
property is permitted. Applicant will have 90 days to return the petition to 
staff. A one-time 30-day extension may be requested and granted at the 
discretion of the Director. If speed study criteria are not met, a denial letter 
will be sent to the applicant and that service area will not be eligible to 
reapply for ﬁve years from the denial date. 
8. If the petition is received within the allotted time, staff will review it to 
ensure level of support and ensure the signatures match the owners of 
record within the County’s database. If the petition is not received within 
the allotted time, a denial letter will be sent to the applicant and that 
service area will not be eligible to reapply for ﬁve years from the denial 
date. If timely petition is accurate and establishes the minimum level of 
support, staff will arrange for a concept plan and a concept cost estimate 
to be developed for traffic calming measures within the service area, as 
funding allows. If funding is not available, the project will go on a priority 
list awaiting funding. If timely petition is not accurate, resulting in a level 
of support less than 70%, a denial letter will be sent to the applicant and 
that service area will not be eligible to reapply for ﬁve years from the denial 
date. 
9. Once the concept level plan is completed, staff will engage with the 
applicant to set up a meeting with the affected property owners to discuss 
the proposed enhancements. The goal of the meeting is to explain the 
concept, respond to questions, and ensure continued support for the 
project. 
10. After the property owner meeting and as funds are available, the concept 
will be developed into construction plans, and will include to the extent 
feasible, feedback from the property owner meeting. An updated 
construction cost will also be developed. 
11. Once funds are available for construction, the project will be completed. 
12. Within 12 months of completion, a post construction traffic study will be 
completed to determine the success of the project. If additional traffic 
calming is required, staff will investigate options. 
13. The City will cover the cost of preliminary engineering, studies, right of way 
acquisition, construction, and maintenance. 
 
 

 
 

6. 
Removal of Traffic Calming Measures 
An applicant may petition the City for removal of traffic calming measures. No 
such petitions will be accepted within ﬁve years of initial project completion, 
barring compelling evidence related to safety and welfare of the residents within 
the service area or adjacent service areas as determined by the City Engineer. The 
petition must indicate 90% of the property owners within the service area are in 
favor of the removal and the City Engineer must concur that removal is in the best 
interest of public safety. Removal is based on availability of funding and is at the 
discretion of the Mayor and Council. 
 
 

APPENDIX 
Examples of Traffic Calming Measures 
Traffic calming measures will be designed as a system of improvements based on the type 
of conditions they can best mitigate within each unique circumstance. Traffic calming 
measures are most effective when applied in a programmatic fashion throughout the service 
area and in conjunction with complimentary elements such as signing and pavement 
marking. 
 
All traffic calming measures will be based on industry standards and all signing and 
pavement marking will conform to GDOT and MUTCD standards. The following list includes 
potential options for consideration. This list is not exhaustive and other measures (not 
listed) may be considered if appropriate. 
 
Chicane: A series of alternating curves or lane shifts that are shaped by mid-block curb 
extensions or bulb-outs, positioning a motorist to steer back and forth out of a straight travel 
path. 
 
Curb & Landscaping (in combination): The addition of a physical barrier/curb line, 
combined with narrowed travel lanes and a beauty strip separating a sidewalk from the travel 
lane. Ground cover and/or landscaping can be added to the beauty strip depending on the 
width. 
 
Curb Extensions: Frequently known as “chokers” or “bulb outs”, these measures reduce the 
number of lanes or the lane width at certain locations to compliment cross walks or parallel 
parking, and to subconsciously slow drivers who pass through the pinch point area. 
 
Diverters: A raised median island built at or in an intersection, often used to restrict left turn 
movements. 
 
Dynamic Speed Display Sign (DSDS): A combination of a static speed limit sign and 
dynamic electronic speed display sign that ﬂashes actual vehicle speeds as vehicles 
approach. 
 
Lateral Shift: A horizontal deﬂection shaped by a combination of curb extensions and 
median islands designed to move the street alignment and cause travel lanes to shift in one 
direction. 

 
Median Island: A raised island located along the street centerline that reduces the width of 
the street. 
 
Mini Roundabout: A raised, and often traversable, center island placed within an existing 
unsignalized intersection, around which traffic circulates. 
 
On Street Parking: Legal parking typically in the form of marked parallel spaces that allow 
for a vehicle to be lawfully parked along the street during any hour of the day or night. 
 
Pavement Treatments: Using texture and/or color to modify the roadway surface and bring 
attention to a crosswalk, intersection, or lane. This may include stamped asphalt, stamped 
concrete, or synthetic street coatings. The additional texture and/or contrasting color can 
offer speed-reducing effects by increasing driver awareness. 
 
Raised Crosswalk: A variation of a ﬂat-topped speed table that is marked and signed as a 
pedestrian crossing, typically elevated three to ﬁve inches above the roadway. 
 
Raised Intersection: A variation of a ﬂat-topped speed table that covers an entire 
intersection, including the crosswalks, typically elevated three to ﬁve inches above the 
roadway. 
 
Roundabout: An intersection conﬁguration in a circular shape with counterclockwise traffic 
ﬂow and yield-at-entry approaches often separated by splitter islands. 
 
Speed Cushion: Two or more raised areas placed laterally across a roadway with gaps that 
provide space to ﬁt the wheel path of large or emergency vehicles. 
 
Speed Hump: A vertical asphalt constructed type of traffic calming device designed to 
reduce motorist speeds along low-volume local roadways. 
 
Speed Table: Extended or elongated speed humps with ﬂat tops that allow for slightly higher 
speeds than speed humps or cushions. 
 
Streetlights: Raised, typically pole mounted, ﬁxtures located along roads, sidewalks, or 
public areas to provide illumination at night.

PRESS RELEASE ANNOUNCING PROPOSED PROPERTY TAX INCREASE 
THE CITY OF DULUTH TODAY ANNOUNCES ITS INTENTION TO 
INCREASE THE 2026 PROPERTY TAXES IT WILL LEVY THIS YEAR BY 
2.91% OVER THE ROLLBACK MILLAGE RATE 
 
The City of Duluth, Georgia in accordance with Georgia State Law (48-5-32-1) is providing the 
following information regarding property taxes and the millage rate. The City of Duluth intends 
to increase the property taxes it will levy this year by 2.91% over the rollback millage rate set 
forth by SB 177, Act 431, of the 1999 Legislative Session. 
 
Each year, the Gwinnett County Tax Assessor is required to review the assessed value of taxable 
property in the county for property tax purposes. When the trend prices of properties that have 
recently sold in the county indicate there has been an increase in the fair market value of any 
specific property, the board of tax assessors is required by law to re-determine the value of such 
property and increase the assessment. This is called a reassessment process. 
 
When the total digest of taxable property is prepared, Georgia Law requires that a rollback 
millage rate must be computed that will produce the same total revenue on the current year’s new 
digest that last year’s millage rate would have produced had no reassessments occurred. 
 
The Fiscal Year 2027 budget adopted by the Duluth City Council on June 8, 2026, requires a 
millage rate higher than the rollback millage rate. The current millage rate is 6.551 mills, and the 
proposed millage rate is 6.551 mills. Therefore, before the Duluth City Council may set a millage 
rate to support the budget, Georgia Law requires that three public hearings be held to allow the 
public an opportunity to express their opinions on the increase. The City is also required to 
distribute this press release. 
 
All concerned citizens are invited to attend the public hearings on this proposed tax increase to be 
held at Duluth City Hall, 3167 Main Street, Duluth, Georgia 30096 as follows:

The City of Duluth, Georgia in accordance with Georgia State Law (48-5-32-1) is providing the following 
information regarding property taxes and the millage rate. The City of Duluth intends to increase the 
property taxes it will levy this year by 2.91% over the rollback millage rate set forth by SB 177, Act 431, of the 
1999 Legislative Session.
Each year, the Gwinnett County Tax Assessor is required to review the assessed value of taxable property 
in the county for property tax purposes. When the trend prices of properties that have recently sold in the 
county indicate there has been an increase in the fair market value of any specific property, the board of tax 
assessors is required by law to re-determine the value of such property and increase the assessment. This is 
called a reassessment process.
When the total digest of taxable property is prepared, Georgia Law requires that a rollback millage rate must 
be computed that will produce the same total revenue on the current year’s new digest that last year’s millage 
rate would have produced had no reassessments occurred.
The Fiscal Year 2027 budget adopted by the Duluth City Council on June 8, 2026, requires a millage rate 
higher than the rollback millage rate. The current millage rate is 6.551 mills, and the proposed millage rate is 
6.551 mills. Therefore, before the Duluth City Council may set a millage rate to support the budget, Georgia 
Law requires that three public hearings be held to allow the public an opportunity to express their opinions 
on the increase. The City is also required to distribute this press release.

assessors is required by law to re-determine the value of such property and increase the assessment. This is 
called a reassessment process.
When the total digest of taxable property is prepared, Georgia Law requires that a rollback millage rate must 
be computed that will produce the same total revenue on the current year’s new digest that last year’s millage 
rate would have produced had no reassessments occurred.
The Fiscal Year 2027 budget adopted by the Duluth City Council on June 8, 2026, requires a millage rate 
higher than the rollback millage rate. The current millage rate is 6.551 mills, and the proposed millage rate is 
6.551 mills. Therefore, before the Duluth City Council may set a millage rate to support the budget, Georgia 
Law requires that three public hearings be held to allow the public an opportunity to express their opinions 
on the increase. The City is also required to distribute this press release.
All concerned citizens are invited to attend the public hearings on this proposed tax increase to be held at

McCLURE BRIDGE ROAD PEDESTRIAN CONNECTOR GRANT MATCH 
 
 
WHEREAS, the Mayor and Council of the City of Duluth, Georgia did approve moving 
forward with development and construction of the McClure Bridge Road Pedestrian 
Connector/Trail (herein referred to as “Project”); and 
WHEREAS, grant funds are being sought to help facilitate the project development 
and construction; and 
 
WHEREAS, the Project proposes a non-motorized transportation alternative route 
connecting the approximately 111-acre tract bounded by Peachtree Industrial Boulevard 
and Pleasant Hill, McClure Bridge, and Howell Springs Roads to downtown Duluth; and 
 
WHEREAS, the Project is part of the City of Duluth’s overall sidewalk and trail plan; 
and 
WHEREAS, the Project will connect existing pedestrian facilities with other existing 
or planned regional bicycle and pedestrian facilities; and 
WHEREAS, the City of Duluth has the capacity to successfully administer any grant 
funds awarded by GTIB for this Project; and 
WHEREAS, the City of Duluth is committed to accepting state and/or federal grant 
monies awarded from GTIB for this Project and will enter into an agreement of acceptance 
with GTIB; and 
WHEREAS, the City of Duluth is committed to matching the state and/or federal 
grant funds awarded with a minimum of 20% of the Project budget, using local funds or 
other eligible grant monies, as allowable. 
NOW THEREFORE, be it resolved by the Mayor and Council City of Duluth, Georgia 
to apply for, accept, and match grant funds as noted above, should they be awarded by the 
Georgia Transportation Infrastructure Bank for this Project.

I. 
Background: 
 
It is staff’s interpretation that certain structures should not be allowed as structures containing 
outdoor storage and/or are inappropriate as accessory structures. 
 
Standards for Code Amendments 
 
The following four standards shall be considered when deciding on a code amendment: 
 
1. Is the proposed amendment consistent with the purpose and intent of this Development 
Code as stated under Article 1? 
2. Does the proposed amendment further or is it compatible with the purpose and intent of 
the Comprehensive Plan? 
3. Is the proposed amendment required to adequately address new or changing conditions or 
to properly implement the Comprehensive Plan? 
4. Does the proposed amendment reasonably promote the public health, safety, or general 
welfare? 
 
 
II. 
Description of the Request: 
 
1. Attached is a redlined copy of the proposed update to Section 203.05. Accessory Buildings and 
Structures and Section 1403. Glossary of Definitions of the Unified Development Code. 
 
 
 
III. 
Exhibits 
 
Exhibit “A”: Redlined copy of the proposed update to Section 203.05. Accessory Buildings and 
Structures and Section 1403. Glossary of Definitions of the Unified Development Code. 
Exhibit “B”: Public Notice 
 

 
 
TA2026-005 
II. Description of the Request 
Exhibit “A” 
 
203.05. Accessory Buildings and Structures. 
a. Accessory uses or structures shall be permitted only in rear yards with the exception of detached 
garages in a residentially zoned area (R-100, R-75, RA-200, or any residential portion of a PUD), 
provided they are no closer to any street than the principal structure, except as otherwise provided in 
this Code. 
b. No accessory building shall be erected on a lot prior to the time of construction of the principal 
building to which it is accessory. 
c. Accessory structure requirements apply only to residential zoning districts. In a residentially zoned 
area, there shall be a minimum setback requirement from side and rear property line of 5 feet and a 
minimum separation requirement between accessory structures of 20 feet. Multiple accessory 
structures are permitted on a single platted lot, provided the combined square footage of the 
accessory structures complies with the size limitations set forth in Section 344 Detached Structures. 
d. Prohibited accessory buildings or structures. Manufactured homes, mobile homes, freight trailers, 
boxcars, trailers, shipping containers, temporary storage buildings or any other structure or former 
vehicle not originally fabricated for use as an accessory building shall be prohibited as an accessory 
building. 
e. Any structure built on commercial or industrial zoned property shall be considered a principal use. 
f. 
The setback requirements of this Code shall not prohibit the placement of any necessary retaining 
wall nor prohibit any wall or fence except that in a residential district. See also Section 304.02 
Fences and Freestanding Walls. 
 
 
Section 1403. Glossary of Definitions 
 
Boxcar. A completely enclosed, roofed railway freight car with sliding side doors, commonly used 
to transport various goods. 
Shipping container (s). A large, standardized steel box designed to store and transport goods 
across ships, trains and trucks. 
Trailer, freight. Non-motorized vehicle designed to be towed by a truck or tractor for transporting 
goods and cargo overland. 
Trailer. An unpowered wheeled vehicle towed by a motorized vehicle.

PRESENT:

Cummings, City Manager, Asst. City Managers, Department Directors, 
City Attorney 
 
 
5:30PM - CALL TO ORDER 
 
I. 
PUBLIC COMMENTS 
 
None. 
 
 
 
II. 
DISCUSSION ITEMS/PRESENTATIONS/UPDATES 
 
1. AI STRATEGY & DATA EFFICIENCY UPDATE 
 
 
 
 
{A} 
 
 
City Manager James Riker introduced recently hired Data Analyst, Dylan 
Schneiderman, to provide the Council with an update on the City’s efforts to improve 
data efficiency and utilization of AI in city operations. He summarized efforts to date, 
including evaluation of existing workflows to determine what type of tool would assist 
staff with accuracy, time savings and overall efficiency. 
 
Mr. Schneiderman outlined the policy, the process and what areas have been 
improved thus far. He gave specific examples and statistics of what departments have 
been affected. A citywide AI policy has been established for safe internal use, with 
clear data input guidelines, and Staff training is ongoing. The Police Department leads 
AI adoption and has been using it already, to assist with report writing, facial 
recognition, transcription, and crime mapping. He emphasized that there is human 
oversight, no autonomous AI decisions are being made. In the Business Office, Mr. 
Schneiderman has worked with property taxes and HR. For taxes, he wrote a small 
program to improve workflow redesigns and monthly property owner changes 
reduced from three days of manual entry to three hours monthly. The HR Wellness 
Program administration workflows were shortened from three days to four hours, 
quarterly. He also discussed financial data consolidation projects, and the need for 
linking departmental data for holistic city insights to give bigger picture trends and 
solutions for inconsistencies. 
 
 

M&C Work Session Notes 
July 27, 2026 
Page 2 of 4 
 
2
 
Questions were raised about security, evaluation of available tools, and cost projections 
for use of AI. Staff reported that some departments are using free versions and are 
satisfied with those. 
 
No action was taken. 
 
2. ACCESSORY STRUCTURES – PROHIBITIONS 
 
 
 
 
 
This item was removed from the July 13th Council agenda for further discussion. 
Community Development/Engineering Deputy Director Aron Hall came forward to 
present. 
 
Mr. Hall explained that the proposed ordinance adds language to Article 2. Use of 
Land and Structures Section 203.05. Accessory Buildings and Structures to 
prohibit the use of certain structures in residentially zoned areas, and Article 14. 
Interpretation and Definitions. 
 
Councilmember Graeder questioned the need for the change. Mr. Hall responded 
that the purpose of this amendment relates to property maintenance aesthetics, 
and would allow code enforcement to address unsightly storage areas and have 
less subjective authority for determining what looks “nice” or is in “good” 
condition. Planning staff felt that clarifying some definitions would prevent 
residents from reusing an item for storage that was not the intended to be used in 
that manner. 
 
Additionally, Mr. Hall felt that the definition of “household” required amending as 
the Article 2 definition is not exactly the same as the one in Article 14. 
 
Staff was authorized to place this item on the September Council agenda. 
 
3. AMENDMENT TO DULUTH CODE ARTICLE III – NOISE 
 
City Manager James Riker reported that Council had recently directed staff to 
investigate a modification to Article III Noise relating to domestic power tools, lawn 
mowers and agricultural equipment. He referenced surrounding communities and 
their day and time restrictions, and said it was truly Council’s preference on how to 
ensure the most courteous guidelines were established. Some people use landscape 
crews who typically like to start the day at 7am to beat the heat and are done by 5pm, 
others who do it themselves would need time after the workday ends on weekdays. 
Most agreed that weekend work should have fewer hours to ensure residents could be 
enjoying their outdoor spaces with minimal disturbance. 
 
Mr. Riker suggested presented proposed modifications to the Municipal Code - Article 
III Noise to change allowable weekday hours from 7am to 8pm, Saturdays from 8am-
5pm, and Sundays/holidays 10am-5pm and including 85 decibel limits. 
 
 

M&C Work Session Notes 
July 27, 2026 
Page 3 of 4 
 
3
 
 
Staff and the City Attorney directed to make changes as discussed and to place this 
item on the next Council consent agenda for authorization. 
 
4. INFILL ORDINANCE 
 
 
 
 
At Mayor and Council's request, staff has been finalizing the details of a proposed infill 
strategy ordinance. Deputy Director Aron Hall came forward to present. Part of this 
strategy included the R-50 zoning category, which is now in use, primarily in Hall Circle, 
the Hill community, and some of Davenport Road. 
 
Mr. Hall showed the various housing types that would qualify, and described the 
purpose and intent as ensuring neighborhood compatibility, maintaining harmony 
and character of existing residential areas, and ensuring that residential infill 
development occurs in an orderly and desirable manner. He referenced allowable 
density by type, setbacks between housing, and parking. Each housing type has a case 
study and examples associated with it so developers can get ideas of what would be 
approved. 
 
Mr. Hall outlined the appearance, associated dimensions and parking for each of the 
housing types, defined as Small lot single family, Duplex, Triplex, Quadplex, Sidecourt, 
Mansion Apartments, Townhomes, Courtyard Buildings, Cottage Courts, Mixed Use, 
and Accessory Dwelling Units. He also discussed allowed materials and fenestration 
requirements. 
 
Mayor and Council asked that guest parking be addressed on the final ordinance. 
Staff will circulate the ordinance to Council for their markup/questions, and will 
present again at the August work session. 
 
5. CAMERA SERVER REPLACEMENT 
 
 
Chief Carruth explained that the camera servers in need of replacement are archive 
servers that store and replay videos from centralized locations at Public Works, WP 
Jones, the Festival Center and City Hall. These servers have a projected lifespan of 5-7 
years. Three of the servers are at their end-of-life now (Public Works, WP Jones and 
Bunten Road Park) and one will be at the end-of-life in January of 2027 (City Hall). The 
cost of replacing the three at end-of-life now is $16,471.00. The cost of replacing the 
City Hall server is $30,018.86. We would like to replace Public Works, WP Jones and 
Bunten servers as soon as possible, and the City Hall server prior to January 2027. A 
budget amendment would be required. 
 
Council recommended performing a benefit analysis on moving to the cloud vs. 
having physical servers. Staff to place this item on the next Council agenda for 
discussion. 
 
 
 

M&C Work Session Notes 
July 27, 2026 
Page 4 of 4 
 
4
 
III. 
MATTERS FROM MAYOR & COUNCIL 
 
1. DOWNTOWN UPDATE 
 
Chris McGahee gave a report on the status of new leases for downtown restaurants 
and retails spaces which have been vacant. 
 
2. RETREAT DISCUSSION NOTES 
 
City Manager James Riker reported that a summary of the notes from the Strategic 
session in June will be presented at the next work session. 
 
3. OVERNIGHT PARKING ORDINANCE 
 
A potential amendment to the hours for the overnight parking restriction is 
forthcoming. 
 
4. DPAC ART PROJECT 
 
The Mayor announced that four artists have been short-listed for the anticipated 
project at Red Clay. 
 
5. ADULT LEAD PROGRAM REBRANDING 
 
Duluth LEAD is being rebranded as “ENGAGE Duluth.” 
 
 
IV. 
ADJOURNMENT 
 
Meeting adjourned at 7:40pm. 
 
 
The next scheduled meeting of the Mayor and Council is a special called meeting for 
Monday, August 10th at 10:00am in the Council Chambers, and the regular meeting on

ORDINANCE 
TO AMEND THE DULUTH CODE CHAPTER 7, ARTICLE IX. - SECONDHAND DEALERS—
DEALERS IN PRECIOUS METALS AND GEMS AND PAWNBROKERS 
 
The Council of the City of Duluth hereby ordains that the Duluth Code of Ordinances is hereby 
amended by deleting in its entirety Article XXIII of Chapter 7 and reserving said Article and 
by deleting in its entirety Article IX of Chapter 7 and replacing Article IX of Chapter with the 
following: 
 
SECONDHAND DEALERS—DEALERS IN PRECIOUS METALS AND GEMS AND 
PAWNBROKERS 
Sec. 7-321. - Penalty. 
Any person violating any of the provisions of this article shall be punished as provided in 
section 1-6 and may also be subject to suspension or revocation of the permit to operate 
under this Chapter. 
Sec. 7-322. - Definitions. 
The following words, terms and phrases when used in this article, shall have the meanings 
ascribed to 
Acquire means to purchase, exchange, transfer, collect, or otherwise obtain physical 
possession of regulated secondhand items from another person or entity not licensed as a 
secondhand dealer. 
Dealer in precious metals and gems means: 
(1) Any person engaged in the business of purchasing precious metals or gems or goods 
made from precious metals or gems from persons or sources other than manufacturers, 
manufacturers' representatives, or other dealers in precious metals or gems; or 
(2) Any person engaged in any other business if, in conjunction with such business, 
precious metals or gems or goods made from precious metals or gems are purchased from 
persons or sources other than manufacturers, manufacturers' representatives, or other 
dealers in precious metals or gems where such purchase is for resale in its original form or 
as changed by remounting, melting, re-forming, remolding, or recasting or for resale as 
scrap or in bulk. 
Employee means any person who works for a secondhand dealer, whether on a part-time 
or fulltime basis, regardless of whether remuneration is received or not, and regardless of 
whether such person is treated as a W-2 employee or a Form 1099 contractor. 
Gems means any precious or semiprecious stone which is cut and polished. 

O2026-25 
Interest in a secondhand dealership means any full or part ownership if the person 
involved, or any member of his or her family, is the outright owner of the secondhand 
dealership; a co-owner of the secondhand dealership; a stockholder in any corporation 
organized for pecuniary gain which owns all or part of the secondhand dealership; a 
stockholder, member, partner or individual with an ownership interest in any corporation, 
partnership, limited liability company or other legal entity organized for pecuniary gain 
which owns all or any part of the secondhand dealership. 
Minor means any person who has not attained the age of 18 years. 
Numismatic coins means coins whose value as collectors' items exceeds the value of the 
content of the precious metals in the coins. 
Pawnbroker means any person engaged in whole or in part in the business of lending 
money on the security of pledged goods, or in the business of purchasing tangible personal 
property on the condition that it may be redeemed or repurchased by the seller for a fixed 
price within a fixed period of time, or in the business of purchasing tangible personal 
property from persons or sources other than manufacturers or licensed dealers as a part of 
or in conjunction with the business activities described in this Chapter. 
Pawnshop means the physical location at which a pawnbroker is licensed to operate. 
Pawn transaction means any loan on the security of pledged goods or any purchase of 
pledged goods on the condition that the pledged goods may be redeemed or repurchased 
by the pledgor or seller for a fixed price within a fixed period of time 
Permit means permission to be employed or work in a secondhand dealership or to be a 
secondhand dealer. 
Person means an individual, partnership, limited liability company, corporation, joint 
venture, trust, association, or any other legal entity however organized. 
Pledged goods means tangible personal property, including, without limitation, all types of 
motor vehicles or any motor vehicle certificate of title, which property is purchased by, 
deposited with, or otherwise actually delivered into the possession of a pawnbroker in 
connection with a pawn transaction. However, for purposes of this section, possession of 
any motor vehicle certificate of title which has come into the possession of a pawnbroker 
through a pawn transaction made in accordance with law shall be conclusively deemed to 
be possession of the motor vehicle, and the pawnbroker shall retain physical possession of 
the motor vehicle certificate of title for the entire length of the pawn transaction but shall 
not be required in any way to retain physical possession of the motor vehicle at any time. 
"Pledged goods" shall not include choses in action, securities, or printed evidences of 
indebtedness. 
Precious metals means gold, silver, or platinum or any alloy containing gold, silver, or 
platinum. 

O2026-25 
Regulated secondhand items means the following goods: 
(1) Precious metal or gems; 
(2) Goods made from precious metals or gems; 
(3) Pledged goods; or 
(4) Tangible property acquired by a pawnbroker. 
Secondhand dealer means any person whose business, in whole or in part, is dealing in 
acquiring, purchasing, selling, or trading regulated secondhand items, and such term 
expressly includes dealers in precious metals and gems and pawnbrokers. 
Secondhand dealership means the physical location at which a secondhand dealer is 
licensed to operate, and such term expressly includes pawnshops. 
Seller means the person from whom a secondhand dealer or employee acquired 
secondhand items or the person from whom a pawnbroker acquired pledged goods. 
Sec. 7-323. -- Annual regulatory permit required. 
All persons, before beginning the business of operating a secondhand dealership (for pawn, 
precious metals, or gems) or similar place where money is advanced on goods or other 
effects, or merchandise of any kind is taken in pawn, shall first file an application with the 
city clerk’s office for a non-refundable annual regulatory permit to conduct such business. 
The fee for such permit is one thousand two hundred dollars ($1,200.00). Such permit shall 
be renewed on or before January 31th. 
Sec. 7-324. - Exempt transactions. 
The following transactions are exempt from the provisions of this article: 
(1) Transactions in which a nonprofit entity, exempt from federal income tax pursuant to 
26 U.S.C. Sections 501(c), 501(d), or 501(e), is a party; and 
(2) Transactions occurring at one-day auctions and/or permitted yard sales, or estate sales, 
unless a dealer in precious metals or gems or pawnbroker is a party to such transaction. 
Sec. 7-325. - Fixed physical location. 
No secondhand dealer or employee may operate except at a fixed permanent physical 
business location with an occupation tax certificate from the city; no secondhand dealer or 
employee may operate as a peddler or transient merchant. Permits acquired under this 
article are valid only for the location stated on the permit and said permit is not 
transferable from one location to another. 
Sec. 7-326. - Secondhand dealer permit qualifications. 

O2026-25 
 (a) Qualifications. All secondhand dealers shall be not less than 18 years of age. Any person 
who has been convicted of or pled guilty to any felony, any crime involving theft or fraud, 
or any crime against property under the laws of this state, any other state of the United 
States, or any federal law shall not be eligible for a secondhand dealer permit under this 
article until five years after the completion by said person of the subject sentence. 
(b) Disclosure. Every secondhand dealer must disclose any ownership or interest in any 
other secondhand dealership, including any other pawnshop(s), whether it is located 
locally or out-of-state and must disclose the nature of such ownership or interest. 
(c) Every secondhand dealer permit holder is required to notify the city of any change in 
information or circumstances which occurs after the original approval was granted. If 
approval is denied, the applicant may, within 15 days of the denial, appeal in writing to the 
city manager for reconsideration pursuant to the provisions of this article. 
Sec. 7-327. -Employee permit qualifications. 
(a) Qualifications. All employees shall be at least 18 years of age. Any person who has been 
convicted of or pled guilty to any felony, any crime involving theft or fraud, or any crime 
against property under the laws of this state, any other state of the United States, or any 
federal law shall not be eligible for an employee permit under this article until five years 
after the completion by said person of the subject sentence. 
(b) Disclosure. Every employee of a secondhand dealer must disclose any ownership or 
interest in any other secondhand dealership, including any other pawnshop(s), whether it 
is located locally or out-of-state and must disclose the nature of such ownership or interest. 
(c) Before any person may work on the premises of a secondhand dealership, he shall file 
an application with the city clerk’s office setting out the information required in 
subsections (a) and (b) of this section. If the application information conforms to the 
requirement of this article, the city shall approve the applicant for a permit authorizing the 
person to be employed at a secondhand dealership. Upon such approval, the applicant may 
begin working on the regulated premises. 
(d) Every permit holder is required to notify the city of any change in information or 
circumstances which occurs after the original approval was granted. If approval is denied, 
the applicant may, within 15 days of the denial, appeal in writing to the city manager for 
reconsideration pursuant to the provisions of this article. 
(d) Independent contractors. For the purpose of this article, independent contractors shall 
be considered as employees and shall be permitted as employees, regardless of the 
business relationship with the owner or occupation tax certificate holder of any 
secondhand dealership.

Sec. 7-329. - Reasons for denial, suspension or revocation of the permit. 
The city clerk or designee may reject an application for a secondhand dealer or employee 
permit, or suspend or revoke a permit for the following reasons: 
(1) The required fees or taxes have not been paid. 
(2) Application does not conform to all the provisions required by this article. 
(3) The owner/employee has failed to fully cooperate with the investigation required by 
this article. 
(4) Any owner/employee has had any license or occupation tax certificate issued under the 
police powers of any county, municipality, or other governmental subdivision involuntarily 
suspended or revoked within the last five years for any reason whatsoever. 
(5) The owner/employee, as a previous holder of a license or occupation tax certificate to 
operate a secondhand dealership has violated any law, regulation or ordinance relating to 
the business within a five-year period immediately preceding the date of the application. 

O2026-25 
(6) Any owner/employee has been convicted of or pled guilty to, in a court of competent 
jurisdiction, any felony, any crime involving theft or fraud, or any crime against property 
within the five years. A pleading of nolo contendere shall be considered as a conviction for 
the purposes of this provision. 
(7) Any owner/employee is less than 18 years of age. 
(8) Any owner/employee has failed to obtain any paper or document necessary in 
pursuance of this business or this application as may be required by any officer, agency or 
department of the city, county, state or United States under authority of any law, ordinance 
or resolution of the city, state or United States or has failed to be properly eligible for legal 
residence in this state or the United States. 
(9) Any owner/employee has made any false statements in the application. 
(10) The applicant or holder of the permit has violated any provisions of this article. 
Sec. 7-330 - Renewal of permits. 
Permits for secondhand dealers and employees may be renewed on a calendar year basis 
provided that the applicants continue to meet the requirements set out in this article. 
Renewal applications shall be submitted by January 30 of the year for which such permit is 
requested along with a fee in the amount of $1,200.00. 
Sec. 7-331. - Permit nontransferable. 
No secondhand dealer or employee permit may be sold, transferred or assigned to any 
other person or persons. Any such sale, transfer or assignment, or attempted sale, transfer 
or assignment, shall be deemed to constitute a voluntary surrender of such permit and such 
permit shall thereafter be null and void; provided and excepting, however, that if the 
permit holder is a partnership and one or more of the partners should die, one or more of 
the surviving partners may acquire, by purchase or otherwise, the interest of the deceased 
partner or partners without affecting a surrender or termination of such permit, and in 
such case, the permit upon notification to the city shall be placed in the name of the 
surviving partner(s). 
Sec. 7-332. - Records and information to be maintained; display of secondhand 
dealer transaction number; identification; digital photographs; fingerprints; records 
storage. 
In the public interest and as set forth herein, all secondhand dealers shall maintain records 
documenting all secondhand transactions. 
(1) All secondhand dealers shall maintain records documenting accurate descriptions of 
all property pledged, traded, pawned, exchanged, or sold to the secondhand dealers. Such 
description shall include, to the extent possible, the manufacturer, model, serial number, 
style, material, kind, color, design, number of stones if jewelry, and all other identifying 

O2026-25 
names, marks, and numbers. The secondhand dealer shall assign a pawn transaction 
number documenting each transaction, and ensure each item received is tagged with the 
secondhand dealer transaction number. 
(2) The tag bearing the secondhand dealer transaction number must remain attached to 
the item until the property is disposed of by sale, trade, or other lawful means. This 
paragraph does not apply to the purchase of property from licensed wholesale or 
distributor businesses for the purpose of retail sales; however the secondhand dealer shall 
be required to maintain all purchasing records for property exempted from this paragraph. 
(3) The secondhand dealer shall require all persons pledging, trading, pawning, 
exchanging, or selling property to show proper identification prior to conducting a 
secondhand dealer transaction. Proper identification is defined as a government issued 
photo identification card such as a driver's license, military identification card, state 
identification card, or passport. 
(4) The secondhand dealer shall also document the name, address, telephone number, 
race, sex, height, weight, driver's license number, and date of birth of the person pledging, 
trading, pawning, exchanging, or selling the property, along with the date and time of 
transaction. This documentation shall be made at the time of the transaction. 
(5) The secondhand dealer shall photograph, with a digital camera or web camera, the 
person pledging, trading, pawning, exchanging, or selling the property. The photograph 
shall clearly show a frontal view of the subject's face along with the pawnbroker's ticket 
transaction number and a photograph of the item being pledged, traded, pawned, 
exchanged, or sold. Digital images shall be labeled and stored in such a manner that they 
are safe from corruption, readily identifiable and readily available for review. 
(6) The secondhand dealer shall obtain from each person pledging, trading, pawning, 
exchanging, or selling any property, the fingerprint of the right hand index finger, unless 
such finger is missing, in which event the print of the next finger in existence on the right 
hand shall be obtained with a notation as to the exact fingerprinted. The fingerprint shall 
be imprinted onto the pawn transaction form in the designated area along with the 
signature of the person pawning, trading, pledging, exchanging, or selling the property. The 
fingerprint must be clear and legible. In the event that more than one (1) pawn transaction 
form is required, a fingerprint and signature should be obtained for each form. Fingerprints 
and the information required herein shall be obtained each time such person pledges, 
trades, pawns, exchanges, or sells any property. 
(7) Items of property that appear to be new, unused, and in their original packaging 
cannot be accepted by the secondhand dealer unless the customer can supply a copy of the 
original sales receipt, or other proof of purchase from the place of purchase, to the 
secondhand dealer who shall retain the receipt or proof of purchase on file. 

O2026-25 
(8) The secondhand dealer shall store the above records, digital images, and fingerprints 
for a period of four (4) years and make them available to law enforcement personnel upon 
request. 
 Sec. 7-333. - Daily report to police; required format. 
Every secondhand dealer shall make a daily report, in such form as may be prescribed by 
the chief of police, of all secondhand dealer transactions that occurred during 24 hours 
ending at 9:00 p.m. on the date of the report. 
(1) Daily reports shall list all property pledged, traded, pawned, exchanged, or sold, the 
secondhand transaction number for each transaction, and a description of the property 
including, to the extent possible, the manufacturer, model, serial number, style, material, 
kind, color, design, number of stones if jewelry, and any other identifying names, marks, 
and numbers. The daily report shall also list the name, address, race, sex, height, weight, 
driver's license number, and date of birth of the person pledging, trading, pawning, 
exchanging, or selling the property along with the date and time of the transaction. 
(2) Every secondhand dealer shall enter each transaction as it occurs into the electronic 
automated reporting system via the internet to the administrator of the electronic 
automated reporting system. The administrator of the electronic automated reporting 
system will electronically transmit all transactions to the police department. 
(3) In the event that the electronic automated reporting system becomes temporarily or 
permanently disabled, secondhand dealer will be notified as soon as possible by the police 
department. In this event, the secondhand dealer will be required to make records of 
transactions in paper form as prescribed by the police department. Such paper forms must 
include all information as enumerated in 7-327. Secondhand dealers shall be responsible 
for maintaining an adequate inventory of these forms. 
(4) The chief of police or his designee shall select and designate the required automated 
reporting system and required equipment needed. There will be a fee assessed to the 
secondhand dealer for each reported transaction. Said fee may be assessed against the 
persons pledging, trading, pawning, exchanging, or selling property. The accessed fee shall 
not exceed fifty (50) percent of the actual cost charged by the police department or the 
third party administrator. This fee will be invoiced to the secondhand dealer and collected 
by the chief of police or his designee, which may be a third party administrator of the 
automated reporting system. 
Sec. 7-334. - Entries to be numbered serially; property to be tagged. 
Every entry required to be made in the secondhand dealer's records shall be numbered 
serially, and the property described in the entry shall have attached to it a tag bearing the 
same serial number until the property is disposed of by sale, trade or other lawful means. 
This paragraph does not apply to the purchase of property from licensed wholesale

distributor businesses for the purpose of retail sales; however, the secondhand dealer shall 
be required to maintain all purchasing records for property exempted from this paragraph. 
Sec. 7-335. - Acquiring articles with serial number mutilated or altered. 
It shall be unlawful for any secondhand dealer to purchase or acquire any watch, clock, 
pistol, gun, automobile tire or battery or any other article commonly branded with a serial 
number upon which the number has been mutilated, altered, or removed. 
Sec. 7-336. - Examination and inspection of articles by police; segregation of 
suspicious articles. 
All property purchased or acquired by a secondhand dealer shall at all times be subject to 
examination and inspection by the police department. If, upon the inspection, a police 
officer shall have reasonable cause to believe that any of the property is stolen, he shall 
segregate it. It shall thereafter be unlawful for the person in possession of the property to 
dispose of it, or in any manner mutilate, melt or disfigure 
Sec. 7-337. - Property to be held after acquisition. 
All property purchased or acquired by a secondhand dealer shall be held for not less than 
30 days, or longer if directed by the police department, before disposing of same by sale, 
transfer, shipment or otherwise. All property and/or titles must be kept on the premises. 
During such 30-day period, these secondhand items will be maintained in an area not 
accessed by customers. 
Sec. 7-338. - Dealing with minors. 
It shall be unlawful for any secondhand dealer to acquire any property of the kinds 
described in this article from any person under the age of 18 years, provided that any 
secondhand dealer will not be held subject to the provisions of this section if the person 
produces a valid identification, as defined in this article, showing he/she is at least 18 years 
of age.

Sec. 7-340. - Redemption; lost or damaged goods. 
Any person properly identifying him or herself and presenting a pawn ticket to the 
pawnbroker shall be presumed to be the pledgor or seller and shall be entitled to redeem 
the pledged goods described in such ticket. In the event such pledged goods are lost or 
damaged while in the possession of the pawnbroker, it shall be responsibility of the 
pawnbroker to replace the lost or damaged goods with like kinds of merchandise. For the 
purposes of this section, lost includes destroyed or having disappeared because of any 
cause, whether known or unknown, that results in the pledged goods being unavailable for 
return to pledgor.

metals and gems. 
In addition to the provisions contained in this article, dealers in precious metals and gems 
shall comply with the requirements of O.C.G.A. § 43-37-1, et seq., and shall register with the 
police department as required by State law, in addition to compliance with this article. It 
shall be unlawful for any person to advertise or transact business as a dealer in precious 
metals and gems without first registering to do so pursuant to this section. It shall be 
unlawful for any dealer in precious metals or gems to purchase precious metals in a melted 
or smelted state unless the purchase is from a registered dealer in precious metals or gems. 
Sec. 7-342. - Additional regulations applicable to pawnbrokers.

provisions.

Unified Development Code 
 
Standards Governing the Exercise of Zoning Power 
 
Section 1104.02 of the UDC establishes the standards governing the exercise of zoning 
power. The following standards are relevant in balancing the interest and promoting the 
public health, safety, morality, and general welfare against the right to the unrestricted 
use of the property: 
 
A. Whether the zoning proposal will permit a use that is suitable in view of the use and 
development of adjacent and nearby property.

adjacent or nearby property.

Comprehensive Plan, transportation plans, or other plans adopted for guiding 
development within the City of Duluth.

development of property that give supporting grounds for either approval or 
disapproval of the zoning or special use proposal.

I. 
PURPOSE AND DESCRIPTION OF THE REQUEST 
The purpose of this Special Use request (SU2026-002) is to allow for the operation of a dual 
language immersion public charter middle school in the M-1 (Light Industrial District). 
Maps detailing the location, zoning district and character area of the subject property are 
attached hereto as Exhibit “A”. The legal description of the subject property is attached 
hereto as Exhibit “B”. Recommended conditions of approval are detailed in Exhibit “C”. 
Applicant’s Response to the Standards Governing Special Use Consideration can be found in 
Exhibit “D”, The proposed circulation plan can be found in Exhibit “E”, and Public Notice can 
be found in Exhibit “F”. 
 
II. 
EXISTING CONDITIONS 
 
The subject property totals +/- 5.29 acres and is located within the +/- 290 acres River Green 
Industrial Park that has construction services, engineering services, manufacturing and 
production facilities, laboratory testing facilities, offices and institutional uses. In addition, 
there is a Gwinnett County Charter School, Notre Dame Academy (a private Catholic school) 
an event facility and a youth behavioral center for pre-school aged kids living with Autism, a 
consulate and Scott Hudgens Park. In total, there are currently 10 (ten) conditional or special 
uses within River Green Business Park. 
 
The subject property is currently zoned M-1 (Light Industrial District) and is surrounded by 
M-1 (Light Industrial District) properties. 
 
 
III. 
REVIEW OF THE REQUEST 
 
1. 
Literal Interpretation of the Unified Development Code (UDC) 
 
A. Table 2-C of the UDC allows schools of this type by way of special use. 
 
B. Section 1101.02 of the UDC states if a proposed use is not allowed by right under the 
existing zoning on a property, a request for an amendment to the Official Zoning 
Map (often called a “rezoning”) must be approved prior to development, 
construction, or occupancy. 
 
C. Section 1105 of the UDC establishes the Special Use Considerations. 
 
The Special Use is designed to apply under any one of the following circumstances: 
1. A Special Use listed under the zoning district is desired for development and a 
more intensive zoning district containing that use, as a use by right would not be 
appropriate for the property; or 
 
2. A Special Use listed under the zoning district is desired for development and no 
zoning district contains that use as a use by right; or 
 
3. A unique use not addressed in any zoning district is desired for development and 
is not likely to be duplicated within the City of Duluth; or 
 
4. The density of development may be affected by the height of a building; or

5. The neighboring properties may be affected by the height of any structure; or 
 
6. The Special Use would be consistent with the needs of the neighborhood or the 
community as a whole, be compatible with the neighborhood and would not be 
in conflict with the overall objective of the Comprehensive Plan. 
 
In order to accommodate these particular uses, Special Use approval allows the City Council 
to approve such a use on a particular parcel without changing the general zoning district. 
Such approval shall be subject to the requirements set forth below and any additional 
conditions deemed necessary to ensure the compatibility of the Special Use with the 
surrounding properties. All Special Use applications shall be for firm development 
proposals only. The Special Use shall not be used for securing early zoning for conceptual 
proposals that may not be undertaken for some time. A Special Use application shall be 
considered only if the application is made by the owner of the property or by his/her 
authorized agent. The minimum requirements for a Special Use approval are: 
1. Any uses allowed under Special Use approval shall also conform to the 
requirements of this Development Code for all uses as found in the zoning 
district. 
 
2. The application and review process for a Special Use shall be the same as for the 
zoning district under which the Special Use is found. In addition to the 
information and/or site plans which are required to be submitted for the 
proposed development, additional information deemed necessary by the 
Director in order to evaluate a proposed use and its relationship to the 
surrounding area shall be submitted. In the review process, particular emphasis 
shall be given to the evaluation of the characteristics of the proposed use in 
relationship to its immediate neighborhood and the compatibility of the 
proposed use with its neighborhood. 
 
3. In the approval process for a Special Use approval application, the City Council 
shall consider the policies and objectives of the Comprehensive Plan, particularly 
in relationship to the proposed site and surrounding area and shall consider the 
potential adverse impacts on the surrounding area, especially in regards but not 
limited to traffic, storm drainage, land values and compatibility of land use 
activities. 
 
4. If an application is approved and a Special Use approval is granted, all conditions 
that may have been attached to the approval are binding to the property. All 
subsequent development and use of the property shall be in accordance with the 
approved plan and conditions. 
 
5. Changes to a Special Use or development of a site for the Special Use, shall be 
treated as an amendment to the Special Use Permit and shall be subject to the 
same application and review process as a new application. 
 
6. An application for Special Use approval in a residential district and which use is 
proposed to operate in a dwelling or as an accessory use to a dwelling is subject 
to the following additional requirements: 
 
a. The Special Use shall operate within the dwelling on the property or, if 
approved by the City Council, in an accessory structure.

b. The exterior character of the dwelling shall be preserved in its residential 
state and there shall be no outside evidence of the operation of a Special Use 
to the neighborhood, except for any accessory structure approved by the City 
Council. 
 
7. The owner of the property approved for a Special Use may voluntarily request 
termination of the Special Use by notifying the Director in writing. The Director 
shall notify the City Council through the Planning Commission of the voluntary 
termination. The approval of a Special Use for a specific use which may be 
operated by a lessee under a private agreement with a lessor in any non-
residential district shall not obligate the City Council to be responsible for or be 
required to resolve any disputes which may arise out of the voluntary 
termination of the Special Use by the property owner. 
 
8. The Community Development and Engineering Department shall have the right 
to periodically examine the operation of the specific use to determine 
compliance with the requirements and any conditions. If the Director 
determines that the requirements and conditions are being violated, a written 
notice shall be issued to the owner of the property outlining the nature of the 
violation and giving the owner of the property a maximum of ten days to come 
into compliance. If after ten days the violations continue to exist, the Director 
shall forward a report to the City Council through the Planning Commission who 
may recommend that action be taken to remove the Special Use from the 
property. 
 
9. Upon approval by the City Council, a Special Use shall be identified on the official 
zoning maps. 
 
10. Upon approval by the City Council of a Special Use, the owner of the property 
shall be issued a notice from the Director that states the specific use permitted, 
the requirements of this Section and any conditions attached to the approval. 
 
11. The Community Development and Engineering Department shall not issue a 
Certificate of Occupancy for the specific use unless all requirements and 
conditions of the Special Use approval have been fulfilled by the owner of the 
property. 
 
2. 
Standards Governing the Exercise of Zoning Power 
 
Section 1104.02 of the UDC establishes the standards governing the exercise of zoning 
power. The following standards are relevant in balancing the interest and promoting 
the public health, safety, morality, and general welfare against the right to the 
unrestricted use of property: 
A. 
How the proposed Special Use will permit a use that is suitable in view of the 
use and development of adjacent and nearby property. 
 
B. 
How the proposed Special Use will adversely affect the existing use or usability 
of adjacent or nearby property. 
 
C. 
Whether the property to be affected by a proposed Special Use has a reasonable

economic use as currently zoned. 
 
D. 
Whether the proposed Special Use will result in a use which will or could cause 
an excessive or burdensome use of existing streets, transportation facilities,

E. 
Whether the proposed Special Use is in conformity with the policy and interest

adopted for guiding development within the City of Duluth. 
 
F.

The Applicant has provided written responses to the above Special Use standards as
