RESOLUTION OF THE CITY OF DULUTH, GEORGIA 
AUTHORIZING PARTICIPATION IN AN AMICUS BRIEF IN CHANG v. CITY OF 
MILTON ON REMAND BEFORE THE GEORGIA COURT OF APPEALS OR, IF 
WARRANTED, THE GEORGIA SUPREME COURT 
WHEREAS, the litigation styled Chang v. City of Milton arises from claims asserted against the City 
of Milton, Georgia, related to a 2016 motor vehicle collision on Batesville Road; 
WHEREAS, on September 16, 2024, the Georgia Court of Appeals issued its decision in City of 
Milton v. Chang, 373 Ga. App. 667 (2024); 
WHEREAS, the Supreme Court of Georgia thereafter granted certiorari and, on March 12, 2026, 
vacated the Court of Appeals decision and remanded the case for further proceedings, holding that a 
municipality's ministerial duty over roadway upkeep and repair did not apply where the alleged unsafe 
condition was outside the lanes of ordinary travel, City of Milton v. Chang, 2026 WL 695364; 
WHEREAS, following remand, the Georgia Court of Appeals will consider the separate question of 
whether a Georgia municipality may nevertheless be subjected to liability under a so-called nuisance theory 
for personal injury claims; 
WHEREAS, the City recognizes that any asserted waiver of sovereign immunity for nuisance claims 
resulting in personal injury does not arise from any express constitutional or statutory waiver applicable to 
municipalities, but instead traces to judicial decisions such as Town of Fort Oglethorpe v. Phillips, 224 Ga. 
834 (1968); 
WHEREAS, the Supreme Court of Georgia explained in Georgia Department of Natural Resources 
v. Center for a Sustainable Coast, Inc., 294 Ga. 593 (2014), that waivers of sovereign immunity must come 
from the Constitution or the General Assembly and that courts may not create new exceptions to sovereign 
immunity; 
WHEREAS, in Mayor & C. of Savannah v. Palmerio, 242 Ga. 224 (1978), Justice Hall, in a 
concurring opinion, advised that “the time is long past for this court to re-examine its opinion in Town of Ft. 
Oglethorpe v. Phillips, 224 Ga. 834, 165 S.E.2d 141 (1968);” 
WHEREAS, in Gatto v. City of Statesboro, 312 Ga. 164, fn. 6 (2021), the Court observed “[s]ome of 
us have doubts about the legal foundations of Phillips, which also divorced municipal nuisance liability from 
its basis in our Constitution's Takings Clause;” 
WHEREAS, a nuisance theory that permits personal-injury claims against cities, but not counties, 
creates an uneven exposure to liability that is not supported by a clear constitutional or statutory waiver; 
WHEREAS, Georgia law has long distinguished between nuisance claims that implicate the Takings 
Clause and nuisance claims seeking damages for personal injury; 
WHEREAS, municipalities across the State have a substantial interest in ensuring that any waiver of 
sovereign immunity remains tied to a constitutional or statutory foundation rather than a judicially created 
expansion; 
WHEREAS, the City finds that it is in the best interests of its citizens and residents to support the 
City of Milton in seeking an appellate ruling that there is no waiver of municipal sovereign immunity for an 
alleged nuisance resulting in personal injury, outside the limited context of a nuisance claim amounting to a 
constitutional taking; and 

R2026-05 
WHEREAS, the City further finds that Georgia cities should have their collective voice heard on this 
issue of statewide importance through coordinated amicus participation before the Georgia Court of Appeals 
and/or the Georgia Supreme Court. 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE CITY OF DULUTH, GA, that: 
• The City authorizes participation in, support for, and joinder with an amicus curiae brief or briefs to be filed 
in Chang v. City of Milton on remand before the Georgia Court of Appeals and/or, if further appellate 
proceedings occur after the Court of Appeals, before the Georgia Supreme Court, and authorizes the City's 
name to be included as an amicus participant. 
• The City supports the position that any purported waiver of a city's sovereign immunity for nuisance claims 
seeking recovery for personal injury is a judicially created doctrine rather than an express waiver grounded 
in the Georgia Constitution or an act of the General Assembly. 
• The City supports the position that, consistent with Sustainable Coast and related sovereign-immunity 
precedent, no waiver of municipal sovereign immunity exists for an alleged nuisance resulting in personal 
injury. 
• The Mayor, City Manager, City Attorney, and such other officers as may be appropriate are authorized to 
take all actions reasonably necessary to implement this Resolution and to coordinate with counsel for the 
City of Milton and other participating municipalities.

CITY OF DULUTH 
 
WHEREAS, the City Council of the City of Duluth has adopted a Stormwater Ordinance for the 
benefit of the public; and

the collection of unpaid stormwater user fees; 
 
NOW THEREFORE, the City Council of the City of Duluth hereby ordains that the City of Duluth 
Municipal Code is hereby amended by deleting in its entirety Section 15-20, Chapter 15, Article II 
and replacing said subsection with the following: 
Sec. 15-20. - Stormwater user fee billing, delinquencies, collections and rates. 
(a) Billing. 
(1) A bill for stormwater user fee charges may be sent through the United States Postal 
Service or by alternative means, notifying the owner of the property being billed of the 
amount of the stormwater user fee charge, less credits, the date the payment is due and the 
date when payment is past due. 
(2) The city council authorizes the city clerk to bill and collect the Duluth Stormwater User 
Fee Charge as part of the property/ad valorem tax bill. The city council further authorizes the 
city clerk to charge and collect penalties and interest as set forth in subsection (b) of this 
section. 
(3) If a bill for a stormwater user fee charge for a particular parcel is generated, failure of the 
customer to receive the bill shall not be justification for nonpayment. 
(4) Regardless of the party to whom the bill is initially directed, the owner of the property, as 
identified from the public land records of Gwinnett County, shall be obligated to pay the 
appropriate stormwater user fee charge for that property and any interest and/or penalties 
that have accrued. 
(5) If a property is unbilled, or if no bill is sent for a particular tract of improved property, the 
Duluth Stormwater Utility may back bill for a period of up to one (1) year, but shall not be 
entitled to any interest or any penalty charges during the back billed period. 
(b) Delinquencies and collection. 
(1) A penalty or late charge in the amount of ten (10) percent of the base amount due and 
unpaid ninety (90) days after the due date shall be assessed against the customer. 
(2) In addition to the penalty stated above, interest in the amount of one (1) percent per 
month shall accrue on all unpaid amounts beginning December 16 of the year in which the 
payment is due.

I. 
PURPOSE AND DESCRIPTION OF THE REQUEST 
The purpose of the request (Z2026-001) from Duluth North Berkeley Industrial Owner, LLC 
is to obtain approval for a modified rezoning of +/- 15.99 acres of property in Land Lot 261 
of the 6th District, Gwinnett County, consisting of tax parcel R6261 130. The subject site is 
currently zoned PUD and therefore has an approved Master Concept Plan. The applicant is 
requesting the modified rezoning to deviate from the existing approved Master Concept Plan 
to allow for a 198,000 square foot warehouse facility. 
Maps detailing the location, zoning and character areas of the site are attached hereto as 
Exhibit “A”. The Master Concept Plan is attached hereto as Exhibit “B”. 
 
II. 
EXISTING CONDITIONS 
 
The site is surrounded by a mixture of uses. The site is bound to the north by a railroad spur. 
Across the spur, are two properties zoned M-2 (Heavy Industrial District) and Gwinnett 
County M-2 (Heavy Industrial District). The site is bound to the east by a large one-story 
warehouse/distribution building zoned PUD. The site is bound to the south by North 
Berkeley Lake Road. Across North Berkeley Lake Road is a multi-tenant one-story 
office/warehouse building zoned PUD. The property is bound to the west by one and two-
story retail buildings zoned PUD. 
 
The subject site contains one seven-story office building shell and associated parking 
partially constructed in 2008. The building has never been occupied and was deemed unsafe 
by the City of Duluth Building Official in 2020. The building was then placed on the City’s 
blighted property list in 2021. 
 
This area of North Berkeley Lake Road, including the subject property, was annexed into the 
City of Duluth in July of 2000 and rezoned to PUD (Planned Unit Development District). In 
2007, the subject property went through a modified rezoning to amend the approved Master 
Concept Plan – the same process the applicant is currently going through. The amended 
Master Concept Plan was approved in November 2007. The current owner of the property 
sought and received another amendment to the approved master concept plan in 2021 and 
subsequent variance to the city’s stream buffer ordinance in 2022 to construct and operate a 
self-storage facility and flex office and warehouse facility. Both the approval of the plan 
amendment and the variance were subject to a number of conditions as outlined in Exhibit 
“G”. 
 
III. 
REVIEW OF THE REQUEST 
Unified Development Code 
 
Article 5 Revisions to Approved PUD 
 
Section 504.08 of the UDC states that additional approval is needed if a change is made to an 
approved Master Concept Plan that the Planning Director does not feel has been conceptually 
approved by the City Council. Such changes may be additions in the types of land use, increases 
to square footage or density or any other substantial changes that are inconsistent with the 
summary report or the master concept plan.

The Applicant has responded to the following Standards Governing the Exercise of Zoning 
Power. 
a) How the proposed rezoning will permit a use that is suitable in view of the use and 
development of adjacent and nearby property. 
b) How the proposed rezoning will adversely affect the existing use or usability of 
adjacent or nearby property. 
c) Whether the property to be affected by a proposed rezoning has a reasonable 
economic use as currently zoned. 
d) Whether the proposed rezoning will result in a use which will or could cause an 
excessive or burdensome use of existing streets, transportation facilities, utilities, or 
schools. 
e) Whether the proposed rezoning is in conformity with the policy and interest of the 
Comprehensive Plan; Land Use Plan; transportation plans and other plans adopted for 
guiding development within the City of Duluth. 
f) Whether there are other existing or changing conditions affecting the use and 
development of the property which give supporting grounds for either approval or 
disapproval of the proposed rezoning. 
 
The Applicant’s responses to the Standards Governing the Exercise of Zoning Power are 
attached hereto as Exhibit “F”. 
 
Master Concept Plan 
 
The Master Concept Plan shows a significant departure from any previous approved master 
plan or subsequent amendment. The current plan proposes a single 198,000 square foot rear 
loaded warehouse facility, 27 tractor trailer parking spaces, a 1.25 acre area identified as a 
parking expansion area, and 183 automobile parking areas. In addition to the amended site 
plan, the applicant is seeking a variance to the city’s minimum number of required parking 
spaces from 224 to the proposed 183. 
 
There are streams located along both side property lines of the subject property. Streams are 
protected by State and City buffers. The State has a 25-foot undisturbed buffer along streams. 
The City has an additional 25-foot stream buffer and a 25-foot impervious buffer where 
grading is allowed but impervious surface is not. The encroachments identified in the current 
application reflect the changes proposed and approved in the 2021 plan amendment and the 
2022 variance request. These encroachments are subject to the conditions outlined in the 
respective land use cases and are listed in Exhibit “G”. 
 
The 1.25 acre area on the proposed site plan labeled “trailer and/or auto parking expansion 
area” is ambiguous to its design and function. It is unclear if this area is to be developed in a 
future phase or if it is the applicant’s intent to utilize this space for trailer and auto parking 
immediately. Regardless, the conditions listed in this staff report make clear that, if this space 
is to be used for the parking or circulation of any vehicle, including tractor trailers or personal 
automobiles, the area will need to be designed to meet all requirements of the city’s unified 
development code. A design allowance is made for tractor trailer trucks allowing enhanced 
landscaping along the North Berkeley Lake Road frontage in lieu of landscaped islands in the 
1.25-acre expansion area, as such islands would make truck circulation difficult. Designs 
shall be submitted to the city for review and approval prior to the area being utilized as 
proposed.

Comprehensive Plan 
 
Every section of Duluth’s Comprehensive Plan, FORWARDuluth Plan 2040, is central to 
implementing the City’s vision and goals. However, the Character Areas and Future Land Use 
Maps are the most influential in terms of daily decision-making and land use changes. The 
Character Area Map is intended to work hand-in-hand with the Future Land Use Map when 
considering city-wide policies and when land-use applications are presented to the Planning 
Commission and City Council. The Character Area Map and related text will set the 
overarching goals for specific areas within the City. The Future Land Use Map gives parcel by 
parcel recommendations for future development. 
 
The subject property is located within the North Berkeley International Village. 
FORWARDuluth states, “North Berkeley International Village will continue to be a magnet for 
small and medium sized minority and internationally owned businesses targeting Duluth’s 
diverse community”. Each Character Area lists aspirations which essentially state the goals 
for the area. FORWARDuluth was adopted in 2019 and at that time the City envisioned the 
subject property as a mixed-use development. However, after consideration, it was 
determined that the property would be better utilized as an industrial or office development. 
When FORWARDuluth was updated in 2020, the subject property’s future land use 
designation was changed from mixed-use to industrial. The aspiration related to the subject 
property was also updated to state, “work with the owner of the seven-story tower to rezone 
and redevelop the property into an economic activity center including office space, 
warehousing, distribution and data centers”. 
 
IV. 
PLANNING STAFF REVIEW 
 
As previously stated, the existing building on the subject property has never been occupied 
and the property has been deemed as blighted and unsafe for human occupancy. The site has 
seen several unsuccessful attempts at redevelopment over the past fifteen years. 
 
There have been numerous police calls and code violations over the past five years. These 
violations consist of: nine (9) code cases involving Code Enforcement; 111 Suspicious Activity 
calls (these calls include people walking around the property, people parked in cars on the 
property including indecent exposure, drug use, squatters and one individual using the inside 
for a gun range); 17 Trespassing calls (these calls include 3 juveniles who broke in to the 
building leading to arrest, 3 juveniles broke glass and used a crowbar to get in, 6 unhoused 
individuals living behind the property, and one individual living in a tent near their car 
parked on the property); 2 burglary calls (these calls involved people breaking into the 
building and stealing tools); Trash dumping (someone had dumped trash behind the building 
prior to the property being fenced). In 2024 the owner installed an alarm system to the 
building. There have been 26 alarm calls with a mix of false alarms and people on the 
property. The property owner is in arrears of $575 for their alarm fees. 
 
The owner is also in arrears over $153k in blight tax. 
 
 The applicant’s request to modify the approved Master Concept Plan aligns with the 
aspirations of FORWARDuluth as well as the Future Land Use Map. Warehouse buildings are

A work session was held prior to the regular scheduled meeting to allow the elected 
officials to discuss this evening’s agenda items. No other items were discussed, and 
no other action was taken.

OVERNIGHT PARKING ORDINANCE CONCERNS 
 
 
Several public comment cards were received from those concerned about the 
City’s Overnight Parking ordinance. 
 
Bill Liss (special assignment editor, WXIA television news Atlanta) of 3596 
Castlegate Dr NW, Atlanta. asked for reasonable amendments to the ordinance. 
 
Mark Keller of 3778 Rogers Cove, Duluth requested modifications as well.

suggested the use of residential parking permits such as those used in residential 
areas downtown.

perhaps based on number of drivers in the home, street width, home repair work 
such as driveway paving, and asked that a more reasonable solution be 
implemented.

V. 
CONSENT AGENDA 
 
1. CONTRACT RENEWAL – APPALACHIAN MOUNTAIN SERVICES 
{A} 
 
As previously discussed at the April 27th Mayor and Council work session, approval 
of this item authorizes the City to renew a contract with Appalachian Mountain 
Services (AMS) to ensure that properties delinquent for more than three years are 
brought into compliance with property tax obligations. If the City does not collect 
the tax, there are no fees paid out. Approval of this item authorizes the Mayor to 
sign the contract, which becomes effective May 11, 2026. 
 
2. RESOLUTION – CHANG VS. MILTON AMICUS BRIEF 
 
 
{B} 
 
As discussed at the April 27th work session of the Mayor and Council, the City of 
Milton is requesting approval of a resolution seeking the city to join the amicus 
brief associated with the ongoing Chang v. Milton case now being heard by the 
Georgia Court of Appeals. Approval of resolution R2026-05 authorizes the City to 
join the amicus brief. 
 
3. APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT - PINE NEEDLE TRAIL PROJECT 
{C} 
 
Approval of this item authorizes the Mayor to execute the Pine Needle Trail Project 
Framework Agreement with the Georgia Department of Transportation (GDOT) as 
approved by staff and the City Attorney, which moves the project forward into the 
next steps in the pre-design process for city project CD-73. 
 
4. ORDINANCE TO AMEND CODE – STORMWATER 
 
 
{D} 
 
As discussed at the April 27, 2026 work session, Mayor and Council to consider a 
revision to the current stormwater ordinance, allowing the City to write off 
uncollectible stormwater fees. Approval of this item approves ordinance O2026-
20 as presented.

5. AD VALOREM/ BUSINESS PERSONAL PROPERTY INSOLVENT LIST {E} 
 
Per Chapter 2, Article 1, Sec 2- 4 of the Duluth Code, approval of this item grants 
insolvency status to property tax accounts determined to be uncollectible for 
years up through 2025 in the base amount of $16,034.98 plus penalties and 
interest for a total of $20,148.59. Business personal property accounts are 
considered insolvent only after every effort to collect them has been exhausted, 
which includes processing late notices, returned mail investigation, cross checks 
with the Gwinnett County' s Tax Assessors' real and personal property tax files, City 
and County Occupational Tax records, and also includes onsite visits by the 
Licensing Compliance inspector. 
 
A motion was made by Councilmember Thomas, seconded by Councilmember 
Doss, to approve the Consent Agenda as presented. 
 
Voted For: 
Council members Park, Thomas, Doss, Graeder, and Cummings 
Motion carried. 
 
 
 
 
VI. 
PUBLIC HEARINGS 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
1. ORDINANCE OF REZONING – CASE Z2026-001- N. BERKELEY LK RD {F} 
 
 
 
Mayor Whitlock opened the public hearing to consider an ordinance to allow the 
rezoning of parcel R6261 130 located at 2641 North Berkeley Lake Road for case 
Z2026-001, and called forward Director of Community Development and 
Engineering Margie Pozin. 
 
Ms. Pozin summarized the request. The owner, Duluth More Space, LLC and 
applicant, Duluth North Berkeley Industrial Owner, LLC are requesting a rezoning 
of this Planned Unit Development (PUD) to allow a change in the master plan. 
The current PUD includes facilities for indoor storage that were never constructed. 
The Owner and Applicant are requesting a change in the master plan to allow for 
demolition of the existing vacant seven story building and the construction and 
operation of roughly 198,000 square feet of flex office/warehouse. 
 
Ms. Pozin showed the location and described the subject property, which is 
approximately 16 acres in the North Berkeley International Village. 
FORWARDuluth envisions this Character Area to continue to be a magnet for 
small and medium sized minority and internationally owned businesses targeting 
Duluth’s diverse community. The Future Land Use Map (FLUM) envisions the uses 
to be Industrial. 
 
Ms. Pozin gave a recent history of the area. The subject site contains a seven-story 
office building shell and associated parking that has remained partially 
constructed since 2008. In 2020 the building was deemed unsafe by the Building 
Official. The property was placed on the blighted property list in 2021. The property 

Draft Minutes of M&C 
May 11, 2026 
Page 5 of 8 
 
5 
went through a PUD amendment in 2021 and was granted an amendment from 
the original Master Plan to use the property for Self-Storage. In 2022 there was a 
variance granted for encroachment into 50’ stream buffer (those conditions still 
hold). 
 
Over the past five years alone there have been nine (9) code cases and 130 cases 
involving police ranging from trespassing and burglary to suspicious activity 
including squatters, drug use and indecent exposure. The owner installed an 
alarm system in 2024 and since then there have been 26 alarm calls. The property 
owner is currently in arrears of $575 for their alarm fees. 
 
Ms. Pozin showed the site plan and discussed an area labeled as 1.25 acres of 
Phase 2. It's considered a future truck parking area. The applicant does not yet 
know who will be renting the space and what their needs will be for truck parking, 
but this is very well conditioned. She showed a sample elevation of what the 
building may look like. She gave a brief synopsis of the conditions, and 
highlighted a few things such as underground utilities, security access gates, 
master signage and outdoor lighting approved prior to development. 
 
The uses that will be underlying for this office and warehouse space will be those 
that are typically found in the M1 zoning, which is light industrial, with no outdoor 
storage. . There will be an enhanced landscape buffer plan, and part of the reason 
is due to the trucking aspect and logistics for large vehicles. Ms. Pozin 
emphasized that there will be no overnight stays in the trucks and explained the 
other parking requirements. 
 
Planning Commission recommended approval with revised conditions at their 
April 6, 2026 hearing. 
 
Mayor Whitlock called for discussion from Council. 
 
Councilmembers Thomas and Graeder asked about enforcement of parking 
conditions and landscaping, and Ms. Pozin said that it would be up to code 
enforcement and depend on the type of business as to what would be deemed 
reasonable. 
 
Councilmember Doss asked about acceleration or deceleration lanes on North 
Berkeley. Ms. Pozin said the trucks have a different entrance than the typical 
single passenger vehicles. 
 
Being no further questions, Mayor Whitlock called forward the applicant. 
 
 
Melanie Glauton with Anderson, Tate and Carr, 1960 Satellite Boulevard in Duluth 
came forward representing the owner. She said they are not asking to change 
that zoning classification. The future land use map specifically identifies this area 
as an industrial area, and they feel this proposal is compatible. The plans are for 
construction of a very large warehouse facility, approximately almost 200,000

square feet with that associated surface parking, with a reserve of 1.25 acres of the 
site for that future parking area. She noted that they agree with staff 
recommended conditions, and felt staff has been very good to work with. 
 
Ms. Glauton noted that there is currently a deceleration lane there on North 
Berkeley Lake, and they do think that the site would still be properly parked even 
with that requested variance of 224 spaces down to 183. 
 
Being no further discussion, the Mayor called the Developer 
 
Hunter Himes of Oakmont Industrial Group, 3520 Piedmont Road, Atlanta came 
forward to explain he is with the development group and happy to answer 
questions. 
 
Mayor Whitlock called for questions/comments from the public. 
 
There being no further comments or questions, Mayor Whitlock closed the public

A motion was made by Councilmember Park, seconded by Councilmember 
Cummings, to approve ordinance O2026-19 for case number Z2026-001 with

Voted For:

Motion carried. 
 
 
 
2. FY2027 BUDGET PRESENTATION 
 
Mayor Whitlock opened the public hearing to receive public comments on the 
FY2027 budget. Prior to this public hearing, council and staff reviewed the 
proposed FY 2027 budget at a budget workshop on May 4th. A second public 
hearing will be held on Monday, June 8, 2026 at the regularly scheduled meeting 
of the Mayor and Council. Following the second public hearing, an ordinance 
adopting the FY 2027 budget will be presented for consideration. 
 
Assistant City Manager/Finance Ken Sakmar came forward to present an overview 
of the proposed FY 2027 Annual Operating and Capital Projects Budget of 
approximately $43 million. On the revenue side, similar figures are presented but 
the budget does require some reserves used to balance the budget. He showed 
the capital projects as well, which are based on the life of the project, not the fiscal 
year. 
 
Mr. Sakmar explained the conservative nature of budget philosophy, but noted 
that last year the proposal anticipated using about $921,000 of reserves to balance 
the budget, but this year it’s approximately $120,000 in excess of that number to 
balance this year's budget. This is the season of review and some of those funds 
that are unobligated would be used to balance prior to tapping into reserves.

He discussed the largest revenues for the city (property taxes) and expenditures 
(salaries) and highlighted various changes between the FY26 and proposed FY27 
budgets. Fortunately some of the approved legislation did not affect the property 
taxes as much as the proposals. The largest increase was a higher than normal 
increase in employee medical insurance. Some large single purchase items were 
included as well such as software, and the TAD transfer was highlighted 
separately. 
 
Mr. Sakmar concluded by noting that the budget was prepared with the millage 
rate remaining the same, but that is up to Council’s discretion and hasn’t been set 
yet for the 2026 tax year. The millage rate has only risen ¼ mills over the last 21 
years, and has remained the same for the last 10. He also noted there are no new 
full-time or permanent part-time positions in the budget except for potential 
stormwater interns which may affect summer 2027. Several items that were listed 
in the budget will be removed if the work can be accomplished prior to June 30 of 
this year, such as the duct cleaning.

in public art money, but said that funds for duct cleaning shouldn’t cost more

1. STORMWATER ORDINANCE REVISIONS 
 
 
 
Staff will introduce discussion on suggested revisions to Chapter 15 of the Duluth 
Municipal Code regarding stormwater that may allow for writing off uncollectible 
amounts. In addition, staff will also make recommendations for potential changes to 
the stormwater fee schedule. 
 
2. HUDGENS TRAIL CONNECTOR 
 
 
 
 
 
With the pending development of the Hudgens property, staff and the developer feel 
it is essential to connect the property to downtown by way of a multi-use trail. This 
would allow cyclists and pedestrians to access both origins/destinations and connect 
the properties in between in a cohesive manner. 

M&C Work Session Agenda 
April 27, 2026 
Page 2 of 2 
 
2 
 
Therefore, staff recommends using the services of an on-call engineer to conduct an 
analysis of trail alternatives. This will allow Council to consider options and decide 
which path to pursue. It is likely that the Hudgens redevelopment would be completed 
prior to the trail connection, but the goal would be at least for trail design and funding 
to be established by that point. 
 
Staff will present a simple graphic to introduce some of the options to initiate 
discussion. 
 
3. APPALACHIAN MOUNTAIN SERVICES CONTRACT RENEWAL 
 
Appalachian Mountain Services has been a valued partner of the City by ensuring that 
properties delinquent for more than three years are compliant with property tax 
obligations. The firm conducts deed research to identify property owners or heirs and 
works to facilitate payment of outstanding taxes, helping to avoid the need for a tax 
sale whenever possible. When no response is received, Appalachian Mountain Services 
assists with coordinating a tax sale at the Gwinnett County Justice Center. 
 
Staff is requesting that the Mayor and Council consider renewing a contract 
agreement with Appalachian Mountain Services, Inc. to continue assisting the City 
with “Sheriff Sales” and the collection of outstanding tax delinquencies. If the City does 
not collect the tax, there are no fees paid out. If approved, the contract will become 
effective May 12, 2026. 
 
4. CHANG V. MILTON REQUEST FOR PARTICIPATION IN AMICUS BRIEF 
 
The City of Milton has sent a resolution seeking the City join the amicus brief 
associated with the ongoing Chang v. Milton case now being heard by the Georgia 
Court of Appeals. 
 
5. STRATEGIC RETREAT DISCUSSION 
 
 
 
 
The upcoming Strategic Retreat will focus on an evaluation of the vision statement 
and aspirational goals of the City.

ADJOURNMENT

RESOLUTION OF THE CITY OF __________________, GEORGIA 
AUTHORIZING PARTICIPATION IN AN AMICUS BRIEF IN CHANG v. CITY OF 
MILTON ON REMAND BEFORE THE GEORGIA COURT OF APPEALS OR, IF 
WARRANTED, THE GEORGIA SUPREME COURT 
WHEREAS, the litigation styled Chang v. City of Milton arises from claims asserted against the City 
of Milton, Georgia, related to a 2016 motor vehicle collision on Batesville Road; 
WHEREAS, on September 16, 2024, the Georgia Court of Appeals issued its decision in City of 
Milton v. Chang, 373 Ga. App. 667 (2024); 
WHEREAS, the Supreme Court of Georgia thereafter granted certiorari and, on March 12, 2026, 
vacated the Court of Appeals decision and remanded the case for further proceedings, holding that a 
municipality's ministerial duty over roadway upkeep and repair did not apply where the alleged unsafe 
condition was outside the lanes of ordinary travel, City of Milton v. Chang, 2026 WL 695364; 
WHEREAS, following remand, the Georgia Court of Appeals will consider the separate question of 
whether a Georgia municipality may nevertheless be subjected to liability under a so-called nuisance theory 
for personal injury claims; 
WHEREAS, the City recognizes that any asserted waiver of sovereign immunity for nuisance claims 
resulting in personal injury does not arise from any express constitutional or statutory waiver applicable to 
municipalities, but instead traces to judicial decisions such as Town of Fort Oglethorpe v. Phillips, 224 Ga. 
834 (1968); 
WHEREAS, the Supreme Court of Georgia explained in Georgia Department of Natural Resources 
v. Center for a Sustainable Coast, Inc., 294 Ga. 593 (2014), that waivers of sovereign immunity must come 
from the Constitution or the General Assembly and that courts may not create new exceptions to sovereign 
immunity; 
WHEREAS, in Mayor & C. of Savannah v. Palmerio, 242 Ga. 224 (1978), Justice Hall, in a 
concurring opinion, advised that “the time is long past for this court to re-examine its opinion in Town of Ft. 
Oglethorpe v. Phillips, 224 Ga. 834, 165 S.E.2d 141 (1968);” 
WHEREAS, in Gatto v. City of Statesboro, 312 Ga. 164, fn. 6 (2021), the Court observed “[s]ome of 
us have doubts about the legal foundations of Phillips, which also divorced municipal nuisance liability from 
its basis in our Constitution's Takings Clause;” 
WHEREAS, a nuisance theory that permits personal-injury claims against cities, but not counties, 
creates an uneven exposure to liability that is not supported by a clear constitutional or statutory waiver; 
WHEREAS, Georgia law has long distinguished between nuisance claims that implicate the Takings 
Clause and nuisance claims seeking damages for personal injury; 
WHEREAS, municipalities across the State have a substantial interest in ensuring that any waiver of 
sovereign immunity remains tied to a constitutional or statutory foundation rather than a judicially created 
expansion; 
WHEREAS, the City finds that it is in the best interests of its citizens and residents to support the 
City of Milton in seeking an appellate ruling that there is no waiver of municipal sovereign immunity for an 
alleged nuisance resulting in personal injury, outside the limited context of a nuisance claim amounting to a 
constitutional taking; and 

WHEREAS, the City further finds that Georgia cities should have their collective voice heard on this 
issue of statewide importance through coordinated amicus participation before the Georgia Court of Appeals 
and/or the Georgia Supreme Court. 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE CITY OF ___________________, that: 
• The City authorizes participation in, support for, and joinder with an amicus curiae brief or briefs to be filed 
in Chang v. City of Milton on remand before the Georgia Court of Appeals and/or, if further appellate 
proceedings occur after the Court of Appeals, before the Georgia Supreme Court, and authorizes the City's 
name to be included as an amicus participant. 
• The City supports the position that any purported waiver of a city's sovereign immunity for nuisance claims 
seeking recovery for personal injury is a judicially created doctrine rather than an express waiver grounded 
in the Georgia Constitution or an act of the General Assembly. 
• The City supports the position that, consistent with Sustainable Coast and related sovereign-immunity 
precedent, no waiver of municipal sovereign immunity exists for an alleged nuisance resulting in personal 
injury. 
• The Mayor, City Manager, City Attorney, and such other officers as may be appropriate are authorized to 
take all actions reasonably necessary to implement this Resolution and to coordinate with counsel for the 
City of Milton and other participating municipalities. 
SO RESOLVED this _____ day of __________________, 2026.

CITY OF DULUTH, GA

PRESENT: Mayor Whitlock, Council members Park, Thomas, Doss, Graeder,
and Holloway, City Manager, Asst. City Managers, Department
Directors, City Attorney

Mayor Whitlock called the meeting to order at 5:30 p.m.
I. PUBLIC COMMENTS

1. NOISE COMPLAINT
Tod and Lynn Madderra of 3385 McClure Bridge Road, Duluth spoke to the Mayor and
Council concerning a neighbor who uses lawn equipment that produces loud noise
and gas fumes during all hours of the day and late evening. The Mayor and Council
directed the staff to look into this matter.
ll. | DISCUSSION ITEMS/PRESENTATIONS/UPDATES

1. STORMWATER ORDINANCE REVISIONS
Stormwater Program Administrator Alyssa Gilhooly introduced a discussion on
suggested revisions to Chapter 15 of the Duluth Municipal Code regarding stormwater
that may allow for writing off uncollectible amounts. In addition, staff will also make
recommendations for potential changes to the stormwater fee schedule.
Staff was directed to develop an ordinance amending the Duluth Code and to
place it on a future agenda, and run some calculation scenarios for a fee increase
structure to be considered at a future work session.

2. HUDGENS TRAIL CONNECTOR
City Manager James Riker came forward to present.
With the pending development of the Hudgens property, staff and the developer feel
it is essential to connect the property to downtown by way of a multi-use trail.

[page 2]
M&C Work Session Notes
April 27, 2026
Page 2 of 3
This would allow cyclists and pedestrians to access both origins/destinations and
connect the properties in between in a cohesive manner.
Staff recommended using an on-call engineer to conduct an analysis of trail
alternatives. Staff presented a simple graphic to introduce some of the options to
initiate discussion. A budget amendment would be required.
Staff was authorized to get costs to move forward with a study.
3. APPALACHIAN MOUNTAIN SERVICES CONTRACT RENEWAL
Appalachian Mountain Services has been a valued partner of the City by ensuring that
properties delinquent for more than three years are compliant with property tax
obligations. The firm conducts deed research to identify property owners or heirs and
works to facilitate payment of outstanding taxes, helping to avoid the need for a tax
sale whenever possible. When no response is received, Appalachian Mountain Services
assists with coordinating a tax sale at the Gwinnett County Justice Center.
Staff requested that the Mayor and Council consider renewing a contract agreement
with Appalachian Mountain Services, Inc. to continue assisting the City with “Sheriff
Sales” and the collection of outstanding tax delinquencies. If the City does not collect
the tax, there are no fees paid out. If approved, the contract will become effective May
12, 2026.
Staff was authorized to place this item on the May 17 consent agenda.
4. CHANG V. MILTON REQUEST FOR PARTICIPATION IN AMICUS BRIEF
The City of Milton has sent a resolution seeking the City join the amicus brief
associated with the ongoing Chang v. Milton case now being heard by the Georgia
Court of Appeals.
Staff was authorized to place this item on the May II'" consent agenda.
5. STRATEGIC RETREAT DISCUSSION
The upcoming Strategic Retreat will focus on an evaluation of the vision statement
and aspirational goals of the City.
Ill. MATTERS FROM MAYOR & COUNCIL
The first budget review session is scheduled for Monday, May 4%. Mayor Whitlock
explained the process.

March 23 work session, approval of this item approves the third contract 
amendment and acknowledges a 2.5% rate increase for solid waste services with 
Republic Services beginning on May 1, 2026 and extending to May 1, 2027. 
 
2. ORD TO AMEND FY26 BUDGET – STORMWATER UTILITY 
 
At the March 23rd council work session, staff gave an update on current 
stormwater rates and projects yet to be completed. At that time, Council 
approved the transfer of $750,000 from the General Fund to the Stormwater 
Utility Fund to address the some of the stormwater system repairs. Approval of 
this item authorizes ordinance BA-FY26-38 to amend the FY26 budget as 
presented.

enter into a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between the Duluth, Lilburn, 
Norcross and Suwanee Police Departments to operate a Joint Special Response 
Team (Joint SRT). 
 
4. ORDINANCE TO AMEND DULUTH CODE – SEC 8-67 – PARKING 
 
Approval of this item approves ordinance O2026-18 to amend section 8-67 of the 
Duluth Code of Ordinances to create three hour parking in front of the Main Street 
City Hall entrance to accommodate city customer parking. The ordinance also 
adds overnight parking restrictions on city controlled parking spaces inside the 
parking deck located at the Marriott/DDA parking deck and Ridgeway Road and 
Hill Street. The approval updates the parking map associated with the ordinance. 
 
5. INTERGOVERNMENTAL AGREEMENT – DDA – PARKING 
 
As discussed at the March 23 work session, approval of this item approves an 
Intergovernmental Agreement (IGA) between the City and Duluth Downtown 
Development Authority (DDA) to allow for consolidated parking enforcement 
inside the parking deck entered from Hill Street and from Ridgeway Road.

exceed $1,552,924.45.

Joint Special Response Team 
Memorandum of Understanding 
I. PURPOSE 
This Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) establishes a cooperative agreement between the 
City of Duluth Police Department, City of Lilburn Police Department, City of Norcross Police 
Department, and City of Suwanee Police Department for the joint operation and administration 
of a multi-agency Special Response Team (SRT). 
The purpose of this agreement is to provide a coordinated, highly trained, and properly 
equipped tactical response capability for incidents that exceed the scope, training, or equipment 
availability of routine patrol operations. This partnership is intended to enhance the safety of 
law enforcement personnel, citizens, and involved subjects through shared resources, training, 
and operational coordination. 
II. PARTICIPATING AGENCIES 
This agreement is entered into by the following agencies, listed in alphabetical order: 
• City of Duluth Police Department 
• City of Lilburn Police Department 
• City of Norcross Police Department 
• City of Suwanee Police Department 
Ill. AUTHORITY 
This Memorandum of Understanding ("MOU") is entered into by and between the City of 
----
Duluth, City of Lilburn, City of Norcross, and City of Suwanee, Georgia, on behalf of their 
respective Police Departments (collectively referred to as the "Participating Agencies" ). 
This MOU shall become effective upon the date of the final signature and shall apply to all 
activities conducted by members assigned to the Special Response Team (SRT). Each 
representative executing this MOU affirms they are authorized to enter into this agreement on 
behalf of their agency. 
IV. MISSION 
The mission of the Special Response Team (SRT) is to provide a unified, multi-agency tactical 
capability to respond to high-risk situations that exceed the capabilities of standard patrol 
response. 
The SRT may be deployed in situations including, but not limited to: 
• High-risk warrant service 
• Barricaded suspects 
• Barricaded gunman incidents 
• Armed suicidal persons 

• Urgent or emergent hostage situations requiring immediate intervention 
• Violent or potentially violent incidents requiring specialized tactics or equipment 
Planned (deliberate} hostage rescue operations are not within the scope of the SRT's mission or 
operational capabilities. However, urgent or emergent hostage situations may be encountered, 
and personnel may take reasonable and necessary action consistent with their training and the 
immediate preservation of life. 
V. DEFINITIONS 
Special Response Team (SRT}: A multi-agency tactical unit composed of selected personnel from 
participating departments. 
High-Risk Warrant: An arrest or search warrant identified through threat assessment as 
requiring specialized equipment, planning, and tactics for safe service. 
Barricaded Person: A situation in which a suspect has confined themselves in a structure, 
vehicle, or location to prevent arrest or investigation, where entry by patrol officers would 
create undue risk. 
Barricaded Gunman: A situation in which an armed suspect has barricaded themselves and is 
known or believed to possess weapons and/or has demonstrated intent to harm others. 
Suicidal Person Tactical Response}: A person exhibiting suicidal behavior while armed or 
presenting a threat level that may require specialized tactical response. 
VI. ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE 
The SRT shall operate as a unified team composed of sworn personnel from each participating 
agency. 
Assignment to the SRT is a collateral duty. Members will maintain their primary roles and 
responsibilities within their respective Participating Agency and respond to SRT activations as 
needed. 
VII. ACTIVATION, COMMAND, AND OPERATIONAL OVERSIGHT 
Any participating agency may request activation of the SRT for incidents occurring within its 
jurisdiction. 
The agency requesting SRT activation shall retain primary responsibility for operational planning, 
command, and oversight of the event prompting the activation. 
A command-level officer, designated SRT commander, or team leader from the 
requesting/originating agency shall be responsible for developing the operational plan, 

coordinating intelligence and briefings, and providing operational direction. 
Example: If Duluth requests SRT assistance for a high-risk warrant service, Duluth personnel will 
oversee planning and command. If Lilburn originates the request, Lilburn personnel will oversee 
the operation. 
Whenever a team member is rendering assistance pursuant to this MOU, the team member 
shall abide by and be subject to the rules and regulations, personnel policies, general orders, 
and standard operating procedures of their own employer. If any such standard is contradicted, 
contravened or otherwise in conflict with a direct order of a superior officer of the Special 
Response Team, then such rule, regulation, policy, general order or procedure shall control and 
shall supersede the direct order. 
VIII. PERSONNEL, TRAINING, AND NEGOTIATION SUPPORT 
SRT personnel must be sworn officers in good standing with their respective agencies. 
Assignment to the SRT is a collateral duty. All members remain employees of their parent 
agency and remain subject to their agency's policies, discipline, and employment protections. 
Each participating agency agrees to support regular training to maintain operational readiness. 
Some participating agencies maintain trained crisis negotiators who may be requested to 
respond in support of SRT operations when available. 
IX. EQUIPMENT AND RESOURCES 
Each Participating Agency agrees to furnish the necessary personal equipment and resources to 
their Participating Agency members assigned to the SRT to render services to each Participating 
Agency. 
Each Participating Agency that furnishes personal equipment pursuant to this MOU must bear 
the cost of loss or damage to that equipment and must pay any expense incurred in the 
operation and maintenance of t hat equipment. Nothing herein shall prevent one Participating 
Agency from lending necessary equipment to any other Participating Agency team member for 
operational purposes pursuant to this MOU. 
Participating agencies may contribute additional equipment and resources for use during SRT 
operations and shall retain sole ownership of said equipment contributed for joint operational 
use. 
The City of Duluth Police Department currently maintains an armored rescue vehicle {armored 
SUV) which may be deployed in support of SRT operations. The vehicle will be operated by a 
qualified Duluth Police Department officer and remains the property of the City of Duluth who 
assumes the vehicle's maintenance, fuel and insurance cost. 

X. LIABILITY, USE OF FORCE, COMPLAINTS 
Each Participating Agency engaging in any assistance pursuant to this MOU agrees to assume 
responsibility for the acts, omissions, or conduct of each of its SRT members or conduct of such 
Participating Agency's/team's own employees while engaged in rendering such assistance 
pursuant to this MOU. 
The Unit Commander for any operation shall conduct an after-action review to document the 
actions taken by the SRT as a team or unit during the course of a given operation. Should a 
concern arise regarding use or force or other actions taken by an individual officer, the 
Commander shall forward a copy of the after-action report to the officer's parent agency along 
with the documented concerns. The review and appropriate remedial response, if any, will be 
the sole responsibility of their respective Agency according to their Agency's policies and 
procedures. Each Participating Agency engaging in any assistance pursuant to this MOU agrees 
to cooperate with such joint investigative efforts. 
Should an application of force on behalf of SRT result in serious injury or death, it is agreed by 
the Participating Agencies that the Georgia Bureau of Investigation will be asked to conduct a 
separate and independent review as appropriate. 
XI. TERM AND TERMINATION 
This MOU shall take effect upon execution by all participating agencies and remain in effect until 
modified or terminated by mutual consent. 
Any participating agency may withdraw from this agreement by providing sixty (60) days written 
notice to the other agencies.

ORDINANCE 
ARTICLE III. STOPPING, STANDING, AND PARKING 
CITY OF DULUTH 
 
WHEREAS, In accordance with O.C.G.A. § 40-6-371(a)(1), the Council of the City of Duluth hereby ordains 
that the Duluth Code of Ordinances Article III of Chapter 8, is hereby amended by deleting Section 8-67 
titled “Downtown Regulations” in its entirety and replacing it with the following: 
Sec. 8-67. Downtown regulations. 
 
a. Designated Time Limited Parking Map - Downtown Duluth. 
The “Designated Time Limited Parking Map - Downtown Duluth” hereby delineates all spaces which 
are time limited in downtown and enforced by this ordinance and is herein described (and 
illustrated as Exhibit “A” of this ordinance). 
 
b. Parking prohibited—Posted signs. 
It shall be unlawful for the owner or operator of any motor vehicle or other vehicle to park the 
vehicle or allow the vehicle to remain parked on any public street, highway or alley, lot or garage, or 
lot controlled or leased by the City of Duluth for the parking of an individual vehicle in violation of 
any posted signs regulating or prohibiting parking in such location. The city manager or designee 
shall have authority to develop regulations governing parking, including establishing time limits 
and directing the posting of signs, for all City of Duluth downtown facilities as displayed in the 
“Designated Time Limited Parking Map - Downtown Duluth.” 
 
c. Three (3) hour parking locations. It shall be unlawful for the owner or operator of any motor 
vehicle or other vehicle to park the vehicle or allow the vehicle to remain parked on any public 
street, highway or alley, lot or garage, or lot controlled or leased by the City of Duluth for the 
parking of an individual vehicle as described herein and depicted in “Designated Time Limited 
Parking Map - Downtown Duluth” for a period in excess of three (3) hours beginning Monday – 
Friday from 6:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. or 0600 hours to 1500 hours described herein: 
 
the parking lot located at the corner of Hill Street NW and Hwy 120 at the rear of Parsons Alley; 
the parking lot entered from West Lawrenceville Street and exited at Hill Street NW; the angled 
and 90 degree parking spaces located along either side of West Lawrenceville Street next to the 
4-way stop at Hill Street and West Lawrenceville Street; the parallel parking spaces on both 
sides of Main Street running from the intersection of West Lawrenceville Street to Knott 
Street/Knox Drive; the parking lot entered from Main Street bounded by Knott Street/Knox 
Drive; the parking lot accessed from Main Street located in front of Main Street city hall 
entrance and accessed from Hill Street by driving through Hill Street city hall parking lot 
and continuing between city hall and the cemetery retaining wall and entered from that 
direction. 
All city vehicles in the official performance of duties are exempt from this requirement. 
d. Fifteen (15) minute parking locations. It shall be unlawful for the owner or operator of any 
motor vehicle or other vehicle to park the vehicle or allow the vehicle to remain parked on any 

public street, highway or alley, lot or garage, or lot controlled or leased by the City of Duluth for the 
parking of an individual vehicle as described herein and depicted in the “Designated Time Limited 
Parking Map - Downtown Duluth” for a period in excess of fifteen (15) minutes and as indicated by 
fifteen (15) minute loading and unloading zone signage described herein: 
 
the parallel parking spaces located along Hwy 120 and the intersection of West Lawrenceville 
Street bounded by Parsons Alley; in the half-round located on West Lawrenceville Street at the 
top of town green; the parallel parking spaces located on both sides of West Lawrenceville Street 
in front of Parsons Alley and in front of 3559 West Lawrenceville Street; the parallel parking 
spaces located at the entrance of the parking lot entered from West Lawrenceville and exited by 
Hill Street; the parallel loading space bounded by the activity lawn on Main Street across from 
the entrance of Knott Street/Knox Drive. 
All city vehicles in the official performance of duties are exempt from this requirement. 
e. Forty-eight (48) hour parking locations. It shall be unlawful for the owner or operator of any 
motor vehicle or other vehicle to park the vehicle or allow the vehicle to remain parked on any 
public street, highway or alley, lot or garage, or lot controlled or leased by the City of Duluth for the 
parking of an individual vehicle as described herein and depicted in the “Designated Time Limited 
Parking Map - Downtown Duluth” for a period in excess of forty-eight (48) hours and as indicated 
by forty-eight (48) hour loading and unloading zone signage described herein: 
 
the parking spaces located on Main Street in front of Coleman Middle School; the parking lot 
entered from Hwy. 120 and from Knott Street/Knox Drive and from Main Street fronted by the 
railroad; the parking spaces located in front of 3176 Main Street; the parking spaces located in 
front of 3150 Main Street; the parking spaces located in front of Taylor Park on Main Street; the 
parking spaces on Main Street located in front of 3151 Main Street; the parking spaces on Main 
Street located in front of the parking lot entered by Main Street bounded by Knott Street/Knox 
Drive; the parking spaces located on Main Street in front of the train observation station parking lot; 
city hall parking spaces accessed by the Hill Street entrance located along the Hill Street 
retaining wall and the Town Green retaining wall stopping at the loading dock attached to 
city hall across from the cemetery retaining wall; the parking spaces located on Main Street in 
front of the Duluth Branch of the Gwinnett County Library; the parallel parking spaces on Main 
Street located next to Church Cemetery; the parallel parking spaces on Hill Street from Hardy Street 
to West Lawrenceville Street; the 90 degree parking spaces located in front of Duluth Festival 
Center on Hill Street; the parking lot on Parkridge Lane entered from Hill Street and from Ridge 
Towne Place; the parking spaces on Ridge Towne Place; the parking spaces on both sides of 
Ridgeway Road and in front of the hotel on Ridgeway Road. 
 
f. No overnight parking locations. It shall be unlawful for the owner or operator of any motor 
vehicle or other vehicle to park the vehicle or allow the vehicle to remain parked on any 
public street, highway or alley, lot or garage, or lot controlled or leased by the City of Duluth 
for the parking of an individual vehicle as described herein and depicted in the “Designated 
Time Limited Parking Map - Downtown Duluth” between the hours of 02:00 A.M. to 5:00 A.M. 
and as indicated by No Parking 2:00 A.M. to 5:00 A.M. signage described herein: 
 
the parking spaces entered and exited from Ridgeway Road through the parking deck 
entrance; the parking spaces entered from Hill Street through the parking deck entrance 
except for those marked for hotel use only, police use, and any spaces behind access 
control devices.

 AGREEMENT 
I. 
PURPOSE 
The purpose of this Agreement is to set forth the terms under which parking areas 
owned by DDA at the Parking Deck located at 3141 Hill Street, Duluth, Georgia 30096 
(hereinafter “3141 Hill Street”) may be utilized by the public. 
II. 
SCOPE OF PROJECT 
A. The DDA agrees to allow the public to park on DDA owned property at 3141 Hill 
Street as shown in the “subject areas” identified on the attached Exhibit A, which 
is incorporated herein by reference. 
 
B. Duluth agrees to install signs directing the public to parking in the subject areas and 
to provide for parking regulation and enforcement through the City of Duluth Police 
Department. 
 
 
 

 
3 
 
III. 
DULUTH RESPONSIBILITIES 
A. Duluth shall be responsible for installing signage informing the public of the 
availability and location of public parking at 3143 Hill Street. Such signs shall 
specify the hours when public parking is allowed. 
B. Duluth shall through its Police Department and Municipal Court system regulate 
and enforce City ordinances regarding public parking at 3143 Hill Street. 
 
IV. 
DDA RESPONSIBILITIES 
A. DDA shall authorize public parking in the subject parking areas at 3141 Hill Street, 
as shown on Exhibit “A” attached hereto and incorporated herein by reference. 
 
V. 
LEGAL ACTIONS 
Unless otherwise specifically provided herein, nothing in this Intergovernmental 
Agreement is intended to create any rights in any individual, firm, corporation, or entity 
not a party to this Intergovernmental Agreement. Neither Duluth nor DDA shall 
indemnify or hold harmless the other party’s agents, officers, servants, vendors and 
employees, past and present, in connection with this Intergovernmental Agreement. 
Both Duluth and DDA shall assume and defend at their own cost, any suit, action or 
other legal proceeding brought against it arising from any actions taken by the that 
party’s agents, officers, servants, vendors, and employees in furtherance of the Project. 
Nothing herein shall be construed to waive sovereign immunity or the immunities of 
either party. 
 
VI. 
TERM & TERMINATION OF AGREEMENT 
A. Term. The term of this Agreement shall be five (5) years commencing upon the 
 
date of the signature of this Agreement. 
 
B. This Agreement may be terminated by either party upon ninety days written 
 
notice of termination by the other party.

2026 LMIG Paving Project on various streets within the City of Duluth 
The City of Duluth is accepting sealed bids from qualified contractors to provide all 
necessary labor, material and equipment necessary to perform asphaltic concrete milling, 
deep patching (as directed), excavation of unsuitable material as needed, replacement, 
grading, compaction of grade aggregate base course as needed, patching, and 
installation or replacement of thermoplastic striping, traffic control, erosion control and 
dust control on various streets within the City limits of Duluth. All work shall be in 
accordance with the specifications, the applicable drawings and subject to the terms and 
conditions of this contract. 
The contract will include multiple road projects for milling, patching and resurfacing. A proposed 
BASE project list as well as a proposed Alternate (additional list of projects) is included in the full 
Invitation to Bid available at www.duluthga.net under the heading “Notices and RFP’s”. 
All sealed bids will be received by the City of Duluth City Clerk, 3167 Main Street, Duluth, Georgia 
30096, until 1:45 P.M. local time on Tuesday, March 31, 2026. Bids received after the 
stated time will not be accepted. Bids will be opened publicly and read aloud on Tuesday, 
March 31, 2026 at 2:00 P.M. on the second floor of Duluth City Hall, 3167 Main Street, Duluth GA 
30096, in the Executive Conference Room. The bid envelope must be marked on the outside with 
the following information: 
City of Duluth 
Bid – 2026 LMIG Paving Project on Various Roads within City of Duluth 
Date and Hour of Bid Opening 
Company Name 
 
Winning contractor will be required to provide an Eighteen month (18) warranty on all 
work completed. 
Pre-Bid Conference will be held at City of Duluth Public Works Facility – 2450 Main Street 
in Duluth, Georgia 30096, on Tuesday, March 10, 2026 at 10:00 A.M. 
Full Invitation to Bid is available on the City of Duluth website, www.duluthga.net under the heading 
“Notices and RFP’s” 
Full Invitation to Bid is also available for viewing at the Duluth Public Works Department, 2450 Main 
Street, Duluth, Georgia 30097. 
Bid will be awarded based upon Base Bid and selected alternates. Alternates will be selected by the 
City at time of bid opening. City retains full discretion on which, if any, alternates will be selected. 
Contract will be awarded, if at all, within sixty (60) calendar days after opening of the proposal. 

Deadline for questions is Tuesday, March 17, 2026 at 5 P.M. Submit all questions to Adam 
Shelton, PE, of Keck & Wood at GAbids2025@keckwood.com No phone calls will be accepted. 
The selected contractor must be able to start work within ten (10) calendar days after the “Notice to 
Proceed” is issued. The time of completion for the project is ninety (90) calendar days from the date 
of the “Notice to Proceed”. 
All bids shall be accompanied by a bid bond in favor of the City, in the amount of five percent (5%) 
of the total bid, (but not less than $5,000); such bid bond representing that the bidder, if awarded a 
contract, will promptly enter into a contract and furnish performance bond and payment bond as 
provided by law and approved by the attorney for the City. Failure to submit a bid bond with the 
proper rating will result in the bid being deemed non-responsive. 
Successful bidder will be required to meet insurance requirements. Performance and Payment bonds 
will be required upon acceptance of the proposal and contract submittal. 
 
The Performance Bond shall be equal to one hundred percent (100%) of the contract 
amount. The Payment Bond shall be equal to one hundred ten percent (110%) of the 
contract amount. 
 
 Insurance and Bonding Company must be licensed to do business by the Georgia Secretary of State, 
authorized to business in Georgia by the Georgia Insurance Department, listed in the Department of 
Treasury’s Publication of Companies holding Certificates of Authority as Acceptable Surety on Federal 
Bonds and as acceptable reinsuring companies. The bid bond, payment bond and performance 
bond must have an A.M. Best rating of A-5 or higher. 
 
Award will be made to the lowest responsible and responsive bidder. The City of Duluth reserves the 
right to reject any and all bids, to waive technicalities and to make an award as deemed in its best 
interest. 
 
Any change to the conditions and specifications must be in the form of a written addendum to be 
valid; therefore, the City will issue a written addendum to document each approved change.

– Management Recommendations for Improvement
1. Segregation of Duties -
During the course of our test work, we noted a couple of areas in which the segregation of duties could be
improved. Segregation of employee’s duties is a common practice in an effective internal control structure. The City has made improvements

New Accounting Pronouncements
• New GASB Pronouncements for Future Years
o
GASB Statement No. 103, Financial Reporting Model Improvements was issued in April 2024 and is effective for
fiscal years beginning after June 15, 2025, and all reporting periods thereafter. Earlier application is encouraged. The
requirements for MD&A will improve the quality of the analysis of changes from the prior year, which will enhance
the relevance of that information. They also will provide clarity regarding what information should be presented in
MD&A. The requirements for the separate presentation of unusual or infrequent items will provide clarity regarding
which items should be reported separately from other inflows and outflows of resources. The definitions of
operating revenues and expenses and of nonoperating revenues and expenses will replace accounting policies that
vary from government to government, thereby improving comparability. The addition of a subtotal for operating
income (loss) and noncapital subsidies will improve the relevance of information provided in the proprietary fund
statement of revenues, expenses, and changes in fund net position. The requirement for presentation of major
component unit information will improve comparability. The requirement that budgetary comparison information
be presented as RSI will improve comparability, and the inclusion of the specified variances and the explanations of
significant variances will provide more useful information for making decisions and assessing accountability.
o
Statement No. 104, Disclosure of Certain Capital Assets was issued in September 2024 and is effective for fiscal
years beginning after June 15, 2025, and all reporting periods thereafter. The objective of this Statement is to clarify
which types of capital assets must be disclosed separately in the notes to the financial statements as well as to
establish disclosure requirements for capital assets that are held for sale.

Other Pending or Current GASB Projects
o
Going Concern Uncertainties and Severe Financial Stress is a major project where the goal is to address issues related to disclosures
regarding going concern uncertainties and severe financial stress. The project will consider (1) improvements to existing guidance for going
concern considerations to address diversity in practice and clarify the circumstances under which disclosure is appropriate, (2) developing a
definition of severe financial stress and criteria for identifying when governments should disclose their exposure to severe financial stress,
and (3) what information about a government’s exposure to severe financial stress is necessary to disclose. This technical topic is being
examined by the GASB due to a wide diversity in practice regarding required presentation on the face of the financial statements,
disclosures, etc. A preliminary views document on this topic is expected by late 2024 with an exposure draft to follow in 2025.
o
Infrastructure Assets is a project that will address issues related to accounting and financial reporting for infrastructure assets. The project
will evaluate standard-setting options related to reporting infrastructure assets to make information (1) more comparable across
governments and more consistent over time, (2) more useful for making decisions and assessing government accountability, (3) more
relevant to assessments of a government’s economic condition, and (4) better reflect the capacity of those assets to provide service and how
that capacity may change over time. Preliminary views document has been issued with comments due back to GASB by the end of January
2025.
o
Subsequent Events—Reexamination of Statement 56 is a project that will improve the accounting and financial reporting for subsequent
events. The project will reexamine existing requirements related to subsequent events in Statement No. 56, Codification of Accounting and
Financial Reporting Guidance Contained in the AICPA Statements on Auditing Standards, to address issues related to (1) confusion about and
challenges associated with applying the existing standards, (2) inconsistency in practice in the information provided about subsequent
events, and (3) the usefulness of the information provided about subsequent events. Exposure draft on this topic is expected by late 2024.
o
Revenue and Expense Recognition is a major project where the overall objective is to develop a comprehensive, principles-based model
that would establish categorization, recognition, and measurement guidance applicable to a wide range of revenue and expense
transactions. Achieving that objective will include: (1) development of guidance applicable to topics for which existing guidance is limited, (2)
improvement of existing guidance that has been identified as challenging to apply, (3) consideration of a performance obligation approach to
the GASB’s authoritative literature, and (4) assessment of existing and proposed guidance based on the conceptual framework. The expected
outcome of the project is enhanced quality of information that users rely upon in making decisions and assessing accountability. The GASB
is currently reviewing comments and other input received from the stakeholder community during the preliminary views stage that was
completed in 2021. An exposure draft is expected in early 2025.

Community Development/Engineering Director Margie Pozin came forward and

report.

Development & Engineering Department for 2025. She highlighted all the projects
that were completed over the past year, highlighted staff and covered statistics for
department operations.

how rates may be adjusted prior to 2026 tax billing.

Stormwater account on the April 13° consent agenda, and to propose fee increases on
a set incremental basis.
4. SOLID WASTE CONTRACT RENEWAL INCREASE
City Manager James Riker reported that_Republic Services submitted a request fora
2.5% rate adjustment for sanitation services, effective May 1, 2026 in the current
franchise agreement.
Company representative Brad Martin came forward and described some of the unique
circumstances surrounding the rate increase request. Although several inflationary
factors point to a higher percentage, Republic Services is requesting a reduced rate

on Chang vs. Milton. No action taken.

hotel parking deck and is proposing an IGA with DDA for enforcing parking regulations
in the deck.

of the Hill Street parking deck is operated by the Duluth Downtown Development
Authority (DDA). The City desires to enter into an Intergovernmental Agreement (IGA)
with DDA to allow enforcement of parking regulations designed to discourage vehicle
storage in DDA parking deck spaces.

a partnership between the Duluth, Lilburn and Suwanee Police Departments.
Members serve in this role as a collateral duty while remaining employees of their
respective departments and operating under their agency's policies and procedures.

longer used parking spaces, directional parking, handicapped parking and parking 
duration in public spaces. Approval also updates the parking map associated with the 
ordinance.

live and work downtown to use the spaces, but not to be used as storage areas for

downtown.

INTERGOVERNMENTAL AGREMENT 
 
THIS INTERGOVERNMENTAL AGREEMENT, is made this ____ day of 
____________, 2026 by and between THE CITY OF DULUTH, GEORGIA, a body 
corporate and politic and a political subdivision of the State of Georgia, (hereinafter 
referred to as "DULUTH") and THE GWINNETT COUNTY SCHOOL DISTRICT, 
a political subdivision of the State of Georgia (hereinafter referred to as GCSD"). 
WHEREAS, Article IX, Section III, Paragraph I (a) of the Constitution of the State 
of Georgia authorizes, among other things, any county, municipality or other political 
subdivision of the State to contract, for a period not exceeding fifty (50) years with any 
county, municipality or political subdivision or with any other public agency, public 
corporation or public authority, for-joint services, for the provision of services, or for the 
joint or separate use of facilities or equipment, provided that such contract deals with 
activities, services or facilities which the contracting parties are authorized by law to 
undertake or to provide; and 
WHEREAS, Duluth and the GCSD desire to continue the current 
Intergovernmental Agreement to set forth the terms and parameters of a parking use 
agreement on GCSD property within the City of Duluth previously approved on March 8, 
2021; 
NOW THEREFORE, for and in consideration of mutual covenants and promises 
contained herein, the sufficiency of which is acknowledged, and pursuant the authority 
granted to Duluth and the GCSD by the Constitution and laws of the State of Georgia, 
Duluth and GCSD, hereby agree as follows: 
 
 
 

2 
 
AGREEMENT 
I. PURPOSE 
The purpose of this Agreement is to set forth the terms under which parking areas 
owned by GCSD at Brooks Coleman Middle School may be utilized by the public. 
II. SCOPE 
A. The GCSD agrees to allow the public to park on GCSD owned property at Brooks 
Coleman Middle School on Hill Street and State Route 120 as shown in the "subject areas" 
identified on the attached Exhibit “A”, which is incorporated herein by reference. Public 
parking shall be allowed in the subject areas on Saturday and Sunday of each week and 
after 5:00 p.m. each day from Monday through Friday. 
B. Duluth agrees to maintain the existing signs directing the public to parking in the 
subject areas, to maintain the existing trash receptacles and to pay an annual sum to GCSD 
for light usage. 
III. DULUTH RESPONSIBILITIES 
A. Duluth shall be responsible for maintaining the existing signage informing the 
public of the availability of public parking at Brooks Coleman Middle School. Such signs 
shall specify the hours when public parking is allowed and provide notice that alcohol is 
not allowed within the parking areas. 
B. Duluth shall maintain two decorative trash receptacles in the parking lot located 
on the Hill Street subject area and one decorative trash receptacle in the State Road 120 
subject area. Duluth will continue to ensure that the trash receptacles are emptied regularly, 
but not less than once per week. 
C. Duluth will pay the GCSD the sum of One Thousand One Hundred and 00/100 
Dollars ($1,100.00) annually, such sum representing the reasonably agreed upon cost of 
lighting the subject area parking lots past normal school hours and on weekends. 

3 
 
IV. GCSD RESPONSIBILITIES 
A. GCSD shall authorize public parking in the subject ·parking areas at Brooks 
Coleman Middle School located off of Hill Street and off of State Road 120, as shown on 
Exhibit "A” attached hereto. 
B. GCSD will ensure that the lights in the subject parking areas at Brooks Coleman 
Middle School located off of Hill Street and off of State Road 120, as shown on Exhibit 
"A" attached hereto remain on until 11:00 p.m. on Sunday through Thursday and until 1:00 
a.m. on Friday and Saturday. 
V. LEGAL ACTIONS 
Unless otherwise specifically provided herein, nothing in this Intergovernmental 
Agreement is intended to create any rights in any individual, firm, corporation, or entity, 
not a party to this Intergovernmental Agreement. Neither Duluth nor GCSD shall 
indemnify or hold harmless the other party’s agents, officers, servants, vendors and 
employees, past and present, in connection with this Intergovernmental Agreement. Both 
Duluth and GCSD shall assume and defend at their own cost, any suit, action or other legal 
proceeding brought against it arising from any actions taken by the that party's agents, 
officers, servants, vendors, and employees in furtherance of the Project. Nothing herein 
shall be construed to waive sovereign immunity or the immunities of either party. 
VI. TERM & TERMINATION OF AGREEMENT 
A. Term. The term of this Agreement shall be five (5) years commencing upon the 
date of the signature of this Agreement. 
B. This Agreement may be terminated by either party upon ninety days written 
notice of termination by the other party. In the event of termination by GCSD, GCSD shall 
reimburse Duluth the pro-rated amount of any sum paid for lighting of the subject parking 
areas.

Il. DISCUSSION ITEMS/PRESENTATIONS/UPDATES
1. TRAFFIC CALMING UPDATE

Community Development/Engineering Director Margie Pozin came forward as a follow up
to the traffic calming presentation made to Council on February 9th.
The program would be self-enforcing, as a system of physical changes along the road
and signing, marking, that will address people's perception of how fast they're going
and cause them to slow down. There is also a perceived problem in terms of the
pedestrian who's standing still or walking on the sidewalk, and their perception of
speed. Evaluation tools/processes are needed to address complaints and then to
determine if a more advanced study is required for traffic calming measures. Such a
study produces results that that data will confirm or deny that there is a problem.
Every location is unique from the next.
Ms. Pozin displayed a map of the complaints she has directly received. Questions were
raised about evaluating, prioritizing, funding and timeframe. There was also
ambiguity in what type of phased approach would align with citizen satisfaction.
Council and staff agreed on including a $50,000 budget item in the 2027 fiscal year as a
base amount for targeted data collection studies and to begin planning an online
reporting platform.

1. APPROVAL OF ENCROACHMENT – KNOX HOUSE HOLDING 
 
As discussed at the February 2nd work session, Knox House Holding, LLC is extensively 
repairing and adapting the 1908 Knox House with both indoor and outdoor 
improvements for its proposed restaurant site. The improvement requires the 
relocation of an existing water line and valve as well as construction of wall and step 
access in the proposed encroachment area. Planning staff have reviewed and 
approved the construction plans in the encroachment. Approval of this item 
authorizes the Mayor and City Manager to execute the agreement as presented. 
 
2. ORD TO AMEND BUDGET - $27,255.75 – POLICE EQUIPMENT 
 
As discussed at the February 2nd work session, staff presented a proposal 
authorizing the approval of ordinance BA-FY26-27 to amend the FY26 budget for 
police vehicles. Recently, the Police Department sold four (4) vehicles and 
miscellaneous parts at auction, after commission and fees the City received 
$14,659. In addition, the Police Department received an insurance settlement of 
$12,596.75 for a police vehicle that was involved in an accident that our insurance
