Exhibit “D” 
Applicant’s Response to the Standards Governing Special Use Consideration 
 
 
A. How the proposed special use will allow a use that is suitable in view of the use and 
development of adjacent and nearby property. 
 
The proposed gold buying business is suitable for this location, as the suite is within a commercial 
shopping center (Parc Walk at River Green) that already supports retail and service-based 
businesses. A professional gold buying operation aligns with the character of surrounding uses, 
such as retail shops, restaurants, and service providers. It will operate during normal business 
hours and will not generate noise, odors, or other disturbances that would be incompatible with 
nearby tenants or properties. 
 
B. How the proposed special use will adversely affect the existing use or usability of 
adjacent or nearby property. 
 
The business will not adversely affect adjacent or nearby properties. Gold buying is a low-traffic, 
appointment-and walk-in-based service with minimal impact on parking or pedestrian flow. Unlike 
higher-intensity uses such as restaurants or event venues, the business requires only a small 
footprint and a limited number of daily customers. Security measures, including surveillance 
cameras and controlled transactions, will further ensure that the business enhances, rather than 
diminishes, the safety and usability of the area. 
 
C. Whether the property to be affected by a proposed special use has a reasonable 
economic use as currently zoned. 
 
The property is currently zoned for commercial use and is located within a retail/service shopping 
center. The proposed special use is consistent with commercial economic activity and represents a 
reasonable economic use of the property. Without this approval, the space would otherwise remain 
limited to general retail/service uses, many of which are similar in intensity and scale to the 
proposed gold buying business. 
 
D. Whether the proposed special use will result in a use which will or could cause an 
excessive or burdensome use of existing streets, transportation facilities, utilities, or 
schools. 
 
The proposed business will not create an excessive or burdensome demand on streets, utilities, or 
public facilities. Customer traffic is minimal compared to restaurants or retail anchors in the center. 
The business does not impact schools or require additional municipal services beyond standard 
water, power, and internet usage. Waste generation is negligible and limited to standard office 
refuse. 
 
E. Whether the proposed special use is in conformity with the policy and interest of the 
Comprehensive Plan; Land Use Plan; transportation plans and other plans adopted for 
guiding development within the City of Duluth. 
 
The proposed use conforms with the City of Duluth’s Comprehensive Plan and Land Use Plan by 
promoting economic development within an existing commercial corridor along Peachtree 

 
 
SU2025-006 
13 | P a g e 
 
Industrial Boulevard. By occupying a vacant suite and providing a legitimate, regulated business 
service, Gold Max supports the City’s goal of encouraging commercial vitality and ensuring safe, 
transparent economic activity within designated retail centers. 
 
F. Whether there is other existing or changing conditions affecting the use and give grounds 
for either approval or disapproval of the special use. 
 
The economic climate and continued demand for precious metals trading provide grounds for 
approving this special use. Gold buying is a regulated, transparent business model that supports 
consumer choice by offering individuals a safe and professional location to sell gold and jewelry. 
The proposed location is within a secure, high-visibility retail center, which is more suitable than 
unregulated or informal buying/selling arrangements. There are no existing conditions at this site 
that would argue against approval, and approval would enhance the commercial viability of the 
cent by diversifying its tenant mix.

CONSULTANT CONTRACT – MASTER SERVICES AGREEMENT 
BUNTEN PARK IMPROVEMENT PROJECT 
 
This CONTRACT made and entered into this ______ day of , 2025 by and between City of 
Duluth, Georgia, a duly chartered municipal corporation (Party of the First Part, hereinafter called the City), and 
Columbia Engineering & Services, Incorporated, (Party of the Second Part, hereinafter called the Consultant and/or 
the Contractor). 
 
WITNESSETH 
 
WHEREAS, Columbia Engineering & Services, Inc. began work on the Bunten Park Improvement Project under a 
separate Master Services Agreement; and 
 
WHEREAS, Columbia Engineering & Services, Inc.’s separate Master Services Agreement expires on December 
31, 2025; and 
 
WHEREAS, it is in the best interest of the City to contract with Columbia Engineering & Services, Inc. for the 
completion of the Bunten Park Improvement Project, without gap in service and without changing the project scope, 
schedule or professional services contract rates. 
 
NOW, THEREFORE, for and in consideration of the mutual promises and obligations contained herein and under 
the conditions hereinafter set forth, the parties do hereby agree as follows: 
 
1. TERM: 
This contract shall commence on January 1, 2026, for a one-year period with four (4) options to renew for 
additional one-year periods until the completion and acceptance of the construction of the Bunten Park 
Improvement Project. The initial term of this contract shall be through December 31, 2026. The contract shall 
terminate absolutely and without further obligation on the part of the City of Duluth at the end of the first one-
year period, however, this contract may be automatically renewed on an annual basis for additional twelve 
month terms, for a total lifetime contract term of five (5) years, upon the same terms and conditions, as 
provided for in this contract. The contract shall automatically renew annually unless the City provides written 
notice to the Contractor that the renewal shall not occur, not less than ten (10) days prior to the annual 
expiration. This renewal shall occur during the life of the on-going construction of the Bunten Park 
Improvement Project for which Columbia Engineering & Services, Inc. was the designer of record. 
 
2. ATTACHMENTS: 
The Consultant's previous professional services rate sheet (Exhibit A) is attached. The all-inclusive year five 
rates will be used for negotiating task orders throughout the duration of construction. 
 
3. PERFORMANCE AND STANDARD OF CARE: 
Consultant agrees to furnish all skill and labor of every description necessary to carry out and complete in 
good, firm and substantial, workmanlike manner, every task order negotiated as a result of this contract. In 
providing services under this Agreement, the Consultant shall perform in a manner consistent with that 
degree of care and skill ordinarily exercised by members of the same profession currently practicing 
under similar circumstances at the same time and in the same or similar locality. 
 
4. PRICE: 
The fee for all task orders assigned from January 1, 2026 through the end of this contract will be negotiated 
and accepted by the City prior to executing the work. The City agrees to pay the Consultant following receipt 
by the City of a detailed invoice, reflecting the actual work performed by the Consultant. 
 
5. COMPLIANCE WITH IMMIGRATION LAWS AND REGULATIONS: 
5.1 The Contractor shall be responsible for complying with the Georgia Security and Immigration Compliance Act 
of 2006 (O.C.G.A. §§ 13-10-90 & 13-10-91) and the Rules of the Georgia Department of Labor implementing the 
Georgia Security and Immigration Compliance Act of 2006 (Rules 300-10-1-.01 through 300-10-1-.09). In accord 
with these provisions the Contractor shall complete attached Exhibits B and C. 
 
5.2 The Contractor affirms and agrees that it is currently registered and participates in the federal work 
authorization program to verify information of all new employees pursuant to O.C.G.A. § 13-10-91(b). 

 
5.3 The Contractor affirms and agrees that any and all subcontractors that it will use on the above-described 
project are registered and participate in the federal work authorization program to verify information of all new 
employees. 
 
5.4 Pursuant to O.C.G.A. §50-36-1, Contractor shall provide information regarding citizenship status and shall 
complete and file with the City the Citizenship Status Affidavit, which is included in Exhibit D. 
 
5.5 The failure to abide by the provisions and agreements set forth in Subsection 5 shall constitute a breach and 
default of this contract. 
 
 
6. INDEMNIFICATION 
The Consultant agrees, to the fullest extent permitted by law, to indemnify and hold harmless the 
Client, its officers, directors and employees (collectively, Client) against all damages, liabilities or 
costs, including reasonable attorneys’ fees and defense costs, to the extent caused by the Consultant’s 
negligent performance of professional services under this Agreement and that of its subconsultants or 
anyone for whom the Consultant is legally liable. 
 
7. INSURANCE REQUIREMENTS: 
Consultant shall maintain the following insurance (a) comprehensive general liability, including blanket 
contractual, covering bodily injuries with limits of no less than $1,000,000.00 per person and $1,000,000.00 per 
occurrence, and property damage with limits of no less than $1,000,000.00 per occurrence; and (b) statutory 
worker’s compensation insurance, including employer’s liability insurance. In addition to above general 
coverages, consultant shall maintain Professional Liability Insurance with limits of $2,000,000 per occurrence 
and in aggregate. All insurance shall be provided by an insurer(s) acceptable to City, and shall provide for thirty 
(30) days prior notice of cancellation to City. Consultant shall deliver to City a certificate or policy of insurance 
evidencing Consultant’s compliance with this paragraph upon contract execution. Consultant shall abide by all 
terms and conditions of the insurance and shall do nothing to impair or invalidate the coverage. 
 
8. TERMINATION FOR CAUSE: 
The City may terminate this Contract for cause upon ten (10) days prior written notice to the Consultant of the 
Consultant's default in the performance of any term of this Contract. Such termination shall be without 
prejudice to any of the City's rights or remedies provided by law. 
 
9. TERMINATION FOR CONVENIENCE: 
The City may terminate this Contract for its convenience upon 30 days written notice to the Consultant. In the 
event of the City's termination of this Contract for convenience, the Consultant will be paid for those services 
actually performed. Partially completed performance of the Contract will be compensated based upon a signed 
statement of completion to be submitted by the Consultant, which shall itemize each element of performance. 
 
10. CONTRACT NOT TO DISCRIMINATE: 
During the performance of this Contract, the Consultant will not discriminate against any employee or applicant 
for employment because of race, creed, color, sex, national origin, age, or disability, which does not preclude 
the applicant or employee from performing the essential functions of the position. The Consultant will also, in 
all solicitations or advertisements for employees placed by qualified applicants, consider the same without 
regard to race, creed, color, sex, national origin, age, or disability which does not preclude the applicant from 
performing the essential functions of the job. The Consultant will cause the foregoing provisions to be inserted 
in all subcontracts for any work covered by this Contract so that such provision will be binding upon each 
subconsultant, providing that the foregoing provisions shall not apply to contracts or subconsultants for 
standard commercial supplies of raw materials. 
 
11. ASSIGNMENT: 
The Consultant shall not sublet, assign, transfer, pledge, convey, sell or otherwise dispose of the whole or any 
part of this Contract or his right, title, or interest therein to any person, firm, or corporation without the previous 
consent of the City in writing. 
 
12. WAIVER: 
A waiver by either party of any breach of any provision, term, covenant, or condition of this Contract shall not 
be deemed a waiver of any subsequent breach of the same or any other provision, term, covenant, or 
condition. 

 
13. SEVERABILITY: 
The parties agree that each of the provisions included in this Contract is separate, distinct and severable from 
the other and remaining provisions of this Contract, and that the invalidity of any Contract provision shall not 
affect the validity of any other provision or provisions of this Contract. 
 
13. GOVERNING LAW: 
The parties agree that this Contract shall be governed and construed in accordance with the laws of the State 
of Georgia. This Contract has been signed in Gwinnett County, Georgia and venue for any litigation arising out 
of this contract shall be in the Gwinnett County Superior Court. 
 
14. MERGER CLAUSE: 
The parties agree that the terms of this Contract include the entire Contract between the parties, and as such, 
shall exclusively bind the parties. No other representations, either oral or written, may be used to contradict the 
terms of this Contract.

E) for Case SU2025-006. 
 
Margie Pozin, Director of Planning and Engineering presented. Owner Anavah, LLC 
and Applicant Suresh Daswani requested a special use permit to obtain a pawn shop 
license for this location. The property is zoned C-2 (General Business District). The 
portion of the business purchasing gold, silver, and fine metals requires a pawn shop 
license by the State and therefore requires a special use permit to operate in this 
zoning district. 
 
Ms. Pozin showed the map location and explained the surrounding uses. The subject 
property totals approximately 1.34 acres and the square footage of the suite is 1,200 sf. 
The subject property is located in the Peachtree Retail Corridor District. 
FORWARDuluth envisions this Character Area to be an attractive and energized retail 
corridor easily accessed by Duluth residents and non-city residents alike.

fine metals. They also sell gold silver, and other fine metals. It is the purchasing of such 
items that requires, through the state, that they be licensed under a pawnshop. One 
of the conditions requires the business to register with the LEADSOnline program 
that inventories the merchandise into a nationwide database which can be scanned 
for any possible stolen goods.

Mayor Whitlock called the meeting to order at 5:30pm 
 
 
I. 
PUBLIC COMMENTS 
 
None. 
 
 
II. 
DISCUSSION ITEMS/PRESENTATIONS/UPDATES 
 
1. DULUTH ECONOMIC INCENTIVE PROGRAM 
 
 
 
{A} 
 
 
Economic Development Director Chris McGahee came forward to present. He 
explained that staff has researched economic development incentive programs 
throughout the Metropolitan Atlanta region to target specific industries and 
improvement projects in the various character areas as outlined in the Duluth 
Comprehensive Plan (FORWARD Duluth). The incentives would impact permitting 
fees and occupational tax licensing fees for approved projects based upon the level of 
investment and job creation. 
 
To be eligible for any waivers and to determine the exact “tier benefit amount,” the 
companies must define the capital investment, number of full-time jobs that will be 
created and project how many years. 
 
Mr. McGahee explained that Council would look at each defined character area of 
the City and question whether or not there is a certain industry or business type 
they would want to attract, and could then incentivize them to create desired 
change. These types of economic development policies can be crafted to match 
the changing landscape Council wishes to see occur. 
 
 
 

M&C Work Session Draft Notes 
November 24, 2025 
Page 2 of 2 
 
2
City Manager James Riker said that staff could start by considering a few of these 
areas, not all of them at once, and provide some reasons why those areas make 
sense to plan on starting there. These regulations would be designed at the 
discretion of Council. 
 
Staff was authorized to pursue the program further, to redefine and present to 
Council again, and initiate an amendment to the Community Agenda (Comp Plan) to 
correspond with an Economic Incentive Program Ordinance and place both on a 
future work session for discussion. 
 
2. PROPOSED 2026-2027 EVENT CALENDAR 
 
 
 
 
{B} 
 
 
Events Coordinator Jessica Gross came forward to present the proposed 2026-2027 
event calendar. She first highlighted the 2025 events and explained any challenges or 
recommended changes to those programs. 
 
In summary, changes are proposed for food truck nights, expanding Multi-cultural 
night to a weeklong event, and discontinuing Haunted Tours and Good Word Les 
Bon festival. Presentation attached for reference. 
 
After discussion, Staff was asked to make small reductions in several events to 
compensate for the anticipated increase to Howl on the Green and the one-time 
events for centennial celebrations, which will be discussed further during budget 
preparations.

Owner Young Yee Woo and Applicant Robert L. Fouse are requesting a special use 
permit to operate a personal care home in this location. The property is zoned R-75 
(single family district), which requires a special-use permit for the operation of a

Deputy Director of Community Development Aron Hall came forward to present. He 
showed a site plan of the location and described the surrounding uses. The subject 
property is located in the Established Neighborhoods District. FORWARDuluth 
envisions this Character Area to serve as the backbone of Duluth’s residential 
community. The Future Land Use Map (FLUM) envisions the uses to be low density 
residential. 
 
Under a personal care home: 
 
• 
This would allow up to six people to be under care. 
• 
Personal care homes are regulated by the Department of Community Health in 
the State of Georgia. 
• 
They are inspected annually. 
• 
There will be a 24-hour full time caregiver on site. 
• 
Doctors make house calls, but there is transportation provided. 
• 
The City owns property to the south and west. 
• 
The property has a two-car garage, a large parking pad, and a long driveway 
(`218’).

Mr. Hall reiterated the six standards governing the special use consideration. They are: 
how the proposed special use will allow a use that is suitable in the view of the use of 
adjacent and nearby properties; how the proposed special use will adversely affect 
the existing use or usability of adjacent or nearby property; whether the property to 
be affected by a proposed special use has a reasonable economic use as currently 
zoned, whether the proposed special use will result in a use which will or could cause 
an excessive or burdensome use of existing streets. Transportation facilities, utilities, 
or schools and whether the proposed special use is in conformity with the policy and 
interest of the comprehensive plan, land use plan, transportation plans, and other 
plans adopted for guiding development within the city of Duluth. Lastly, whether 
there are other existing or changing conditions affecting the use and give grounds for 
either approval or disapproval of this special use. 
 
Mr. Hall detailed each of the proposed conditions. Planning Commission 
recommended approval (4-1) at their September 15, 2025 hearing. 
 
Mayor Whitlock called for discussion from Council. 
 
Questions were raised regarding the definition of personal care home, what staff 
recommendation was for this case and the timing of the approval. 
 
Mr. Hall said that the applicant could give the state definition; staff findings did not 
present an issue with the request, and the date of approval starts the 90 day period 
for the applicant to begin operations. 
 
Mayor Whitlock called the applicant forward. 
 
Mr. Robert Faust of 136 Summer Drive, Atlanta GA came forward representing the 
applicant to address questions from the Mayor and Council. He complimented staff 
and the Planning Commission. He noted that their application illustrates that they are 
consistent with the guidelines and parameters for minimal impact on the 
surrounding properties. He said that personal care is defined in the state of Georgia 
by the department of community health as a facility that participates both in room 
and board housing, for persons of not necessarily an age, but about 98% of residents 
of this type of housing in the state of Georgia are seniors in age. There are occasions 
where a younger person with another type of condition that might cause this housing 
to be appropriate for them, but the specific language of the department of 
community health involves “activities of daily living.” 
 
In addition to just room and board, residents of this housing option are receiving 
levels of care identified by the department of community health as activities of daily 
living. Within the state of Georgia there is a limitation of six occupants eligible to live 
in a community of this kind within this zoning designation. 
 
 
Mr. Faust addressed the 90 day limit and said the City’s approval is a requirement of 
their application to the state of Georgia for their approval. It typically takes less than 
90 days but there is a very rigid procedure that the state follows before a license is 
issued. A staff person must be living in that house before residents are invited to move 
in, the pantry has to be full of food, and all of the facilities have to be in place to

2. AMEND DULUTH CODE – CHAPTER 8 - SECTION 8-68 PARKING 
 
Chief Carruth came forward to discuss proposed additions to the City of Duluth parking 
ordinance (8-68) in order to enhance enforcement, clarify existing regulations, and reflect 
current community needs. The additions include code sections for handicapped parking 
violations; parking opposite of traffic violations; and abandoned vehicles parked on city 
property. 
 
Staff also discussed implementing 48 hour parking restrictions to prohibit public spaces 
from being used as storage areas or for other undesirable uses. The intent is to ensure the 
downtown spaces provide frequent turnover for availability. Currently, cars parking in 
spots over 5 days are considered “abandoned” and can be ticketed at that point. This 
reduction to 2 days may also help the Charleston Bay neighborhood with their parking 
complaints. 
 
Staff also mentioned that, in the hotel parking lot, some cars are left for 30-60 days. There 
was also discussion on catering vehicles for the downtown businesses and perhaps some 
type of permitting for those, since they have no other options than to utilize public city 
parking.

was authorized to place this item on the December consent agenda for approval.

The Alcohol Review Board met with staff and the City Attorney on September 17th to 
discuss recommended amendments to the City's Code of Ordinances, Chapter 3 -

changes. The policy changes match the current state laws/regulations, assist with 
administrative/governmental operations, and /or change any older policies that are no 
longer applicable or feasible. Following review and discussion, the Alcohol Board voted 
unanimously to recommend approval of the amendments as discussed.

I. 
PURPOSE AND DESCRIPTION OF THE REQUEST 
The purpose of this Special Use request (SU2025-005) is to allow for a Fitness Center/Health 
Club in CBD (Central Business District). 
Maps detailing the location, zoning district and character area of the subject property are 
attached hereto as Exhibit “A”. The legal description of the subject property is attached 
hereto as Exhibit “B”. Recommended conditions of approval are detailed in Exhibit “C”. The 
Applicant’s Response to the Standards Governing Special Use Consideration can be found in 
Exhibit “D”, and the Public Notice is found in Exhibit “F.” 
 
II. 
EXISTING CONDITIONS 
 
The subject property totals +/- .37 acres. What is known as the “Thrive Building” is a three-
story building with two-stories facing Main Street and a basement level in the rear facing the 
Railroad tracks. On the Main Street side, there is a coffee shop and the Thrive Coworking 
space. The applicant is proposing a fitness center/ health club for children from toddler age 
to age 12 on the daylit basement level. The interior finish would occupy 4,000 square feet, 
which is the entire basement level of Thrive. The property is within the CBD (Central 
Business District) and is surrounded by CBD (Central Business District) save for the railroad 
tracks, which are zoned M-1 (Light Industrial District). Beyond the railroad is HC-R (Highway 
Commercial – Retail District). 
 
 
III. 
REVIEW OF THE REQUEST 
 
1. 
Literal Interpretation of the Unified Development Code (UDC) 
 
A. Table 2-C of the UDC allows “Fitness Centers/Health Clubs” in CBD (Central Business 
District) as a special use. 
 
B. Section 1101.02 of the UDC states if a proposed use is not allowed by right under the 
existing zoning on a property, a request for an amendment to the Official Zoning 
Map (often called a “rezoning”) must be approved prior to development, 
construction, or occupancy. 
 
C. Section 1105 of the UDC establishes the Special Use Considerations. 
 
The Special Use is designed to apply under any one of the following circumstances: 
1. A Special Use listed under the zoning district is desired for development and a 
more intensive zoning district containing that use, as a use by right would not be 
appropriate for the property; or 
 
2. A Special Use listed under the zoning district is desired for development and no 
zoning district contains that use as a use by right; or 
 
3. A unique use not addressed in any zoning district is desired for development and 
is not likely to be duplicated within the City of Duluth; or 
 
4. The density of development may be affected by the height of a building; or 
 
5. The neighboring properties may be affected by the height of any structure; or 

 
 
SU2025-005 
3 | P a g e 
 
 
6. The Special Use would be consistent with the needs of the neighborhood or the 
community as a whole, be compatible with the neighborhood and would not be 
in conflict with the overall objective of the Comprehensive Plan. 
 
In order to accommodate these particular uses, Special Use approval allows the City Council 
to approve such a use on a particular parcel without changing the general zoning district. 
Such approval shall be subject to the requirements set forth below and any additional 
conditions deemed necessary to ensure the compatibility of the Special Use with the 
surrounding properties. All Special Use applications shall be for firm development 
proposals only. The Special Use shall not be used for securing early zoning for conceptual 
proposals that may not be undertaken for some time. A Special Use application shall be 
considered only if the application is made by the owner of the property or by his/her 
authorized agent. The minimum requirements for a Special Use approval are: 
1. Any uses allowed under Special Use approval shall also conform to the 
requirements of this Development Code for all uses as found in the zoning 
district. 
 
2. The application and review process for a Special Use shall be the same as for the 
zoning district under which the Special Use is found. In addition to the 
information and/or site plans which are required to be submitted for the 
proposed development, additional information deemed necessary by the 
Director in order to evaluate a proposed use and its relationship to the 
surrounding area shall be submitted. In the review process, particular emphasis 
shall be given to the evaluation of the characteristics of the proposed use in 
relationship to its immediate neighborhood and the compatibility of the 
proposed use with its neighborhood. 
 
3. In the approval process for a Special Use approval application, the City Council 
shall consider the policies and objectives of the Comprehensive Plan, particularly 
in relationship to the proposed site and surrounding area and shall consider the 
potential adverse impacts on the surrounding area, especially in regards but not 
limited to traffic, storm drainage, land values and compatibility of land use 
activities. 
 
4. If an application is approved and a Special Use approval is granted, all conditions 
that may have been attached to the approval are binding to the property. All 
subsequent development and use of the property shall be in accordance with the 
approved plan and conditions. 
 
5. Changes to a Special Use or development of a site for the Special Use, shall be 
treated as an amendment to the Special Use Permit and shall be subject to the 
same application and review process as a new application. 
 
6. An application for Special Use approval in a residential district and which use is 
proposed to operate in a dwelling or as an accessory use to a dwelling is subject 
to the following additional requirements: 
 
a. The Special Use shall operate within the dwelling on the property or, if 
approved by the City Council, in an accessory structure. 
 

 
 
SU2025-005 
4 | P a g e 
 
b. The exterior character of the dwelling shall be preserved in its residential 
state and there shall be no outside evidence of the operation of a Special Use 
to the neighborhood, except for any accessory structure approved by the City 
Council. 
 
7. The owner of the property approved for a Special Use may voluntarily request 
termination of the Special Use by notifying the Director in writing. The Director 
shall notify the City Council through the Planning Commission of the voluntary 
termination. The approval of a Special Use for a specific use which may be 
operated by a lessee under a private agreement with a lessor in any non-
residential district shall not obligate the City Council to be responsible for or be 
required to resolve any disputes which may arise out of the voluntary 
termination of the Special Use by the property owner. 
 
8. The Community Development and Engineering Department shall have the right 
to periodically examine the operation of the specific use to determine 
compliance with the requirements and any conditions. If the Director 
determines that the requirements and conditions are being violated, a written 
notice shall be issued to the owner of the property outlining the nature of the 
violation and giving the owner of the property a maximum of ten days to come 
into compliance. If after ten days the violations continue to exist, the Director 
shall forward a report to the City Council through the Planning Commission who 
may recommend that action be taken to remove the Special Use from the 
property. 
 
9. Upon approval by the City Council, a Special Use shall be identified on the official 
zoning maps. 
 
10. Upon approval by the City Council of a Special Use, the owner of the property 
shall be issued a notice from the Director that states the specific use permitted, 
the requirements of this Section and any conditions attached to the approval. 
 
11. The Community Development and Engineering Department shall not issue a 
Certificate of Occupancy for the specific use unless all requirements and 
conditions of the Special Use approval have been fulfilled by the owner of the 
property. 
 
2. 
Standards Governing the Exercise of Zoning Power 
 
Section 1104.02 of the UDC establishes the standards governing the exercise of zoning 
power. The following standards are relevant in balancing the interest and promoting 
the public health, safety, morality, and general welfare against the right to the 
unrestricted use of property: 
A. 
How the proposed Special Use will permit a use that is suitable in view of the 
use and development of adjacent and nearby property. 
 
B. 
How the proposed Special Use will adversely affect the existing use or usability 
of adjacent or nearby property. 
 
C. 
Whether the property to be affected by a proposed Special Use has a reasonable 
economic use as currently zoned. 

 
 
SU2025-005 
5 | P a g e 
 
 
D. 
Whether the proposed Special Use will result in a use which will or could cause 
an excessive or burdensome use of existing streets, transportation facilities, 
utilities, or schools. 
 
E. 
Whether the proposed Special Use is in conformity with the policy and interest 
of the Comprehensive Plan; Land Use Plan; transportation plans and other plans 
adopted for guiding development within the City of Duluth. 
 
F. 
Whether there are other existing or changing conditions affecting the use and 
give grounds for either approval or disapproval of the Special Use. 
 
The Applicant has provided written responses to the above Special Use standards as 
part of the application. That document is attached hereto as Exhibit “D”. 
 
3. 
Literal Interpretation of FORWARDuluth, Plan 2045 (Comprehensive Plan) 
 
The subject property is located in the Downtown Core District. FORWARDuluth 
envisions this Character Area to serve as the cultural and entertainment heart of the 
City and region. The Future Land Use Map (FLUM) envisions the uses to be 
commercial/retail/office. 
 
IV. 
PLANNING STAFF REVIEW 
 
The “Thrive Building” obtained its Certificate of Occupancy (CO) in 2024 and quickly filled 
the co-working office spaces. Land of a Thousand Hills Coffee opened in 2025. There remains 
two vacant suites in the Thrive Building. One on Main Street and one in the walk-out 
basement perpendicular to the railroad tracks. With an entrance at the rear of the building 
off of main street, there is very limited visibility for a viable commercial space. A facility such 
as the one being proposed is a destination that does not rely on foot traffic, but advertising, 
word of mouth and is membership based – making it an ideal tenant for the space they are 
proposing to occupy. 
 
Except for City Hall, all buildings in the CBD (Central Business District) are zero lot lines. The 
City owns and maintains all of the parking downtown. Though not dedicated to this space, 
there are 37 parking spaces right outside the doors of this suite. 
 
The Little Gym is a franchise that, according to the website, opened in 1976 in Bellevue, 
Washington with the owner’s mission to create a “nurturing place where children could 
explore their physical development, while also growing socially, emotionally, and 
intellectually.” 
 
The gym would occupy 4,000 square feet, which is the entire basement suite of the “Thrive 
Building.” The Little Gym has several different class offerings from Parent/Child classes (4 
months – 3 Years Old), Pre-K Gymnastics (3-6 Years Old), Grade School Gymnastics (6-12 
Years Old) and Dance (3-12 Years Old). For children under 3, a parent (or caregiver) must 
participate in the class. For children 3 and up, parents are invited to watch class from the 
lobby. The class model is 10-15 kids per session. Therefore, parking will be dictated by class 
attendance and teachers and overlap would be minimal. 
 

 
 
SU2025-005 
6 | P a g e 
 
Although Thrive co-working is open to its members 24 hours a day/7 days a week, it is only 
open to the public and staffed from 9-5 Monday-Friday. Therefore, the demand for parking is 
less on the weekend. The “Thrive Building” is toward the south end of downtown. With City 
Hall closed on the weekends and limited hours at the library on Sunday, there is limited foot 
traffic this far south in the downtown core. The addition of the Little Gym, has the potential 
to bring additional foot traffic to this part of downtown, which could activate the Land of a 
Thousand Hills Coffee shop on days when Thrive Co-working is it its lowest occupancy as the 
current hours of Land of a Thousand Hills Coffee are 8:30 am -9:30 pm on Saturday and 9:00 
am – 6:00 pm on Sunday. 
 
V. Recommendation

1. ORDINANCE OF SPECIAL USE-CASE SU2025-005 - LITTLE GYM {H}
Mayor Whitlock opened the public hearing to consider an ordinance to allow a special
use permit on parcel R6293 039 located at 3176 Main Street (lower level of the Thrive
building) for case SU2025-005.
Community Development/Engineering Director Margie Pozin came forward to explain
the request from owner Alan Solon and Applicant Melissa Mitchell for a special use
permit to operate a fitness center/health club in this location. The property is zoned
CBD (central business district), which requires a special use permit for the operation of
a fitness center/health club. They plan to lease the lower level basement of the Thrive
Building, which is about 4,000 square feet. The surrounding zoning is Central Business
District with the exception of the railroad, which is light industrial. Located in the
character area called the downtown core, which is intended to be the cultural
entertainment heart of our city, the future land use map envisions this to be
commercial retail office.
Ms. Pozin said the business will cater to four-month to 12-year-old children, and the
location is more of a destination rather than a walk-by use, which staff feels is
beneficial. While parents are here during weekday and weekend hours, they would
likely support other downtown businesses.
The Planning Commission recommended approval at their October 6, 2025 hearing.
Mayor Whitlock called for discussion from Council.
Councilmember Harkness asked what staff's recommendation was, and if there was
adequate parking.
Ms. Pozin replied that staff had not provided one but would recommend approval and
did feel that parking was sufficient.
Councilmember Graeder questioned the conditions, as the timeframe in the printed
ordinance seemed different from the power point presentation.

2. AMEND DULUTH CODE – CH 8-68 PARKING 
 
SUMMARY: 
Staff is proposing additions to the City of Duluth parking ordinance (8-68) to enhance 
enforcement, clarify existing regulations, and reflect current community needs. The 
additions include a code section for handicapped parking violations; parking opposite 
of traffic violations; and abandoned vehicles parked on city property. 
 
IMPACT TO BUDGET: N/A 
 
3. ALCOHOL ORDINANCE AMENDMENTS 
 
SUMMARY: 
The Alcohol Review Board met with staff and the City Attorney on September 17th to 
discuss recommended amendments to the City's Code of Ordinances, Chapter 3 - 
Alcoholic Beverages. The proposed amendments consist of Housekeeping and Policy 
Changes: The policy changes match the current state laws/regulations, assist with 
administrative/governmental operations, and /or change any older policies that are no 
longer applicable or feasible. Following review and discussion, the Board voted 
unanimously to recommend approval of the amendments as discussed. 
 
IMPACT TO BUDGET: N/A 
 
4. HEALTH DEPARTMENT ORDINANCE AMENDMENTS 
 
SUMMARY: 
At the request of Gwinnett County Health Department, staff recommends 
approval of amendments to Chapter 5 and Chapter 7 of the Duluth Code in the 
best interest of public health. The changes are necessary to update regulations 
and clarify the authority for enforcement in the following areas: Tattoo and Body 
Piercing establishments, Swimming Pools, Tourist Accommodations, On-site 
Sewage Management, and Food Service. 
 
IMPACT TO BUDGET: N/A 
 
5. STORMWATER UPDATE 
 
Stormwater team members will update Mayor and Council on recent projects and will 
be available to answer questions.

ORDINANCE TO AMEND DULUTH CODE 
WHEREAS, the Mayor and Council of the City of Duluth desire to make various changes to 
Chapter 3 of the City of Duluth Code of Ordinances regarding the licensing and permitting 
of alcohol sales and handling; 
NOW THEREFORE, the Mayor and Council of the City of Duluth hereby ordains that the 
Code be amended as follows: 
PART I 
The Council of the City of Duluth hereby further ordains that the Duluth Code of 
Ordinances is hereby amended by deleting in its entirety Sec. 3-100, Article I, Chapter 3 of 
the Duluth Code of Ordinances and replacing same with a new Sec. 3-100, Article I, Chapter 
3 to read as follows: 
Sec. 3-100. Purpose. 
This article chapter has been enacted for the purposes, among others, of promoting the 
health and general welfare of the community, to establish reasonable and ascertainable 
standards for the regulation and control for the licensing and sales of alcoholic beverages 
and retail package alcohol; to protect and preserve schools and churches; to give effect to 
existing land use; and to preserve certain residential areas, with reasonable considerations, 
among others, to the character of the areas and their peculiar suitability for particular uses, 
the congestion in the roads and streets, and with a general view of promoting desirable 
living conditions and sustaining the stability of neighborhoods and property values; to 
protect against the evils of concentration of the retail outlets for liquor in one (1) family 
and/or in one (1) corporation; and to prevent undesirable persons in engaging in or having 
any interest in alcoholic beverages. 
PART II 
The Council of the City of Duluth hereby further ordains that the Duluth Code of 
Ordinances is hereby amended by deleting in its entirety Sec. 3-101, Article I, Chapter 3 of 
the Duluth Code of Ordinances and replacing same with a new Sec. 3-101, Article I, Chapter 
3 to read as follows: 
Sec. 3-101. Sales to be licensed; compliance with ordinance and state law required. 
It shall be unlawful for any person to sell or offer for sale at wholesale or retail any 
alcoholic beverages, or to offer for sale for consumption on the premises, or to offer free of 
charge as a promotional activity or incentive any alcoholic beverages within the city 
without having first complied with the provisions of this article chapter. No person shall 
sell or possess for the purpose of sale any alcoholic beverage unless such person has a 
license from the city to sell or possess for sale alcoholic beverages, or sell or make

and restrictions contained in O.C.G.A., Title 3, and regulations promulgated there under,

ORDINANCE 
TO AMEND DULUTH CODE – HEALTH AND SANITATION 
 
WHEREAS, 
 The City of Duluth Mayor and Council desire to clarify and specifically designate that certain 
regulatory rule making, and enforcement falls to the Gwinnett County Board of 
Commissioners and the Gwinnett County Health Department; and 
 
WHEREAS The City of Duluth Mayor and Council desire to comport its Code with those set 
forth in the Gwinnett County Code and other applicable State laws regulating health and 
safety. 
 
NOW THEREFORE, The City of Duluth ordains as follows: 
 
PART I: 
 
The Council of the City of Duluth hereby ordains that the Duluth Code of Ordinances is hereby 
amended by deleting in its entirety Article XVIII of Chapter 7 of the Code, and replacing 
Article XVIII of Chapter 7 as follows: 
 
ARTICLE XVIII. – TATTOO AND BODY PIERCING ESTABLISHMENTS 
Sec. 7-750 
 
(a) The regulations of the Gwinnett County Board of Health, adopted by resolution February 
12, 2024, based upon rules of the Georgia Department of Public Health, as referenced in 
chapter 511-3-8, as now or hereafter amended, and having been adopted by resolution of 
the board of commissioners on May 14, 2024, as the health regulations governing body art 
studios for the county are made a part of this Code as though fully set out at length in this 
section. Copies of the body art regulations are on file in the office of the clerk of the Gwinnett 
County Board of Commissioners. 
 
(b) The Gwinnett County Health Department is designated as the enforcement authority for 
this 
 ordinance. 
 
PART II: 
The Council of the City of Duluth hereby further ordains that the Duluth Code of Ordinances 
is hereby amended by deleting in its entirety Section 5-61.5 of Article III, Chapter 5 of the 
Code, and replacing Section 5-61.5 of Article III, Chapter 5 of the Code as follows: 
 
Sec. 5-61.5. – Swimming pool code. 
 
(a) The regulations of the Gwinnett County Board of Health, adopted by resolution April 9, 
2018, containing sections 1 through 26, as now or hereafter amended, and having been 

2 
 
adopted by ordinance of the board of commissioners on May 14, 2024, as the health 
regulations governing public swimming pools, spas and recreational water parks are made 
a part of this Code as though fully set out at length in this section. Copies of the regulations 
are on file in the office of the clerk of the Gwinnett County Board of Commissioners. 
 
(b) The Gwinnett County Health Department is designated as the enforcement authority for 
this ordinance. 
 
 
PART III: 
 
The Council of the City of Duluth hereby further ordains that the Duluth Code of Ordinances 
is hereby amended by adopting a new Article XI of Chapter 7 of the Code to read as follows: 
 
ARTICLE XI: Tourist Accommodations 
Sec. 7-370 Tourist Accommodations. 
 
(a) The regulations of the Gwinnett County Board of Health, adopted by resolution February 
12, 2024, based upon rules of the Georgia Department of Public Health, as referenced in 
chapter 511-6-2, as now or hereafter amended, and having been adopted by resolution of 
the Gwinnett County Board of Commissioners on May 14, 2024, as the health regulations 
governing tourist accommodations for the county are made a part of this Code as though 
fully set out at length in this section. Copies of the tourist accommodations regulations are 
on file in the office of the clerk of the Gwinnett County Board of Commissioners. 
 
(b) The Gwinnett County Health Department is designated as the enforcement authority for 
this 
 ordinance. 
 
 
PART IV: 
 
The Council of the City of Duluth hereby further ordains that the Duluth Code of Ordinances 
is hereby amended by adopting a new code Section 5-73 of Article III of the Code to read as 
follows: 
 
Sec. 5-73. On-site sewage management systems. 
 
(a) Rules and regulations of the state department of public health; adopted. The regulations of 
the Gwinnett County Board of Health, adopted by resolution February 12, 2024, based upon 
rules of the Georgia Department of Public Health, as referenced in chapter 511-3-1, as now 
or hereafter amended, as now or hereafter amended, and having been adopted by resolution 
of the Gwinnett County Board of Commissioners on May 14, 2024, as the health regulations 
governing on-site sewage management systems for the county are made a part of this Code 

3 
 
as though fully set out at length in this section. Copies of the on-site sewage management 
systems regulations are on file in the office of the clerk of the Gwinnett County Board of 
Commissioners. 
 
(b) Rules and regulations of the state department of public health; enforcement. 
 
(1) The rules and regulations cited in subsection (a) of this section shall be enforced 
by the Gwinnett County Board of Health as a duly adopted ordinance of the City of 
Duluth. 
 
(2) Violations of this section may be prosecuted upon citations issued by officers of 
the Gwinnett County Police Department, the Gwinnett County Department of Water 
Resources, or by designated employees of the Gwinnett County Board of Health. Any 
person violating any provision in these regulations shall be guilty of violating a duly 
adopted ordinance of the county, and upon conviction by a court of competent 
jurisdiction shall be punished either by a fine not to exceed $1,000.00, or by 
confinement in the county jail for a total term not to exceed 60 days, or both. The 
court shall have the power and authority to place any person found guilty of a 
violation of this regulation on probation and to suspend or modify any fine or 
sentence. As a condition of such suspension, the court may require payment of 
restitution or impose other punishment allowed by law. 
 
(c) New community sewage treatment systems prohibited. 
 
(1) A community sewage treatment system shall mean a privately owned sewage 
treatment system which collects sewage from two or more residents or other 
establishments, and which may consist of collector lines, pumps, sewage tanks and/or 
soil treatment units. Community sewage treatment systems are characterized by 
having relatively few residents or establishments which contribute flow and are not 
staffed by qualified operators licensed by the state 24 hours a day, seven days a week. 
 
(2) New community sewage treatment systems are prohibited in the county, 
notwithstanding any and all provisions of Ga. Comp. R. & Regs., chapter 511-3-1 that 
may otherwise allow such systems to be permitted. 
 
(3) Upon the effective date of the ordinance from which this section is derived, no 
new community sewage treatment facilities that may be permitted in any 
municipality in the county shall be permitted to send sewage flows to the POTW. 
 
(d) Authority to disconnect water service. 
 
(1) The director of the county department of water resources (DWR director) or the 
DWR director's designee is authorized to disconnect water service from any property 
where a pattern of repeated refusal to repair a failed septic tank system has resulted 
in harm to public health, safety, welfare, the environment or the public interest, as set 
forth herein. Three bacteriological tests showing 200 or more colony forming units of 

4 
 
fecal coliform bacteria taken from affected surface water shall be presumptive 
evidence of harm to public health, safety, welfare, the environment or the public 
interest. 
 
(2) The DWR director or designee is authorized to work with the county health 
department, an agency of the state, to coordinate measures to protect public health, 
safety, welfare, the environment or the public interest from contamination caused by 
failed septic tanks. 
 
(3) The DWR director or designee is directed to work with the county health 
department and with the owners of property affected by failed septic tanks to repair 
the maximum possible number of such systems, giving due regard to protecting 
health, safety, welfare, the environment or the public interest. 
 
(4) Upon following the notification procedures established by the county health 
department directing a property owner of the need to repair a failed septic tank 
system, the DWR director or designee is authorized to disconnect water service 
connected to that failing septic tank system whether or not the property owner has 
paid any civil penalties or whether or not the property owner or occupant is current 
with any bills from the water and sewer utility. 
 
(e) The Gwinnett County Health Department is designated as the enforcement authority for 
this ordinance. 
 
 
PART V: 
 
The Council of the City of Duluth hereby further ordains that the Duluth Code of Ordinances 
is hereby amended by deleting in its entirety Article XVII of Chapter 7 of the Code, and 
replacing Article XVII of Chapter 7 as follows: 
 
ARTICLE XVII- FOOD SERVICE 
 
Sec. 7-730 – Food Service 
 
(a) The regulations of the Gwinnett County Board of Health, adopted by resolution February 
12, 2024, based upon rules of the Georgia Department of Public Health, as referenced in 
chapter 511-6-1, as now or hereafter amended, and having been adopted by resolution of 
the Gwinnett County Board of Commissioners on May 14, 2024, as the health regulations 
governing food service for the county are made a part of this Code as though fully set out at 
length in this section. Copies of the food service regulations are on file in the office of the 
clerk of the Gwinnett County Board of Commissioners. 
 
(b) The Gwinnett County Health Department is designated as the enforcement authority for 
this ordinance.

8 - SECTION
8- 68 PARKING
Chief Carruth came forward to discuss proposed additions to the City of Duluth parking
ordinance (8-68) in order to enhance enforcement, clarify existing regulations, and reflect
current community needs. The additions include code sections for handicapped parking
violations; parking opposite of traffic violations; and abandoned vehicles parked on city
property.
Staff also discussed implementing
48 hour parking restrictions to prohibit public spaces
from being used as storage areas or for other undesirable uses. The intent is to ensure the
downtown spaces provide frequent turnover for availability. Currently, cars parking in
spots over 5 days are considered " abandoned" and can be ticketed at that point. This
reduction to 2 days may also help the Charleston Bay neighborhood with their parking
complaints.
Staff also mentioned that, in the hotel parking lot, some cars are left for 30- 60 days. There
was also discussion on catering vehicles for the downtown
businesses and perhaps some
type of permitting for those, since they have no other options than to utilize public city
parking.
Staff was asked to review all the variables and make recommended amendments, and
was authorized to place this item on the December consent agenda for approval.
3. ALCOHOL
ORDINANCE
AMENDMENTS
The Alcohol Review Board met with staff and the City Attorney on September 17th to
discuss recommended amendments to the City's Code of Ordinances, Chapter 3 -
Alcoholic Beverages. The proposed amendments consist of housekeeping and policy
changes. The policy changes match the current state laws/ regulations, assist with
administrative/ governmental
operations, and / or change any older policies that are no
longer applicable or feasible. Following review and discussion, the Alcohol Board voted
unanimously to recommend approval of the amendments as discussed.
City Attorney Stephen Pereira mentioned that Council was provided the full presentation
for review. He highlighted several of the " policy" changes for council comment, such as
Sunday sales on New Year' s Eve, Handling permit fees and repeat training requirements,
indoor commercial recreation changes, and changes to the catering permit policies to
strike out overly restrictive
requirements.
Staff was authorized to place this item on the next Council agenda for approval.
4. HEALTH DEPARTMENT ORDINANCE AMENDMENTS
At the request of Gwinnett County Health Department, staff recommended approval
of amendments
to Chapter 5 and Chapter 7 of the Duluth Code. The changes are
necessary to update regulations and clarify the authority for enforcement in the
following areas: Tattoo and Body Piercing establishments, Swimming Pools, Tourist
Accommodations, On- site Sewage Management, and Food Service.

1. BUFORD HWY DECORATIVE CROSSWALKS/ORD TO AMEND BUDGET 
 
At the October 28, 2024 work session, Mayor and Council discussed and approved 
the addition of decorative crosswalks on Buford Highway at SR 120 and at Brock 
Road. Staff lined up a contractor who agreed to hold his prices until the City was 
ready to begin construction. StreetScapes is ready to begin work upon contract 
execution and Notice to Proceed. Therefore, approval of this item authorizes staff 
to contract with StreetScapes in the amount of $109,791 to complete both 
crosswalks. In addition, staff recommends a contingency of $20,209, a new 
handicap ramp at Brock Road in the amount of $1500 (to be completed by a third 
party), and $2500 in construction oversight for a total budget amendment (BA-FY-
13) request of $134,000 in 2023 SPLOST Transportation Funds to (CD-65) Buford 
Highway - Transfer from SPLOST 2023 line item and $2,500 to Buford Highway - 
Sidewalks & Crosswalks - Professional Services line item and $131,500 to Buford 
Highway - Sidewalks & Crosswalks - Site Improvements line item, including 
associated transfers.

Owner Young Yee Woo and Applicant Robert L. Fouse are requesting a special use 
permit to operate a personal care home in this location. The property is zoned R-
75 (single family district), which requires a special-use permit for the operation of a 
personal care home.

2. ORDINANCE TO AMEND COMPREHENSIVE PLAN – TA2025-005 
 
Mayor and Council to consider amendments to the FORWARDuluth 2045 
Comprehensive Plan. Staff felt it necessary to update the Hudgens Small Area 
Plan to better address current needs of the community. In addition, Council 
recently approved the R-50 zoning category, which requires an update to the 
comprehensive plan. 
 
The Planning Commission recommended approval of the text amendments at 
their October 6, 2025 hearing. Ordinance is attached for reference. 
 
 
VII. 
NEW BUSINESS 
 
1. AWARD OF BID/ORD TO AMEND BUDGET – PUBLIC SAFETY ROOF 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The roof system at the Public Safety Building is original to the building and circa 
2006. Accordingly, staff published a Request for Proposal (RFP) for replacement of 
the roof. Staff received four proposals and following an evaluation by an outside 
consultant, staff is recommending that the contract be awarded to CGS LLC, 
in the amount of $ 108,329.21. Given the complexity of the roof, staff is also 
recommending a 20% contingency be added for a total request of $ 130,000. 
 
Additionally, staff is requesting approval of a budget amendment BA-FY26-11 to 
add $130,000 in unallocated 2023 SPLOST Public Safety funds to Police Capital 
Projects - Police - Buildings line item, including associated transfers. 
 
2. AWARD OF BID – SUNRISE RETAINING WALL 
 
 
 
Several months ago, code compliance noticed the existing railroad tie retaining 
wall on Sunrise Lane in the Chattahoochee Hills Subdivision was in need of repairs. 
The HOA contacted us to assist in determining ownership of the wall. The wall 
was built on the right of way line, and it is likely to have tie back anchors that 
protrude into the right-of-way itself. Therefore, the City is taking ownership of and 
replacing the wall. 
 
Repairs to a wall of this age and type were determined not to be cost effective. 
Three bids were received to replace the existing wall with an engineered modular 
concrete block wall. This includes removal of the existing wall, removal of any 
trees that have grown near or into the wall, construction of the new wall, 
restoration/stabilization of the roadway shoulder, and the planting of bushes along 
the top of the wall to act as an edge barrier. The three trees removed for 
construction will be replaced.

contractor's use. 
 
The following bids were received: 
 
IP Construction $34,500.00 
Triscapes $35,385.00 
Zaveri Enterprises, Inc. $76,300.00 
 
Staff recommends awarding a contract in the amount of $34,500.00 to IP 
Construction. 
 
3. ORDINANCE TO AMEND BUDGET - $44,850 – SUNRISE RETAINING WALL 
 
Mayor and Council to consider a budget amendment for the retaining wall 
replacement on Sunrise Lane in the Chattahoochee Hill Subdivision. 
 
With a contract award to IP Construction in the amount of $34,500, staff request 
approval of a budget amendment BA-FY26-09 for construction, contingency and 
project oversight. as follows: 
 
Construction $34,500.00 
Construction Oversight: 3,450.00 
Material Testing: 2,000.00 
Contingency: 6,900.00 
 
TOTAL BUDGET: $46,850.00 
 
Approval of this ordinance adds $46,850 in 2023 SPLOST Transportation Funds to 
Sunrise Lane Retaining Wall - Transfer from SPLOST 2023 and to add $3,450 to 
Sunrise Lane Retaining Wall - Paved Streets - Professional Services line item and 
$43,400 to Sunrise Lane Retaining Wall - Paved Streets - Infrastructure line item, 
including associated transfers. 
 
4. RESOLUTION TO ACCEPT GRANT - PINE NEEDLE PEDESTRIAN 
 
As previously authorized by Council, staff submitted a grant application through 
the Atlanta Regional Commission in February of 2025 for the Pine Needle 
Pedestrian Connector. On October 6, staff received notice from the Georgia 
Department of Transportation that we were successful and will be awarded grant 
funding for the Preliminary Engineering (PE) phase of the project. This phase is 
estimated to cost $860,000. The federal match would include $688,000 with a 
required local match of $172,000. Accepting this grant requires a resolution to be 
signed by Council stating the City will contribute the required 20% grant match.

5. ORDINANCE TO AMEND BUDGET - $860,000 – PINE NEEDLE TRAIL 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Should Council approve the Resolution to provide matching funds of $172,000 to 
support the Pine Needle Pedestrian Connector Project federal grant through the 
Georgia Department of Transportation, staff is requesting approval of a budget 
amendment (BA-FY26-14) to add the federal and local matching funds to the Pine 
Needle Drive Improvements capital project. Matching funds will come from 2023 
SPLOST Transportation Funds. 
 
Approval of this item approves budget amendment (BA-FY26-14) to add $172,000 
to Pine Needle Drive Improvements - Transfer from SPLOST 2023 line item and 
$688,000 to Pine Needle Drive Improvements - Federal Grants line item and 
$860,000 to Pine Needle Drive Improvements - Roadways & Walkways - 
Professional Services line item, including associated transfers. 
 
 
VIII. MATTERS FROM DEPT HEADS/CITY ATTORNEY 
 
1. POLICE DEPARTMENT STAFFING REQUEST/ORD TO AMEND BUDGET 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
In response to requests to Mayor and Council for additional police presence 
throughout our neighborhoods, and to meet the growing public safety needs in 
our City, staff would like to request four additional police officer positions. For the 
first time in several years, the City is at full capacity for police officer positions. The 
additional police officers would be used for patrol functions and would allow for 
the addition of one more officer per shift to answer citizen calls for service. 
 
The Police Department anticipates seven months of funding for the new officer 
positions in the FY26 budget. For this reason, staff is requesting approval of a 
Budget Amendment BA-FY26-10 for $232,000 to fund the salaries and benefits for 
these new positions from prior year reserves to add funds to the following line

1. PROPOSED 2025 TAX MILLAGE RATE/ORDINANCE OF APPROVAL 
{B}
 
 
 
 
 
Mayor Whitlock opened the public hearing and called Asst. City Manager/Finance and 
Redevelopment Director Ken Sakmar forward to present. 
 
Each year, the Gwinnett County Tax Assessor reviews the assessed value of taxable 
property in the County. When the total digest of taxable property is prepared, Georgia Law 
requires calculation of a "rollback" millage rate (RMR) that produces the same total 
revenue on the current year's new digest that last year's millage rate would have 
produced, had no reassessments occurred. The City of Duluth is considering maintaining 
the same millage rate as last year, which is 6.551 mills. For the 2025 digest, the current 
millage rate exceeded the rollback millage rate by 0.184 mills, or stated another way, as a 
percentage of the rollback millage rate, the current millage rate represents a 2.89% 
"increase." The reassessment revenue would add approximately $530,861. 
 
Mr. Sakmar continued by noting that the City has implemented the provisions of 
House Bill 581 which provides tax relief to homeowners who have a homestead 
exemption, and it offers a “floating” homestead exemption amount. This calculates to 
be a little bit over $100 million. Also, in the digest, there are other changes to the 
digest as a result of growth of roughly $55 million, or 2.1% of real property. There are 
also reassessments of existing property, and those reassessments are projected to 
result in a net increase of $183 million, or 6.92% of real property. Breaking that number 
down that I just mentioned in the reassessments, you arrive at $271 million. There 
would be a projected loss of roughly $88 million, so it nets down to $183 million, 
broken out between residential and commercial. 
 
The specific detail was calculated down to the per parcel value by residential and 
commercial. Comparing the current millage rate to the rollback millage rate, it comes 
out to .184%. or roughly $531,000 speaking as a dollar amount. Looking at the value of 
the average home, Mr. Sakmar gave examples of calculations based on home values 
of $350,000, $450,000, and $550,000. 
 
Mr. Sakmar explained that the City's budget was projected to use reserves to balance the 
budget of almost a million dollars and property tax is the largest share of the city's revenue 
side of the budget. He further explained the exemptions, amounts given, and detailed the 
floating homestead this year with estimated dollar amount. He showed the millage rate 
history back to 1985, and noted it would be 10 years that we've had the same rate, and that 
is the longest period of time it has remained the same. 
 
Georgia law requires that the City publish a "Notice of Property Tax Increase" in the legal 
organ when the tentative adopted millage rate exceeds the rollback millage rate. In 
addition, three public hearings must be scheduled to allow the public an opportunity to 
express their opinion on the proposed tax millage. This was the third and final public 
hearing; an ordinance was presented for adoption. 
 
Mayor Whitlock clarified that, under HB 581, values are capped at increasing based on 
the consumer price index. But this year for residential homestead properties, the 2024 
values; the increases only apply to non-homestead residential and commercial

4. ORDINANCE OF ADOPTION–UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT CODE 
 
{E} 
 
Mayor Whitlock opened the public hearing and called Deputy Director for 
Community Development & Engineering Aron Hall forward to present. 
 
Staff proposed an ordinance adopting a new City of Duluth Unified Development 
Code (UDC). The current UDC was originally adopted in 2015 and had undergone 
several text amendments. Over the past two years, staff has dissected the text and 
created a newer version intended to eliminate inconsistencies, redundancies, and 
errors. The new code is intended to reflect Council's current policies regarding land 
use. Some sections have been simplified, some sections have been rewritten for 
clarity, and some sections remain unchanged. 
 
To gather input and feedback from stakeholders, staff advertised and held two joint 
work sessions with the Planning Commission and the Zoning Board of 
Appeals as well as two work sessions with Mayor and Council. He explained that the 
25 text amendments have been approved over the past two years, and provided a 
brief overview of the changes to the UDC during the hearing; those articles that were 
affected were, number one, adoption, purpose, and applicability, number two, use of 
land and structures, three, restrictions on particular uses, four, parking and loading 
requirements, five, subdivision and plan developments, seven, landscaping buffers 
and tree protection, and then nine, project design and construction standards. 
Chapter 14 had a lot of changes only because we moved all of the definitions that 
were in all the articles to 14, so 14 is now acting as a glossary. 
 
Mr. Hall detailed the changes, referencing removing the word “morals” as subjective, 
changing “urban” to “suburban” sprawl, defining “yards,” adding R50 as a zoning class, 
lot coverage clarification and amended setbacks. Further amendments were 
regarding principal uses, rooming/boarding houses, changing zoning allowances for 
mixed use building requirements, continuing/retirement care, day care etc. Mr. Hall 
detailed the other proposals moving many uses from “special use” to “allowed by 
right” based on previous requests, department experience and current updated 
practices/nearby compatibility. 
 
Other updates included describing the R50 guidelines, lighting requirements, 
carports, dumpster enclosures, animals and bees, distance requirements for 
junkyards and tattoo establishments. Mr. Hall referenced temporary events, distances 
from places that serve alcohol, and sale of spring/summer items. Additionally, short-
term rental requirements were detailed, parking sections were updated, definitions 
added to Article 14, and tree density/calculations were simplified.

I. 
PURPOSE AND DESCRIPTION OF THE REQUEST 
The purpose of this Special Use request (SU2025-004) is to allow for a personal care home in 
R-75 (Single-Family District) zoning. 
Maps detailing the location, zoning district and character area of the subject property are 
attached hereto as Exhibit “A”. The legal description of the subject property is attached 
hereto as Exhibit “B”. Recommended conditions of approval are detailed in Exhibit “C”. The 
existing site plan is shown in Exhibit “D”. The Applicant’s Responses to the Standards 
Governing Special Use Considerations is provided in Exhibit “E”. 
 
II. 
EXISTING CONDITIONS 
 
The subject property totals +/- 1.40 acres. The applicant is proposing a personal care home 
which would allow up to six persons under care. The property abuts two single-family houses 
to the north (both currently zoned R-75 (Single-Family Residential District), a single-family 
house to the east (currently zoned R-75 (Single-Family Residential District) on the other side 
of Pine Needle Drive , and an R-100 (Single-Family District) undeveloped property owned by 
the City of Duluth to the south and west. 
 
 
III. 
REVIEW OF THE REQUEST 
 
1. 
Literal Interpretation of the Unified Development Code (UDC) 
 
A. Table 2-C of the UDC allows “Personal Care Homes, Family (2 to 6 under care)” in R-
75 zoning district as a special use. 
 
B. Section 1101.02 of the UDC states if a proposed use is not allowed by right under the 
existing zoning on a property, a request for an amendment to the Official Zoning 
Map (often called a “rezoning”) must be approved prior to development, 
construction, or occupancy. 
 
C. Section 1105 of the UDC establishes the Special Use Considerations. 
 
The Special Use is designed to apply under any one of the following circumstances: 
1. A Special Use listed under the zoning district is desired for development and a 
more intensive zoning district containing that use, as a use by right would not be 
appropriate for the property; or 
 
2. A Special Use listed under the zoning district is desired for development and no 
zoning district contains that use as a use by right; or 
 
3. A unique use not addressed in any zoning district is desired for development and 
is not likely to be duplicated within the City of Duluth; or 
 
4. The density of development may be affected by the height of a building; or 
 
5. The neighboring properties may be affected by the height of any structure; or

6. The Special Use would be consistent with the needs of the neighborhood or the 
community as a whole, be compatible with the neighborhood and would not be 
in conflict with the overall objective of the Comprehensive Plan. 
 
In order to accommodate these particular uses, Special Use approval allows the City Council 
to approve such a use on a particular parcel without changing the general zoning district. 
Such approval shall be subject to the requirements set forth below and any additional 
conditions deemed necessary to ensure the compatibility of the Special Use with the 
surrounding properties. All Special Use applications shall be for firm development

authorized agent. The minimum requirements for a Special Use approval are: 
1. Any uses allowed under Special Use approval shall also conform to the 
requirements of this Development Code for all uses as found in the zoning 
district. 
 
2. The application and review process for a Special Use shall be the same as for the 
zoning district under which the Special Use is found. In addition to the 
information and/or site plans which are required to be submitted for the 
proposed development, additional information deemed necessary by the 
Director in order to evaluate a proposed use and its relationship to the 
surrounding area shall be submitted. In the review process, particular emphasis 
shall be given to the evaluation of the characteristics of the proposed use in 
relationship to its immediate neighborhood and the compatibility of the 
proposed use with its neighborhood. 
 
3. In the approval process for a Special Use approval application, the City Council 
shall consider the policies and objectives of the Comprehensive Plan, particularly 
in relationship to the proposed site and surrounding area and shall consider the 
potential adverse impacts on the surrounding area, especially in regards but not 
limited to traffic, storm drainage, land values and compatibility of land use 
activities. 
 
4. If an application is approved and a Special Use approval is granted, all conditions 
that may have been attached to the approval are binding to the property. All 
subsequent development and use of the property shall be in accordance with the 
approved plan and conditions. 
 
5. Changes to a Special Use or development of a site for the Special Use, shall be 
treated as an amendment to the Special Use Permit and shall be subject to the 
same application and review process as a new application. 
 
6. An application for Special Use approval in a residential district and which use is 
proposed to operate in a dwelling or as an accessory use to a dwelling is subject 
to the following additional requirements: 
 
a. The Special Use shall operate within the dwelling on the property or, if 
approved by the City Council, in an accessory structure.

The subject property is located in the Established Neighborhoods District. 
FORWARDuluth envisions this Character Area to serve as the backbone of Duluth’s

IV. 
PLANNING STAFF REVIEW 
 
A personal care home with two – six persons under care is allowed by right in C-1 
(Neighborhood Business District) and by Special Use in RA-200 (Residential-Agricultural 
District), R-100 (Single-Family Residential District), R-75 (Single-Family Residential 
District), RM (Residential-Multi-Family District), MH (Manufactured Housing District) and O-
N (Office-Neighborhood District). The last personal care home to be permitted in the City was 
in December of 2005, when a 12-person personal care home was approved by Mayor and 
Council at the property 3089 Duluth Highway 120, which is zoned O-N (Office-Neighborhood 
District). 
 
Personal care homes are regulated by the Department of Community Health for the state of 
Georgia and are inspected annually. A full-time dedicated care giver lives on site with the 
residents. The residents of a personal care home are active and independent; however, many 
have chronic illnesses that warrant extra care, such as Alzheimer’s. House calls are made by 
doctors, who administers medication. 
 
While transportation is provided by the management of the personal care home, residents 
have the option of having their own vehicle; however, this is uncommon. There is currently 
a long driveway (~218’), a two-car garage, and ample parking space. Though unlikely, if each 
person in the home had a car, there would be enough space for the seven cars and any guests 
that may be visiting (e.g. doctors or other medical professionals). 
 
The home is well buffered from Craig Drive to the south. The closest house is roughly 109’ 
from primary structure to primary structure. The parcel in question is well above the 
minimum for an R-75 lot at 1.4 acres (60,984). The required lot size for R-75 is 12,000 sf. 
 
Staff does not foresee any unintended consequences by allowing a personal care home at this 
location.

Proposed Comprehensive Plan 
 
 
 
The 110-acre tract of land known locally as the Hudgens Property remains one of the largest 
undeveloped properties in western Gwinnett County situated at the corner of one of the county’s 
busiest intersections. As such, the City recognizes the importance of creating a small area plan for this 
property in an effort to encourage development that aligns with the goals and aspirations of Duluth’s 
residents, elected officials, and planning staff. 
The Hudgens Property’s proximity to Northside Hospital provides a unique opportunity to expand the 
intersection’s capacity for retail, office space, and diverse housing opportunities for the doctors, nurses, 
and staff of the hospital. The proposed plan demonstrates the capability of the subject property to fulfill 
an increasing demand within the City of Duluth for quality housing, entertainment, and regional 
interconnectedness within the City of Duluth. 
A variety of land uses should be allocated across the property through the Principles of New Urbanism, 
which advocate for human-scaled, walkable and mixed-use communities that prioritize people over cars, 
fostering community, diversity, and sustainability. Mixed-use blocks should not exceed dimensions of 
200’ by 200’ to provide pedestrians with a variety of routes to travel throughout ground floor retail and 
office centers. Residential blocks should not exceed dimensions of 200’ by 200’ to break up monotonous 
rows of homes and reduce vehicular travel times. Streets throughout the developed property should 
always prioritize the pedestrian over the vehicle through the use of street trees, wide sidewalks, and 
traffic calming measures, including roundabouts, planted medians, on-street parking, etc. 

 
 
TA2025-05 
There are four distinct districts within the small area plan: Mixed-Use Commercial District, Mixed-Use 
Residential/Park District, Medical District and Residential District. 
Mixed-Use Commercial District 
The Mixed-Use Commercial District will be the densest district with 15+ units an acre. The district can 
support two multi-family apartment buildings with a total maximum unit count of 500. The district 
covers roughly 15 acres of the 110 acre site with concentrations at the north end of Peachtree Industrial 
Boulevard and in the center of the property along Pleasant Hill Road. 
Surface parking shall be avoided except for on-street parking. Most of the parking should come from 
shared deck parking between the commercial, office and residential uses. Buildings with on-street 
parking and street frontage should provide retail and entertainment on the ground floor, and office or 
residential on upper floors. Ground floor retail and other convenient uses shall be of a human-scale with 
12’-16’ ceiling heights, large windows and breaks in massing. Heights of the buildings should be between 
50-75’, which could accommodate a 16’ ground floor and four to five -stories of residential and/or office 
space.

Mixed-Use Residential/Park District 
The Mixed-Use Residential/Park District will be less dense than the Mixed-Use Commercial District and 
will expand over a larger area of roughly 25 acres. The density is anticipated to be 6-15 units an acre, 
which will net up to 375 units over the 25 acres. Most of the district is anticipated to be internal to the 
site, with a small portion of the district expanding parallel to Pleasant Hill Road and the corner of 
McClure Bridge Road. 
This district will support smaller scale commercial, live-work units, and mixed-use residential. A mix of 
housing and intimate retail and restaurant or café space is preferred. Vertical mixed-use and horizontal 
mixed-use is contemplated with smaller storefronts intermingled with residential units on the ground 
floor. The housing should be a mix of townhomes, small -plexes from 2-12 units and small footprint 
single-family. Small lot surface parking may be supported depending on the context; however, on-street 
parking is preferred, and townhomes shall be required to have two-car enclosed garages. The height for
