the Residential District. 
The natural topography and hydrology of the property, especially in this district, allow for the provision 
of unprogrammed park space. Passive or low-impact recreation such as walking trails and open fields 
provide for the greatest amount of accessibility to public open spaces. Stormwater facilities should act 
as amenity areas in this district provided their aesthetics meet amenity expectations. The stream and its 
buffer allow for the preservation of open space and a pedestrian trail system for the residents of this 
community and for the city at large to enjoy.

Medical District 
With roughly 15 acres devoted to medical and medical support uses, the property’s relationship to 
Northside Hospital should be considered carefully. The intersection of Peachtree Industrial Boulevard 
and Pleasant Hill is an extremely busy and prominent corner within the City of Duluth and carries a 
distinct character related to the hospital and its corresponding medical services. This corner of the 
property should engage with the hospital in a creative way. There is potential to expand the doctors’ 
and medical offices into the Hudgens property, especially at the corner of Pleasant Hil and McClure 
Bridge Road, and there is also an opportunity to expand Northside’s role as a regional medical center. 
With such a large tract of developable land, a medical school or conference center could be an 
appropriate land use at this intersection with smaller medical offices intermingled with commercial 
properties. 
Residential District 
Within the Residential District there shall be a gradation of density and a strong diversity of housing. The 
Residential District is the largest land use within the development and encompasses roughly 55 acres of 
the site. ForwardDuluth contemplates low density as 1-6 units per acre. The northern end of the 
property is most suitable for larger lot single-family executive-style or luxury-style homes. Positioning 
these larger lots in this location creates a natural transition from the single-family neighborhood north 
of the Hudgens property to the higher intensities proposed at the southern end. While the northern end 
of the property is suitable for larger lot single-family homes, as one moves into the property heading 
south, there should be a range of lot sizes including R-100, R-75 and R-50. This district also has the

opportunity to include creative single-family home designs and layouts, such as skinny houses and 
cottage courts.

should predominate the front plane of the house. And heights should be limited to 35’.

clusters on small lots. R-50 is the newest zoning category that is promoted in the Core Neighborhood, 
which offers the smallest lot sizes of any single-family residential zoning category with a minimum area 
of 7500 square feet.” 
 
Add to Aspirations: 
Promote R-50 zoning as redevelopment on North Street.

interest of the comprehensive plan, land use plan, transportation plans, and other
plans adopted for guiding development within the city of Duluth. Lastly, whether
there are other existing or changing conditions affecting the use and give grounds for
either approval or disapproval
of this special use.
Mr. Hall detailed each of the proposed
conditions. Planning Commission
recommended
approval ( 4- 1) at their September
15, 2025 hearing.
Mayor Whitlock called for discussion
from Council.
Questions were raised regarding the definition
of personal care home, what staff
recommendation
was for this case and the timing of the approval.
Mr. Hall said that the applicant could give the state definition; staff findings did not
present an issue with the request, and the date of approval starts the 90 day period
for the applicant to begin operations.
Mayor Whitlock called the applicant forward.
Mr. Robert Faust of 136 Summer Drive, Atlanta GA came forward representing the
applicant to address questions from the Mayor and Council. He complimented staff
and the Planning Commission. He noted that their application illustrates that they are
consistent with the guidelines
and parameters
for minimal
impact on the
surrounding
properties. He said that personal care is defined
in the state of Georgia
by the department of community health as a facility that participates both in room
and board housing, for persons
of not necessarily an age, but about 98% of residents
of this type of housing in the state of Georgia are seniors in age. There are occasions
where a younger person with another type of condition that might cause this housing
to be appropriate
for them, but the specific language of the department
of
community health involves "activities of daily living."
In addition to just room and board, residents of this housing option are receiving
levels of care identified by the department of community health as activities of daily
living. Within the state of Georgia there is a limitation of six occupants eligible to live
in a community of this kind within this zoning designation.
Mr. Faust addressed the 90 day limit and said the City's approval is a requirement of
their application
to the state of Georgia for their approval. It typically takes less than
90 days but there is a very rigid procedure that the state follows before a license is
issued. A staff person must be living in that house before residents are invited to move
in, the pantry has to be full of food, and all of the facilities have to be in place to
4

Minutes of M& C
October
13, 2025
Page 5 of 12
illustrate the ability to take a resident in at the time the state comes for their
inspection.
Questions were also raised as to how many bedrooms are in the house and whether a
commercial
container
would
be allowed
if residential
trash
containers
were not
suitable.
Mr. Faust said there are three bedrooms, with areas suitable to convert to sleeping
space for staff, and at this time it would likely be a small six or eight yard dumpster
needed but it would still not be out by the street, but near the structure of the home
itself.
Questions were raised about the typical resident status, type and level of care
provided, and configuration
of the house.
Mr. Faust confirmed that it would be medical care in nature, supported
by outside
physicians etc. and the type of occupancy they would attract is a much younger,
healthier, lower level of acuity resident than you might see in some of the larger care
communities, likely a younger, healthier group of seniors who are making primarily a
lifestyle choice to be a part of a housing and living condition that provides them a
little bit more interaction. It also provides that overlay of health care, not in the
medical sense, but health care activities of daily living. Most of the time what ADLs-
that' s the language you' ll hear in the industry- anticipates
is showering
assistance,
transportation
in and out of a wheelchair
assistance, medication
reminders, etc. The
existing three bedrooms in the home are all on the top floor and residents would
therefore
be physically able to access them.
There was a general discussion about the creek and the property being classified in
floodplain area, the upcoming construction that will be in close vicinity to the
property, and questions as to the desirability of this location.
Mr. Faust did not feel the creek/floodplain would be hazardous for the residents, said
that they are aware of construction, and the size of the property is desirable for
outdoor enjoyment and also an advantage that three of the four property lines of this
tract of land are not abutting an adjacent neighbor. Also having a hospital right
around the corner from there is a very strong attribute and the proximity of
downtown Duluth are also a big attraction.

1. PROPOSED 2025 TAX MILLAGE RATE/ORDINANCE OF APPROVAL 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Each year, the Gwinnett County Tax Assessor reviews the assessed value of taxable 
property in the County. When the total digest of taxable property is prepared, Georgia 
Law requires calculation of a "rollback" millage rate (RMR) that produces the same 
total revenue on the current year's new digest that last year's millage rate would have 
produced, had no reassessments occurred. The City of Duluth is considering 
maintaining the same millage rate as last year, which is 6.551 mills. For the 2025 digest, 
the current millage rate exceeded the rollback millage rate by 0.184 mills, or stated 
another way, as a percentage of the rollback millage rate, the current millage rate 
represents a 2.89% "increase." The reassessment revenue would add approximately 
$530,861. 
 
Georgia law requires that the City publish a "Notice of Property Tax Increase" in the 
legal organ when the tentative adopted millage rate exceeds the rollback millage rate. 
In addition, three public hearings must be scheduled to allow the public an 
opportunity to express their opinion on the proposed tax millage. This is the third and 
final public hearing; an ordinance is presented for adoption.

4. ORDINANCE OF ADOPTION–UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT CODE 
 
Mayor and Council to consider adopting a new City of Duluth Unified 
Development Code (UDC). 
 
The current UDC was originally adopted in 2015 and had undergone several text 
amendments. Over the past two years, staff has dissected the text and created a 
newer version intended to eliminate inconsistencies, redundancies, and errors. 
The new code is intended to reflect Council's current policies regarding land use. 
Some sections have been simplified. Other sections have been better explained. 
And some sections remain unchanged. 
 
To gather input and feedback from stakeholders, staff advertised and held two 
joint work sessions with the Planning Commission and the Zoning Board of 
Appeals as well as two work sessions with Mayor and Council. Staff will give a brief 
overview of the changes to the UDC during the hearing.

Mr. Leventhal came forward to present. He reported that One-person households

III. 
REVIEW OF THE REQUEST 
 
1. 
Literal Interpretation of the Unified Development Code (UDC) 
 
A. Table 2-C of the UDC allows “Day Care Center (more than 18 persons in care)” in M1 
(Light Industrial District) zoning as a special use. 
 
B. Section 1101.02 of the UDC states if a proposed use is not allowed by right under the 
existing zoning on a property, a request for an amendment to the Official Zoning Map 
(often called a “rezoning”) must be approved prior to development, construction, or 
occupancy. 
 
C. Section 1105 of the UDC establishes the Special Use Considerations. 
 
The Special Use is designed to apply under any one of the following circumstances: 
1. A Special Use listed under the zoning district is desired for development and a 
more intensive zoning district containing that use, as a use by right would not be 
appropriate for the property; or 
 
2. A Special Use listed under the zoning district is desired for development and no 
zoning district contains that use as a use by right; or 
 
3. A unique use not addressed in any zoning district is desired for development and 
is not likely to be duplicated within the City of Duluth; or 
 
4. The density of development may be affected by the height of a building; or 
 
5. The neighboring properties may be affected by the height of any structure; or 
 
6. The Special Use would be consistent with the needs of the neighborhood or the 
community as a whole, be compatible with the neighborhood and would not be 
in conflict with the overall objective of the Comprehensive Plan. 

 
 
SU2025-002 
3 | P a g e 
 
 
In order to accommodate these particular uses, Special Use approval allows the City Council 
to approve such a use on a particular parcel without changing the general zoning district. 
Such approval shall be subject to the requirements set forth below and any additional 
conditions deemed necessary to ensure the compatibility of the Special Use with the 
surrounding properties. All Special Use applications shall be for firm development 
proposals only. The Special Use shall not be used for securing early zoning for conceptual 
proposals that may not be undertaken for some time. A Special Use application shall be 
considered only if the application is made by the owner of the property or by his/her 
authorized agent. The minimum requirements for a Special Use approval are: 
1. Any uses allowed under Special Use approval shall also conform to the 
requirements of this Development Code for all uses as found in the zoning 
district. 
 
2. The application and review process for a Special Use shall be the same as for the 
zoning district under which the Special Use is found. In addition to the 
information and/or site plans which are required to be submitted for the 
proposed development, additional information deemed necessary by the 
Director to evaluate a proposed use and its relationship to the surrounding area 
shall be submitted. In the review process, particular emphasis shall be given to 
the evaluation of the characteristics of the proposed use in relationship to its 
immediate neighborhood and the compatibility of the proposed use with its 
neighborhood. 
 
3. In the approval process for a Special Use approval application, the City Council 
shall consider the policies and objectives of the Comprehensive Plan, particularly 
in relationship to the proposed site and surrounding area and shall consider the 
potential adverse impacts on the surrounding area, especially in regards but not 
limited to traffic, storm drainage, land values and compatibility of land use 
activities. 
 
4. If an application is approved and a Special Use approval is granted, all conditions 
that may have been attached to the approval are binding to the property. All 
subsequent development and use of the property shall be in accordance with the 
approved plan and conditions. 
 
5. Changes to a Special Use or development of a site for the Special Use, shall be 
treated as an amendment to the Special Use Permit and shall be subject to the 
same application and review process as a new application. 
 
6. An application for Special Use approval in a residential district and which use is 
proposed to operate in a dwelling or as an accessory use to a dwelling is subject 
to the following additional requirements: 
 
a. The Special Use shall operate within the dwelling on the property or, if 
approved by the City Council, in an accessory structure. 
 
b. The exterior character of the dwelling shall be preserved in its residential 
state and there shall be no outside evidence of the operation of a Special Use 
to the neighborhood, except for any accessory structure approved by the City 
Council.

7. The owner of the property approved for a Special Use may voluntarily request 
termination of the Special Use by notifying the Director in writing. The Director 
shall notify the City Council through the Planning Commission of the voluntary 
termination. The approval of a Special Use for a specific use which may be 
operated by a lessee under a private agreement with a lessor in any non-
residential district shall not obligate the City Council to be responsible for or be 
required to resolve any disputes which may arise out of the voluntary 
termination of the Special Use by the property owner. 
 
8. The Community Development and Engineering Department shall have the right 
to periodically examine the operation of the specific use to determine 
compliance with the requirements and any conditions. If the Director 
determines that the requirements and conditions are being violated, a written 
notice shall be issued to the owner of the property outlining the nature of the 
violation and giving the owner of the property a maximum of ten days to come 
into compliance. If after ten days the violations continue to exist, the Director 
shall forward a report to the City Council through the Planning Commission who 
may recommend that action be taken to remove the Special Use from the 
property. 
 
9. Upon approval by the City Council, a Special Use shall be identified on the official 
zoning maps. 
 
10. Upon approval by the City Council of a Special Use, the owner of the property 
shall be issued a notice from the Director that states the specific use permitted,

the owner or occupier to resume the nonconforming use.

Mayor Whitlock opened the public hearing and called Asst. City Manager/ Finance and
Redevelopment Director Ken Sakmar forward to present.
Each year, the Gwinnett County Tax Assessor reviews the assessed value of taxable
property in the County. When the total digest of taxable property is prepared, Georgia Law
requires calculation of a " rollback" millage rate ( RMR) that produces the same total
revenue on the current year' s new digest that last year' s millage rate would have
produced, had no reassessments occurred. The City of Duluth is considering maintaining
the same millage rate as last year, which
is 6.551 mills. For the 2025 digest, the current
millage rate exceeded the rollback millage rate by 0.184 mills, or stated another way, as a
percentage of the rollback millage rate, the current millage rate represents
a 2.89%
increase." The reassessment
revenue would add approximately $ 530, 861.
Mr. Sakmar continued by noting that the City has implemented the provisions of
House Bill 581 which provides tax relief to homeowners who have a homestead
exemption, and it offers a " floating" homestead exemption amount. This calculates to
be a little bit over $ 100 million. Also, in the digest, there are other changes to the
digest
as a result of growth of roughly $ 55 million, or 2. 1% 
of real property. There are
also reassessments of existing property, and those reassessments are projected to
result
in a net increase of$ 183 million, or 6. 92% of real property. Breaking that number
down that
I just mentioned
in the reassessments, you
arrive at $ 271 million. There
would be a projected loss of roughly $ 88 million, so it nets down to $ 183 million,
broken out between residential and commercial.
The specific detail was calculated down to the per parcel value by residential and
commercial. Comparing the current millage rate to the rollback millage rate, it comes
out to .184%. or roughly $ 531, 000 speaking as a dollar amount. Looking at the value of
the average home, Mr. Sakmar gave examples of calculations based on home values
of $350, 000, $ 450, 000, and $ 550, 000.
Mr. Sakmar explained that the City' s budget was projected to use reserves to balance the
budget of almost a million dollars and property tax is the largest share of the city's revenue
side of the budget. He further explained the exemptions, amounts given, and detailed the
floating homestead this year with estimated dollar amount. He showed the millage rate
history back to 1985, and noted it would be 10 years that we' ve had the same rate, and that
is the longest period of time it has remained the same.
Georgia law requires that the City publish a " Notice of Property Tax Increase" in the legal
organ when the tentative adopted millage rate exceeds the rollback millage rate. In
addition, three public hearings must be scheduled to allow the public an opportunity to
express their opinion on the proposed tax millage. This was the third and final public
hearing; an ordinance was presented for adoption.
Mayor Whitlock clarified that, under HB 581, values are capped at increasing based on
the consumer price index. But this year for residential homestead properties, the 2024
values; the increases only apply to non- homestead residential and commercial

Staff proposed an ordinance adopting a new City of Duluth Unified Development
Code ( UDC). The current UDC was originally adopted in 2015 and had undergone
several text amendments. Over the past two years, staff has dissected the text and
created a newer version intended to eliminate inconsistencies, redundancies, and
errors. The new code is intended to reflect Council' s current policies regarding land
use. Some sections

25 text amendments have been approved over the past two years, and provided a
brief overview of the changes to the UDC during the hearing; those articles that were
affected were, number one, adoption, purpose, and applicability, number two, use of
land and structures, three, restrictions on particular uses, four, parking and loading
requirements, five, subdivision and plan developments, seven, landscaping buffers
and tree protection, and then nine, project design and construction standards.
Chapter 14 had a lot of changes only because we moved all of the definitions that
were in all the articles to 14, so 14 is now acting as a glossary.

lot coverage
clarification

Each year, the Gwinnett County Tax Assessor reviews the assessed value of taxable 
property in the County. When the total digest of taxable property is prepared, 
Georgia Law requires calculation of a "rollback" millage rate (RMR) that produces 
the same total revenue on the current year's new digest that last year's millage 
rate would have produced, had no reassessments occurred. The City of Duluth is 
considering maintaining the same millage rate as last year, which is 6.551 mills. For

the legal organ when the tentative adopted millage rate exceeds the rollback

The City of Duluth, Georgia in accordance with Georgia State Law (48-5-32-1) is 
providing the following information regarding property taxes and the millage rate. The 
City of Duluth intends to increase the property taxes it will levy this year by 2.89% 
over the rollback millage rate set forth by SB 177, Act 431, of the 1999 Legislative 
Session.
Each year, the Gwinnett County Tax Assessor is required to review the assessed 
value of taxable property in the county for property tax purposes. When the trend 
prices of properties that have recently sold in the county indicate there has been an 
increase in the fair market value of any specific property, the board of tax assessors 
is required by law to re-determine the value of such property and increase the 
assessment. This is called a reassessment process.
When the total digest of taxable property is prepared, Georgia Law requires that a 
rollback millage rate must be computed that will produce the same total revenue on 
the current year’s new digest that last year’s millage rate would have produced had 
no reassessments occurred.
The Fiscal Year 2026 budget adopted by the Duluth City Council on June 9, 2025, 
requires a millage rate higher than the rollback millage rate. The current millage 
rate is 6.551 mills, and the proposed millage rate is 6.551 mills. Therefore, before 
the Duluth City Council may set a millage rate to support the budget, Georgia Law 
requires that three public hearings be held to allow the public an opportunity to 
express their opinions on the increase. The City is also required to distribute this 
press release.

Frequently

Gwinnett County with on-demand, flexible 
shared rides. It’s available to anyone needing local 
transportation for work, shopping, appointments, 
connecting to other transit options, and more. 
On-demand trips mean you can use the service 
when you need it instead of having to plan your trip 
around a bus route schedule.

system, addressing equity, reliability, and efficiency.

We recommend that you be ready to board or take 
your trip at the start of your pick-up time window. 
You will receive an updated estimated arrival time as

ride has reached the pick-up location. Updates are 
sent via SMS and the Ride Gwinnett app. You can also

PROPOSED TAX MILLAGE RATE - 2025 
 
Each year, the Gwinnett County Tax Assessor reviews the assessed value of taxable 
property in the County. When the total digest of taxable property is prepared, Georgia 
Law requires calculation of a "rollback" millage rate (RMR) that produces the same 
total revenue on the current year's new digest that last year's millage rate would have 
produced, had no reassessments occurred. The City of Duluth is considering 
maintaining the same millage rate as last year, which is 6.551 mills. For the 2025 digest, 
the current millage rate exceeded the rollback millage rate by 0.184 mills, or stated 
another way, as a percentage of the rollback millage rate, the current millage rate 
represents a 2.89% "increase". The reassessment revenue would add approximately 
$530,861. 
 
Georgia law requires that the City publish a "Notice of Property Tax Increase" in the 
legal organ when the tentative adopted millage rate exceeds the rollback millage rate. 
In addition, three public hearings must be scheduled to allow the public an 
opportunity to express their opinion on the proposed tax millage. 
 
This is the first public hearing. The second public hearing is scheduled for this evening, 
August 25, 2025, at 5:30 pm in the Community Room, the third public hearing is 
scheduled to be heard, Monday, September 8, 2025 in the City Hall Council Chambers, 
after which an ordinance will be presented for adoption.

a portion of Peachtree Road and dedication of new public roadway. 
 
Resolution R2025-10 proposes abandonment of a .593 acre portion of Peachtree 
Road pursuant to O.C.G.A. §32-7-2(c) following proper notice to all property owners 
located on the portions of the municipal street system closed and abandoned by 
this action. This abandonment is subject to any and all previous utility easements 
conveyed to Gwinnett County or any other public or private entity or franchise 
holder, and these easements or other property rights previously conveyed shall 
not be extinguished or altered by this action. 
 
The abandonment resolution authorizes the Mayor, City Manager, City Clerk, and 
the City Attorney to take such action and execute such documents as are 
necessary to exchange the property where the now abandoned Peachtree Road 
existed with Embry Development Company, LLC for construction and dedication 
of a new public road.

along Buford Highway and Peachtree Road for Case Z2025-001. 
 
Several owners, along with applicant Embry Development Company, LLC, are 
requesting the rezoning of the properties from HC-A (Highway Commercial Auto) 
and HC-R (Highway Commercial Retail) to PUD (Planned Unit Development) to 
allow for a 77-unit townhome development. 
 
The Planning Commission recommended approval with conditions at their July 7, 
2025 hearing. Staff will outline the location of the development along with said 
conditions in the public hearing. Ordinance and staff report are attached for 
reference.

The Mayor and Council to consider an ordinance to modify a condition of rezoning 
for Parcels R6264 496 and R 6264 037 located at 3282 Davenport Road. These 
parcels were rezoned on March 10, 2025 as part of Case Z2024-005 to allow for a 
single family detached residential subdivision. 
 
The Planning Commission recommended approval at their July 7, 2025 hearing. 
Ordinance and staff report are attached for reference. 
 
4. ORDINANCE - PUD MODIFICATION CASE Z2025-002 – FOUNDRY APTS 
 
Mayor and Council to consider an ordinance to amend an existing PUD (Planned 
Unit Development) to allow for a change in density for Case Z2025-002. 
 
Owner/Applicant FP Peachtree Industrial, LLC, is requesting a modification to the 
existing PUD (Planned Unit Development) to allow for the conversion of 64 3-
bedroom apartment units into 128 1-bedroom apartment units to meet current 
market demand. 
 
The Planning Commission recommended approval with conditions at their July 7, 
2025 hearing. Staff will outline those conditions in the public hearing. Ordinance 
and staff report are attached for reference.

3. PURCHASING POLICY AMENDMENT – HB 137 
 
 
 
 
{C} 
 
Mr. Sakmar explained that, effective July 1, 2025, House Bill 137 increased the threshold 
for public works public bidding from $100,000 to $250,000. HB 137 exempts public 
works projects under $250,000 from certain bidding and procedural obligations. Thus, 
projects under $250,000 would be governed by the city's adopted purchasing policy.

Given the ongoing rise in costs for construction materials, labor, and services, raising 
the city's internal threshold for public bidding from $100,000 to $250,000 would

project needs while still maintaining transparency and essential projects can proceed 
without delays.

Council consent agenda for authorization.

Purchases Over $99,999 But Less Than $250,000 
Obtaining competitive prices is a requirement for purchases of this dollar amount. 
However, the competitive sealed bid requirements are much less than the formal 
competitive procedures for purchases greater than $250,000. 
The competitive sealed bid process is a procurement method which allows bidders to 
submit bids in sealed envelopes by a specific date specified in the invitation to bid. 
Departments are required to obtain a minimum of three (3) bids or explain why they could 
not obtain three bids. 
Departments should prepare an invitation to bid which clearly describes the project scope 
and requirements. The invitation to bid should include the timeline of the process for 
awarding the contract, location, date and deadline for submitting bids, how the bids will be 
evaluated or scored, any meeting to be held prior to the bid award and if they are 
mandatory or optional. Any bonding requirements for the project, the time and place the 
bids will be opened, estimate of the time and place the bid will be awarded and how the 
winning bidder will be notified. 
Contractor/Vendor bids should be submitted in sealed envelopes, clearly labeled with their 
name and the name of the project they are bidding on. The sealed envelopes should be 
stamped or marked with the date and time they were received and kept in a secure location 
until the bid opening. Bids received after the deadline for submitting bids should not be 
considered and the bidder should be notified their bid will not be considered. 
All qualified sealed bids received should be recorded on the City of Duluth Competitive 
Sealed Bid Form (Exhibit XX) along with the documents received from each qualified 
bidder. Departments should note on the form the winning bidder and submit this 
documentation to Accounts Payable when requesting a purchase order (PO) or submitting 
an invoice for payment.

I. 
PURPOSE AND DESCRIPTION OF THE REQUEST 
The purpose of the rezoning request (Z2025-001) is to rezone the current parcels
 
from HC-A (Highway Commercial – Auto) and HC-R (Highway Commercial – Retail) 
 
to PUD (Planned Unit Development) to allow for a 77-unit townhome development. 
 
Maps detailing the location, zoning district and character area of the subject 
properties are attached hereto as Exhibit “A”. The legal description of the subject 
properties are attached hereto as Exhibit “B”. Recommended conditions of rezoning 
are detailed in Exhibit “C”. Applicant’s Responses to the Standards Governing Special 
Use Consideration are provided in Exhibit “D”. Applicant’s Letter of Intent is provided 
in Exhibit “E”. The Master Concept Plan is located in Exhibit “F”. An illustrative site 
plan is included as Exhibit “G”. Elevations are included as Exhibit “H”. And, the public 
notice and ad exhibits are included in Exhibit “I”. 
In order for the applicant to achieve their desired land use on the overall site, they 
are required to rezone the subject properties. 
 
II. 
EXISTING CONDITIONS 
 
The overall subject properties total +/- 6.12 acres and consists of 11 parcels with 
various property owners. Tax parcel R6264 065 (3375 Buford Highway) is currently 
a carwash zoned HC-A (Highway Commercial – Auto). Tax parcel 6292 043 (3355 
Buford Highway) contains three single-family detached units (two of which are 
boarded up) zoned HC-A (Highway Commercial – Auto). Tax parcel 6292 043A (3355 
Buford Highway) contains a boarded up quadplex zoned HC-A (Highway Commercial 
– Auto). Tax parcels 6292 057 (3366 Buford Highway), 6292 042 (3356 Peachtree 
Road), 6292 069 (3346 Peachtree Road), 6292 041 (3305 Peachtree Road), 6292 049 
(3357 Peachtree Road), 6292 056 (3337 Peachtree Road) are all undeveloped and 
zoned HC-A (Highway Commercial – Auto). Tax parcels 6292 050 (3307 Buford 
Highway) and 6293 644 (3435 Davenport Road) are both undeveloped and zoned 
HC-R (Highway Commercial-Retail). The subject property abuts the railroad. 
Northwest of the railroad is a residential Planned Unit Development (PUD) called 
Willbrooke. Properties to the southeast include: Sherwood Crossing, a PUD (Planned 
Unit Development) townhome community, Waterbug Properties LLC at 3330 Buford 
Highway (zoned HC-A (Highway Commercial-Auto)), Atlanta Pine Straw at 3320 
Buford Highway (zoned HC-A (Highway Commercial-Auto)), and the City of Duluth’s 
Public Safety facility at 3276 Buford Highway (zoned HC-A (Highway Commercial-
Auto)). 
 
There is a portion of Peachtree Road that separates several of these properties. This 
right-of-way will be abandoned through a formal process with Mayor and Council at 
their August 11th Voting meeting. Peachtree Road will be reconfigured with an equal 
or greater portion being rededicated as public right-of-way prior to the closeout of 
the townhome project.

III. 
REVIEW OF THE REQUEST 
 
1. 
Literal Interpretation of the Unified Development Code (UDC) 
 
 
A. Section 1101.02 of the UDC states if a proposed use is not allowed by right 
under the existing zoning on a property, a request for an amendment to the 
Official Zoning Map (often called a “rezoning”) must be approved prior to 
development, construction, or occupancy. In addition, a zoning change for 
approval of a subdivision, multi-family, or nonresidential project must 
include a subdivision sketch plan, preliminary site development plan, or PUD 
(planned unit development) master concept plan as applicable, showing the 
proposed layout of the project. The master concept plan can be found in 
Attachment “F”. 
 
2. 
Standards Governing the Exercise of Zoning Power 
 
Section 1104.02 of the UDC establishes the standards governing the exercise of 
zoning power. The following standards are relevant in balancing the interest 
and promoting the public health, safety, and general welfare against the right to 
the unrestricted use of property: 
A. 
Whether the zoning proposal will permit a use that is suitable in view 
of the use and development of adjacent and nearby property. 
 
B. 
Whether the zoning proposal will adversely affect the existing use or 
usability of adjacent or nearby property. 
 
C. 
Whether the zoning proposal will result in a use that will or could cause 
an excessive or burdensome use of existing streets, transportation 
facilities, utilities, or schools. 
 
D. 
Whether the zoning proposal is consistent with the Land Use Policy Plan, 
Comprehensive Plan, transportation plans, or other plans adopted for 
guiding development within the City of Duluth. 
 
E. 
Whether there are other existing or changing conditions affecting the use 
and development of property that give supporting grounds for either 
approval or disapproval of the zoning or special use proposal. 
 
The Applicant has provided written responses to the above Rezoning Standards 
as part of the application. Those documents are attached hereto as Exhibit “E”. 
 
3. 
Literal Interpretation of FORWARDuluth, Plan 2045 (Comprehensive 
Plan) 
 

 
 
Z2025-001 
 
4 | P a g e 
 
 
 
 
 
The subject properties that constitute the proposed project straddle two 
character areas. The western portion is part of the Core Neighborhood District. 
FORWARDuluth envisions this area to be denser, connected neighborhoods, 
easily accessible to Downtown through a system of trails, sidewalks and road 
connections, while capitalizing on existing traditional street fabric and 
opportunities for redevelopment and infill. 
The eastern portion of the project is located in the Downtown Core District 
Character Area. FORWARDuluth envisions this Character Area to be the cultural 
and entertainment heart of the City and region, celebrating the hometown, 
historic character while utilizing big city aesthetic and amenities. 
The Future Land Use Map (FLUM) calls for Medium Density Residential. 
Residential and planned unit development zoned properties consisting of 
detached single-family homes and townhomes with a density between 6-12 
units per acre. 
 
IV. 
PLANNING STAFF REVIEW 
 
Density 
 
The Planned Unit Development application is requesting 77 townhomes over 6.21 
acres. With the right-of-way excluded from the acreage, the density will be 12.39 units 
per acre, which is consistent with the Future Land Use Map. 
Walkability 
The proposed development will be an extension of the downtown core residential 
development as seen within and around South on Main. The furthest point of the 
development will be roughly a half mile walk to the library with the nearest unit being 
less than 1,000 feet to the library. With less than a mile walk to Parsons Alley, all of 
downtown will be accessible through alternative modes of transportation, greatly 
reducing vehicle trips for residents of the development. There will also be 
connectivity via sidewalks throughout the development and along Buford Highway 
and a small trail connection directly to Davenport Road. 
Landscaping 
A key feature of this development includes an enhanced landscape plan fronting 
Buford Highway. This landscape buffer should incorporate a mix of region- 
appropriate evergreen trees and shrubs along with a mix of native deciduous trees. 
This mix of deciduous trees should incorporate small, medium and large canopy trees 
within the buffer and throughout the site. This enhanced buffer is in addition to the 
required Tree Density Units for the rest of the site. An approved landscape plan shall 
be reviewed and approved prior to development. 
 

 
 
Z2025-001 
 
5 | P a g e 
 
 
 
 
 
Open Space 
The applicant is proposing 15% of the development be open space, which is 
approximately 40,000 square feet of open space. The amount of open space is over 
13,000 square feet more than required. The programing for the open space is a mix 
of passive pocket parks, green space and a dog park. With its proximity to downtown, 
the greatest amenity remains town green and access to all adjacent activities. 
Architecture 
The architecture, along with the landscaping, will be a key feature of the development. 
The proposed elevations show a timeless classic brick design with large industrial 
looking windows. The look of the architecture is reminiscent of the post-industrial-
looking façade of the Thrive Building giving a clear connection to the downtown. 
 
 
V. 
RECOMMENDATION 
Planning Commission recommended Approval with Conditions.

I. 
PURPOSE AND DESCRIPTION OF THE REQUEST 
The purpose of the modification of rezoning request (MZ2025-001) is to remove a 
condition of zoning which required a 10’ ADA compliant concrete or asphalt trail 
through the property in question connecting to city owned property with a trailhead 
at Hall Circle. 
 
Maps detailing the location, zoning district and character area of the subject 
property are attached hereto as Exhibit “A”. The legal description of the subject 
property is attached hereto as Exhibit “B”. Revised conditions of approval are 
detailed in Exhibit “C”. Applicant’s Letter of Intent is provided in Exhibit “D”. The 
Master Plan is located in Exhibit “E”. And public notice is located in Exhibit “F”. 
 
II. 
EXISTING CONDITIONS 
 
The subject property totals +/- 7.91 acres and currently has a single-family house on 
tax parcel R6264 037. Tax parcel R6264 037 is currently undeveloped. These two 
properties were rezoned from R-100 (Single-Family Residential District) to PUD 
(Planned Unit Development) for the construction of 29 Single-Family detached homes 
at the March 10th 2025 hearing . The subject property abuts a residential Planned Unit 
Development (PUD) to the north called Windsor Gate. Properties to the east are 
currently zoned R-75 (Single-Family Residential District) and are part of the Hall 
Circle neighborhood. The three parcels to the immediate west are zoned R-100 
(Single-Family Residential District), each containing a single-family home. Across 
Davenport Road the properties are zoned RM (Residential Multi-family District) and 
contain duplexes. The property to the south is zoned R-100 (Single-Family 
Residential District). It is currently undeveloped with much of the property in a utility 
easement. 
 
 
 
III. 
REVIEW OF THE REQUEST 
 
1. 
Literal Interpretation of the Unified Development Code (UDC) 
 
 
A. Section 504.08 of the UDC states that any changes that, in the opinion of the 
Planning and Development Director, result in a development of such intent 
and character that has not been conceptually approved by the City Council 
shall require additional approval in accordance with procedures established 
in the Procedures and Permits Article for a revision of conditions of rezoning 
approval.

2. 
Standards Governing the Exercise of Zoning Power 
 
Section 1104.02 of the UDC establishes the standards governing the exercise of 
zoning power. The following standards are relevant in balancing the interest 
and promoting the public health, safety, and general welfare against the right to 
the unrestricted use of property: 
A. 
Whether the zoning proposal will permit a use that is suitable in view 
of the use and development of adjacent and nearby property. 
 
B. 
Whether the zoning proposal will adversely affect the existing use or 
usability of adjacent or nearby property. 
 
C. 
Whether the zoning proposal will result in a use that will or could cause 
an excessive or burdensome use of existing streets, transportation 
facilities, utilities, or schools. 
 
D. 
Whether the zoning proposal is consistent with the Land Use Policy Plan, 
Comprehensive Plan, transportation plans, or other plans adopted for 
guiding development within the City of Duluth. 
 
E. 
Whether there are other existing or changing conditions affecting the use 
and development of property that give supporting grounds for either 
approval or disapproval of the zoning or special use proposal. 
 
The Applicant has provided letter of intent for the modification of the PUD. The 
letter is attached hereto as Exhibit “D”. 
 
3. 
Literal Interpretation of FORWARDuluth, Plan 2045 (Comprehensive 
Plan) 
 
The subject property is located in the Core Neighborhood District Character 
Area. FORWARDuluth envisions this Character Area to be denser, connected 
neighborhoods, easily accessible to Downtown through a system of trails, 
sidewalks and road connections, while capitalizing on existing traditional 
street fabric and opportunities for redevelopment and infill. The Future Land 
Use Map (FLUM) envisions this parcel as Low Density Residential with density 
between 1-6 units per acre.

IV. 
PLANNING STAFF REVIEW 
 
The original Planned Unit Development proposal was approved by City Council at 
their March 10, 2025 meeting. Staff finds the following facts: 
 
The original condition was as follows: 
 
The developer shall install a 10’ ADA compliant concrete paved walking trial and 
 
creek crossing with a 20’ easement between the project property and Hall Circle. The 
 
HOA shall maintain the trail until its terminus on City Parcel R6293 083. The City shall 
 
grant a temporary construction easement to the developer for completion of the 10’ 
 
concrete paved walking trail and creek crossing through City property at parcel 
 
R6293 083. Details of the trail and creek crossing shall be approved by the 
 
Community Development and Engineering Department prior to issuing a Land 
 
Disturbance Permit. 
 
A second condition relating to the first was written as follows: 
 
As part of the walking trail connecting the development to Hall Circle, the developer 
 
shall install lighting and conduit along the totality of the trail. Details of the lighting 
 
and conduit shall be approved by the Community Development and Engineering 
 
Department prior to issuing a Land Disturbance Permit. 
When the city is reviewing Planned Unit Development applications, the UDC requires 
a master plan showing the development in as much detail as possible. Staff require 
approved conditions to be met. However, this is all prior to full plan sets with 
engineering that takes topography fully into consideration. Once the developer had 
initial engineered plans of what the trail would require, staff and the developer 
determined construction of such a trail would be prohibitive given the topography of 
the subject location. 
 
V. 
RECOMMENDATION 
Planning Commission recommended Approval with Conditions.

I. 
PURPOSE AND DESCRIPTION OF THE REQUEST 
The purpose of the rezoning request (Z2025-002) is to modify the current PUD to 
allow for the modification of three-bedroom units into one-bedroom units. 
 
Maps detailing the location, zoning district and character area of the subject 
property are attached hereto as Exhibit “A”. The legal description of the subject 
property is attached hereto as Exhibit “B”. Recommended conditions of approval are 
detailed in Exhibit “C”. Applicant’s Responses to the Standards Governing the 
Exercise of Zoning Power are provided in Exhibit “D”. Applicant’s Letter of Intent is 
provided in Exhibit “E”. The Master Plan is located in Exhibit “F”. Elevations are 
provided in Exhibit “G”. and Public Notices are included in Exhibit “H”. 
In order for the applicant to achieve their desired land use on the subject property, 
they are required to rezone the subject property. 
 
II. 
EXISTING CONDITIONS 
 
The subject property totals +/- 32.00 acres and currently has 256 units with a mix of 
1-, 2-, and 3-bedroom units, with a density of 8 units per acre. The subject property 
abuts a large undeveloped commercially zoned property to its south. It abuts R-100 
properties to its east. It abuts a mix of residential and commercial office PUD 
properties (Hampton Arbors, Woodhaven, and River Parc) along with a Montessori 
school to its west. And it abuts a residential PUD (Chattahoochee Landing) and 
commercial auto repair center to its north. 
 
 
 
III. 
REVIEW OF THE REQUEST 
 
1. 
Literal Interpretation of the Unified Development Code (UDC) 
 
Section 504.08 of the UDC states that any changes that, in the opinion of the Planning 
and Development Director, result in a development of such intent and character that 
has not been conceptually approved by the City Council shall require additional 
approval in accordance with procedures established in the Procedures and Permits 
Article for a revision of conditions of rezoning approval. Such changes may be 
additions in the types of land uses, increases in square footage or density, decreases 
in lot sizes, changes in the location or dimensions of major streets, decreases in 
dwelling unit floor areas, major alterations in the land use patterns, or other 
substantial changes that are inconsistent with the summary report or the master 
concept plan approved for the PUD. The master concept plan can be found in 
Attachment “F”. 
 
2. 
Standards Governing the Exercise of Zoning Power 
 
Section 1104.02 of the UDC establishes the standards governing the exercise of 
zoning power. The followpublicrds are relevant in balancing the interest and

The Applicant has provided written responses to the above Rezoning Standards

3. 
Literal Interpretation of FORWARDuluth, Plan 2045 (Comprehensive 
Plan) 
 
The subject property is located in the Urban Neighborhood District Character 
Area. FORWARDuluth envisions this Character Area to be a high-quality multi-
family corridor with connection through multi-modal transportation to 
regional employment opportunities. The Future Land Use Map (FLUM) 
envisions this parcel as Mixed Use, which includes properties zoned PUD. 
 
IV. 
PLANNING STAFF REVIEW 
 
 
The original Planned Unit Development was approved in 1985. The applicant could 
not locate the original PUD approval through Gwinnett County, however, the City’s 
records show that this parcel was annexed into the City of Duluth through a new 
charter, “so as to clarify the corporate limits of said city,” which was signed into law 
on March 31, 1995. Therefore, this property was brought into the city as having been 
rezoned to PUD by Gwinnett County.

Density 
 
The property has had 256 units since its original zoning approval in 1985. The owner 
is now requesting a modification for all the three-bedroom units to become one 
bedroom units, which would increase the overall unit count from 256 units to 320 
units. This change would increase the density from 8 units an acre to 10 units an acre. 
 
Parking 
 
There are currently 503 parking spaces. By today’s standards, set forth in the current 
Unified Development Code, this development would be required to have 640 covered 
parking spaces plus 64 guest parking spaces for a total of 704 parking spaces. By 
comparison, the District at Duluth has 153 two-bedroom and 218 one-bedroom 
apartments and required a ratio of no less than 1.59 parking spaces per unit for a 
total of 590 parking spaces. If the same logic is applied to this development, 509 
parking spaces would be required. Therefore, 6 additional parking spaces should be 
included in the PUD amendment. Garden style apartments such as this development 
are not conducive to covered parking, since the units are spread out throughout the 
site. Staff does not recommend requiring parking to be covered for this development. 
 
Walkability 
When this development was built in 1985-1986 there was no known requirement for 
sidewalk along Peachtree Industrial Boulevard. There is now a noticeable gap in 
sidewalk along Peachtree Industrial Boulevard. This sidewalk gap is also shown as 
proposed sidewalk in the City’s master sidewalk plan. Any development would 
trigger the developer to have to build the frontage sidewalk. The developer will have 
to coordinate with Gwinnett County Department of Transportation. This gap will 
become even more pronounced when the large property to the south develops with 
a required sidewalk; therefore, staff is recommending a 5’ sidewalk from property 
line to property line along Peachtree Industrial Boulevard connecting to the sidewalk 
to the north of the property. 
Landscaping 
It is staff’s opinion that a key feature of this development would be an enhanced 
landscape plan fronting Peachtree Industrial Boulevard. The landscape plan should 
enhance the buffer between Peachtree Industrial Boulevard and the subject property. 
The buffer should incorporate a mix of region-appropriate evergreen trees and 
shrubs along with a mix of native deciduous trees. This mix of deciduous trees should 
incorporate small, medium and large canopy trees. An approved landscape plan shall 
be reviewed by the City and approved prior to development. 
V. 
RECOMMENDATION 
Planning Commission recommended Approval with Conditions.

Applicant’s Response to the Standards Governing Exercise of Zoning Power 
 
1. Whether the zoning proposal will permit a use that is suitable in view of the use and 
development of adjacent and nerby property. 
 
Yes The proposed unit conversion is suitable within the context of existing adjacent 
multifamily and residential developments. The Foundry is already an established residential 
community, and the proposal does not introduce a new use, but rather reconfigures existing 
units to better meet current market demands. The increase in one-bedroom units will create a 
more balanced housing mix that aligns with the demographic and economic evaluation of the 
area, complementing surrounding properties rather than conflicing with them. 
 
2. Wheter the zoning propsal will adversely affect the existing use or usability of adjacent or 
nearby property. 
 
No. The proposal is expected to enhance the usability and desirability of nearby properties. By 
reducing the average number of residents per unit and minimizing household size, the 
conversion will lead to less strain on shared infrastructure, quieter living environments, and 
lower traffic and congestion. These improvements can increase property values and make the 
surrounding neighborhood more attractive to new residents and investors. 
 
3. Whether the zoning proposal will result in a use that will or could cause an excessive or 
burdensome use of existing streets, transportation facilities, utilities, or schools. 
 
No. Although the total unit count will increase, the actual resident population is projected to 
decrease due to the shift from large 3-bedroom units to smaller 1-bedroom units. This will 
result in reduced traffic generation and a lower burden on utilities and public schools. The 
proposal is designed to optimize existing infrastructure without requiring any expansions or 
upgrades, making it a low-impact and sustainable solution for housing needs. 
 
4. Whether the zoning proposal is consistent with the Land Use Policy Plan, Comprehensive 
Plan, transportation plans, or other plans adopted for guiding development within the City of 
Duluth. 
 
Yes. The proposal directly supports the goals and recommendations of the 2040 Forward 
Duluth Comprehensive Plan. The plan encourages the redevelopment of aging multifamily 
properties into more efficient, diverse, and denser residential configurations. It also promotes 
smart growth strategies that improve housing affordability and expand workforce housing 
options—all of which are accomplished through the Application. Additionally, the plan favors

infill and redevelopment projects that reduce the strain on public services without expanding 
the City’s physical footprint, which this project achieves. 
 
5. Whether there are other existing or changing conditions affecting the use and development 
of property that give supporting grounds for either approval or disapproval of the zoning or 
special use proposal. 
 
Yes. Regional and local housing trends clearly indicate increased demand for smaller, more 
affordable units, especially from young professionals, retirees, and smaller households. The 
Foundry’s current stock of large 3-bedroom units is no longer the most efficient or desirable 
format for today’s renters. The project modernizes the property in line with shifting 
demographics and helps fulfill Duluth’s goals for economic vitality and housing diversity. 
These evolving conditions make a strong case for approval of the rezoning. 
 
6. Whether the property to be affected by a proposed rezoning has a reasonable economic use 
as currently zoned. 
 
While the property does have a somewhat reasonable economic use under current zoning, the 
current unit configuration is not aligned with modern market demand. Approval of the 
Application would offer a more economically viable long-term use, ensuring the continued 
relevance and financial performance of the property while also enhancing community 
compatibility and stability.

AN ORDINANCE FOR THE REZONING OF +/- 32.00 ACRES OF PROPERTIES IN LAND LOTS 322, 6TH 
DISTRICT, GWINNETT COUNTY CONSISTING OF TAX PARCEL R6322 133 AS LEGALLY DESCRIBED 
ON THE ATTACHED EXHIBIT “B”. THE ORDINANCE PROVIDES FOR FINDINGS, ESTABLISHES 
CONDITIONS OF APPROVAL AS SHOWN ON ATTACHED EXHIBIT “C”, PROVIDES FOR 
SEVERABILITY, REPEALS CONFLICTING ORDINANCES, ESTABLISHES AN EFFECTIVE DATE, AND IS 
FOR ALL OTHER LAWFUL PURPOSES. 
WHEREAS, the applicant, FP Peachtree Industrial, LLC C/O Fargos Properties has filed a complete 
application (Z2025-002) with the City of Duluth seeking a rezoning. Said rezoning plan includes, but is not 
limited to, the rezoning of +/- 32.00 acres of property from PUD (Planned Unit Development) to PUD 
(Planned Unit Development); and 
WHEREAS, per Article 5 of the Duluth Unified Development Code, a substantial revision to an approved 
Planned Unit Development (PUD) must be approved by the Governing Body; and 
WHEREAS, the City of Duluth Planning Commission held a public hearing at the meeting of July 7, 2025, 
duly noticed as prescribed by law and published in the Gwinnett Daily Post, regarding the application. At 
the July 7, 2025 meeting, the Planning Commission recommended approval with conditions as is set forth 
in the minutes of said meeting; and 
WHEREAS, the City Council held a public hearing at the meeting of August 11, 2025, duly noticed as 
prescribed by law and published in the Gwinnett Daily Post, regarding said application, as shall be set 
forth in the minutes of said meeting. 
NOW THEREFORE, the City Council of the City of Duluth hereby ordains that the City of Duluth Unified 
Development Code is hereby amended as follows: 
SECTION 1. FINDINGS. 
Pursuant to Article 5 of the Duluth Unified Development Code, the City Council finds that it is appropriate 
to grant a modification to the original PUD, for the following reasons:: 
A. The modification is suitable given the use and development of adjacent and nearby properties. 
 
B. The proposed modification is not anticipated to adversely affect the existing use or usability of 
adjoining or nearby properties as conditions will be imposed on the development that address uses 
and intensities, architecture and design, landscape and screening, transportation and parking, 
roadways, stormwater facilities, street lighting and signage. 
 
C. The proposed modification is not anticipated to cause an excessive or burdensome use of existing

INTERGOVERNMENTAL AGREEMENT 
 
This INTERGOVERNMENTAL AGREEMENT (hereinafter “IGA”) is made and entered 
into as of the 11th day of August 2025, by and between the CITY OF DULUTH, GEORGIA, a 
Georgia municipal corporation (the “City”), and the URBAN REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY OF 
THE CITY OF DULUTH, GEORGIA, a public body corporate and politic duly created and 
existing under the laws of the State of Georgia (the “URA”). This IGA is intended to and shall be 
construed as an intergovernmental agreement under the provisions of the Constitution of the State 
of Georgia. 
 
W I T N E S S E T H: 
 
 
WHEREAS, the URA desires to purchase a certain parcel of property known as 3135 
Buford Highway within the incorporated limits of the City of Duluth Georgia in Gwinnett County, 
Georgia, in furtherance of its Urban Redevelopment Plan. Said property being more particularly 
described in Exhibit “A” and Shown on Exhibit “B” attached hereto and incorporated herein by 
reference (hereinafter the “Subject Property”); and 
 
WHEREAS, the City has acquired funds through a blight tax which are restricted but 
which may be used to purchase the subject property and desires that the blight tax funds be used 
to purchase the subject property for remediation, including demolition of existing structures. 
 
NOW THEREFORE, for and in consideration of the payment of Ten (10 Dollars 
($10.00), the covenants and promises set forth herein intended to benefit the citizens of Duluth by 
providing for future development in the Downtown Development Area which will be consistent 
with the Urban Redevelopment Plan and will assist in the redevelopment and revitalization of the 
Downtown Development Area, and for other good and valuable consideration the receipt and 
sufficiency of which is hereby acknowledged, the parties do hereby agree to the following terms: 
 
1. 
The City shall transfer to the URA FIVE HUNDRED THREE THOUSAND FIVE 
HUNDRED TEN DOLLARS and NINETY ONE CENTS ($503,510.91) to 
facilitate the purchase of the subject property. 
 
2. 
The Mayor, Mayor Pro Tem, City Manager, City Clerk, and City Attorney, and/or 
their appropriate designees are hereby authorized to complete the transfer of the 
funds and to take any and all action necessary and appropriate to carry out the intent 
of this Agreement between the parties. 
 
3. 
The URA will use the transferred funds to purchase the subject property and 
demolish existing structures on the subject property; 
 
4. 
The URA agrees that in the event the subject property is sold for more than EIGHT 
HUNDRED FIFTY THOUSAND and 00/100 DOLLARS ($850,000.00) all such 

 
 
excess funds shall be remitted to the City of Duluth, Georgia. 
 
5. 
This Agreement and the rights and obligations of the parties hereto shall be 
governed, construed, and interpreted according to the laws of the State of Georgia. 
 
6. 
This Agreement expresses the entire understanding and agreement between the 
parties hereto. 
 
7. 
The invalidity of any one or more phrases, sentences, clauses or sections contained 
in this Agreement shall not affect the remaining portions of this Agreement or any 
part thereof. 
 
8.

original, and all of which shall constitute but one and the same instrument. 
 
9. 
No waiver, amendment, release, or modification of this Agreement shall be 
effective unless made in writing and executed by both parties hereto.

Community Development & Engineering, Margie Pozin forward to present an 
ordinance to amend an existing PUD (Planned Unit Development) for parcel 
R6322 133 to allow for a change in density for Case Z2025-002. 
Ms. Pozin said that Owner/Applicant FP Peachtree Industrial, LLC, is requesting a 
modification to the existing PUD (Planned Unit Development) on approximately 
32 acres to allow for the conversion of 64 three bedroom apartment units into 128 
one bedroom apartment units to meet current market demand. She described 
the existing conditions, nearby zoning, and Character Area for the Urban 
Neighborhood District. She showed the site plan, elevations and noted staff 
findings showing consistency with the Comprehensive Plan. 
 
Ms. Pozin referenced the reduction in number of three bedroom apartment units 
and noted that the City would still have approximately 345, which is still a 
considerable number. She discussed the sidewalk gap and landscape buffers that 
will both be improved as part of this project. All of the requirements from the 
original PUD are still going to be applied, and this follows the property, not the 
ownership of the property, so if the property sells, the conditions remain. They are 
limited to a maximum of 168 one-bedroom units and 152 two-bedroom units, so 
they will have a total unit count of 320. They are also required to develop six 
additional parking spaces, with administrative leeway to approve up to twelve 
additional spots if the need arises. 
 
The roofing equipment must be screened from public view, and the sidewalk and 
buffer enhancements will happen prior to certificate of occupancy issuance. The 
Planning Commission recommended approval with conditions at their July 7, 
2025 hearing.

Dakota Carruthers of 1075 Peachtree Street NE and Jeremy Leventhal of 100 South 
Commons, Pittsburgh, PA presented additional information regarding the 
renovation. The existing multifamily community was developed in 1985. The 
property was acquired in 2021 and there have since been upgrades to amenities, 
additions of amenities, and even some renovations in the units. Staff visited the 
site and toured some of the units to see where the wall would go up, where the 
new kitchen would go, and how these would be separated. They are proposing no 
changes other than a walkway to the new doorway that will be created for the 
new units. 
 
Ms. Carruthers further explained that they feel this meets the Comprehensive Plan 
especially where it references optimizing the land use without expanding the 
existing footprint. The project is slated to take place over a long period of time as 
the units vacate, so this is not something that's happening immediately. The 
Conditioned property site improvements would be completed before the first CO 
was issued, and gradually the interiors of the individual units would be renovated. 
 
Mr. Leventhal came forward to present. He reported that One-person households 
are the fastest-growing household type in the U.S., now approximately 30 percent 
of all households, up from about 19 percent in 1974. The Foundry, our apartment 
complex, conversion proposal directly serves professionals, empty-nesters, young 
employees seeking smaller, affordable, individual homes. Duluth's rental market is 
missing one-bedrooms. one-bedroom units account for about 27% of the rental 
market in Duluth with approximately 1,500 units out of 5,500 units in total. In 
Atlanta 1-bedroom units compose of 39% of the market and the national average 
is 40%. If you include total inventory of housing, not just rentals, but homes in the 
area, Gwinnett County has only 6 percent of all housing as one-bedrooms. The 
Foundry is requesting the ability to transform all of the 3-bedroom units into 1-
bedroom units over time to not vacate residents. 
 
Councilmember Doss asked about the relational makeup of the residents 
currently renting three-bedroom units, if they are roommate or family situations. 
 
Mr. Leventhal stated that there is a variety in rentals, and the relationship makeup 
extends from roommates to family dwellings. A total of eight buildings are 
included in the plan to restructure the units.

to vacate in order to get the units constructed in a quicker time period, however,

Mayor Whitlock shared a search from Realtor.com for rental units in Duluth. The

1. UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT CODE WORKSHOP 2 
 
 
SUMMARY: 
Staff has been working on reviewing, editing, updating, and correcting items within 
the City's Unified Development Code since mid-2023. 
 
This is the second of two Council workshops where staff will update Mayor and Council 
with proposed content edits to date and answer questions regarding any proposed 
revisions. 
 
IMPACT TO BUDGET: N/A 
 
2. STORMWATER TRANSFER REQUEST 
 
 
 
 
 
SUMMARY: 
The Stormwater Division has approached administration about several emergency 
projects. Accordingly, staff will present to Council an overview of the city's financial 
reserves and the recommended transfer of $1,000,000 to the stormwater utility fund. 
 
IMPACT TO BUDGET: transfer from prior year reserves 
 
3. PURCHASING POLICY AMENDMENT – HB 137 
 
 
 
 
SUMMARY: 
Effective July 1, 2025, House Bill 137 increased the threshold for public works public 
bidding from $100,000 to $250,000. HB 137 exempts public works projects under 
$250,000 from certain bidding and procedural obligations. Thus, projects under 
$250,000 would be governed by the city's adopted purchasing policy. 
 
Given the ongoing rise in costs for construction materials, labor, and services, raising 
the city's internal threshold for public bidding from $100,000 to $250,000 will provide 
staff greater flexibility to manage smaller projects without triggering the formal 
bidding process. Such flexibility would allow staff to respond more efficiently to project 
needs while still maintaining transparency and essential projects can proceed without 
delays.

consistent with limits identified within HB 137. Staff will provide a presentation 
identifying the recommended changes to our adopted policy.

SUMMARY:

opened for a month, during which five applications were received. All five candidates 
were interviewed in the months of June and July by a selection panel composed of a 
council member, the commission chair, and city staff. After thoughtful discussion and 
vote, Marisa Tontaveetong "Ginger" and Shaena Leuthe were selected and 
recommended to fill the vacant seats. They will serve for the remainder of the 
unexpired terms, which end in March 2026. 
 
These two vacancies are “off cycle” appointments: 
• Marisa Tontaveetong "Ginger" to serve the unexpired term of Sheila Harmony, 
which ends in March 2026. 
• Shaena Leuthe to serve the unexpired term of Augustine Emmanuel, which also 
ends in March 2026. 
 
IMPACT TO BUDGET: N/A

Deputy Planning Director Aron Hall came forward to present. The City of Duluth is 
the applicant and is requesting a text amendment to the UDC to allow certain 
office uses with the O-I (Office-Institutional) and O-N (Office – Neighborhood) 
Districts. He showed the current use chart and noted that it should include all 
administrative, financial and professional offices and furthermore to add from the 
NAICS code 561 and 561110. Code 561 are industries in the administrative and 
supportive service subsector group establishments engaged in activities that

Mr. Hall said that the processes employed in this sector are general management, 
personal administration, clerical activities, cleaning activities are often integral 
parts of the activities of establishments found in all sectors of the economy. Code 
561110 is defined as industries that comprise establishments primarily engaged in 
providing a range of day-to-day office administrative services such as financial 
planning, billing, record-keeping, personnel, physical distribution, and logistics for 
others on a contract or fee basis. These establishments do not provide operating 
staff to carry out the complete operations of a business, so these are all just 
clerical. The new use chart would add to C1, C2, HC retail, HC auto, OI, ON, M1, M2,

3. ORDINANCE OF SPECIAL USE – SU2025-001 – 3285 HOWELL MEADOW DR 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Mayor Whitlock opened the public hearing to consider an ordinance to allow a 
special use permit on Parcel 6323 086 located at 3285 Howell Meadow Dr for Case 
SU2025-001. Applicant Susan Clark requested a special use permit to allow the 
keeping of bees on R-100 (Single-Family Residential District). 
 
Deputy Planning Director Aron Hall came forward to present. He summarized the 
location of the property and surrounding zonings. A special use is required to 
allow beekeeping in R100 single-family residential districts. The character area is 
the established neighborhoods district. Forward Duluth, the comprehensive plan 
envisions this character area to serve as the backbone of Duluth's residential 
community. The future land use map envisions this the uses to be low density 
residential. 
 
Mr. Hall provided pertinent bee and beekeeping facts. Beekeepers usually have at 
least two hives for a healthy bee colony. They usually travel between one to two 
miles to forage but are known to travel up to five miles to forage. Bees are not 
aggressive, but they will defend their hives. In early spring, hives contain roughly 
ten to fifteen thousand bees. By summer's end populations can reach from sixty to 
eighty thousand per hive. The honeybee is one of 542 species of bees living in 
Georgia, and it has seen a sharp decline over the last several decades. 
 
Mr. Hall said the proposal is for three beehives. The hives would be placed within 
the side yard and set back from the property line ten feet. The back setback is 80 
feet from the property line. There is an evergreen buffer between the beehives 
and the neighboring property. The property to the rear also has a small evergreen 
hedge and there have not been any code of case violations on this property since 
the Clark's obtained the property over a year ago. 
 
The conditions were outlined, and Staff is recommending approval of conditions 
and Planning Commission recommended approval with conditions at their last 
meeting. Mr. Hall clarified what was meant by the “side” yards; Irvindale is 
considered a front yard (referenced as the northeastern section).

RESOLUTION OF THE CITY OF DULUTH, GEORGIA (the “CITY”) 
AUTHORIZING PARTICIPATION IN AN AMICUS BRIEF IN THE CHANG V. CITY 
OF MILTON APPEAL PENDING BEFORE THE GEORGIA SUPREME COURT 
 
 
WHEREAS, the Chang v. Milton litigation involves a claim of liability against the City 
of Milton, Georgia, for personal injuries due to a 2016 vehicle collision with a fixed obstruction 
(a masonry planter) located on City-owned right of way where the obstruction was outside the 
motoring lanes of travel; 
 
 
WHEREAS, the masonry planter had been at the same location since 1992 and had never 
been the subject of a complaint or prior accident; 
 
 
WHEREAS, at the trial court, the City of Milton was found to be partially at fault and a 
jury awarded money damages against the City of Milton of $35,000,000; 
 
 
WHEREAS, on September 16, 2024, the Court of Appeals affirmed the findings of the 
trial court, City of Milton v. Chang, et. al., 373 Ga. App. 667 (2024) (Court of Appeals ruling); 
 
 
WHEREAS, on June 24, 2025, the Supreme Court of Georgia granted certiorari, Supreme 
Court docket number S25G0476; 
 
 
WHEREAS, the Georgia Supreme Court identified three issues upon which it wanted the 
Parties to focus in their appellate briefing: 
 
1. Is the design and placement of objects on a shoulder of a roadway part of the ministerial 
duty of a municipality to keep its “streets and sidewalks in a reasonably safe condition” 
or is it a governmental function? Compare Mayor, Etc., of Dalton v. Wilson, 118 Ga. 
100 (44 SE 830) (1903) with Town of Fort Oglethorpe v. Phillips, 224 Ga. 834 (165 
SE2d 141) (1968). See generally OCGA § 36-33-1. 
 
2. Is the placement of a planter on the shoulder of a roadway a “defect[] in the public roads 
of [the municipality’s] municipal street system”? See OCGA § 32-4-93 (a). 
 
3. For municipal immunity to be waived under the circumstances of this case, must the 
plaintiff show that the municipality violated its ministerial duty to keep its “streets and 
sidewalks in a reasonably safe condition” and that the planter on the shoulder of the 
roadway is a “defect[] in the public roads of [the municipality’s] municipal street 
system”? Please address the interplay between OCGA § 36-33-1 and OCGA § 32-4-93 
(a). 
 
 
WHEREAS, the CITY believes that answers to the above legal questions are of significant 
value to its citizens and residents; 
 
WHEREAS, the CITY believes that Supreme Court guidance on such questions may lead 
to the Court of Appeals ruling being overturned 

R2025-08 
 
 
WHEREAS, the CITY believes the Court of Appeals ruling is inconsistent with existing 
legal precedent; and, 
 
WHEREAS, the CITY believes that it is in the best interests of the health, welfare, and 
safety of its citizens that the Court of Appeals ruling be reversed and that the questions presented 
by the Supreme Court be answered in a way that benefits Georgia’s’ cities. 
 
NOW THEREFORE, the CITY does hereby authorize participation in an amicus brief 
before the Georgia Supreme Court asking that the Court of Appeals ruling be reversed and that 
the Supreme Court’s three proffered questions be answered in a way that is legally advantageous 
to Georgia’s cities. An amicus brief so tendered may include the City’s name as a participating 
party. 
 
IT IS SO RESOLVED this

A. Table 2-C of the UDC allows “Bees and Bee Products” in R-100 zoning district as a

C. Section 1105 of the UDC establishes the Special Use Considerations. 
 
The Special Use is designed to apply under any one of the following circumstances: 
1. A Special Use listed under the zoning district is desired for development and a

appropriate for the property; or 
 
2. A Special Use listed under the zoning district is desired for development and no

is not likely to be duplicated within the City of Duluth; or

IV. 
PLANNING STAFF REVIEW 
 
The proposal is for three (3) beehives on the approximately half-acre property. Staff was 
made aware of the beehives from the applicant who, after putting up the bee boxes (without 
the bees), was advised that there may be certain laws about keeping bees within the city 
limits. It was at this time that the applicant contacted the Community Development and 
Engineering Department and was informed that their property (R-100, Single-Family 
Residential) would be required to obtain a Special Use Permit. 
 
Staff went out to the property and saw that the bee hives were roughly 80’ from the back 
property line and 10’ from the side property line. Additionally, the side property line has a 
thick evergreen buffer consisting of holly bushes. An accessory structure can be as close as 5’ 
from the property line in the side and rear yard. Staff is recommending in the conditions that 
as long as the bee hives are on the property, there must be an evergreen buffer along the side 
property line. There is also a small evergreen buffer along the back property line which acts 
as a visual buffer between the neighboring property and the bee hives. 
 
Bees are an extremely important part of any ecosystem, our urban ecosystem included. 
According to the website Bees of Georgia (native-bees-of-georgia.ggc.edu) bees pollinate 1 of 
every 3 bites of food we eat (native-bees-of-georgia.ggc.edu). Bees pollinate nearly every 
fruit, nut, and vegetable crop. “Recent estimates suggest that bees contribute $15 billion in 
pollination services to the U.S. economy each year” (id.). While Georgia has 542 species of 
bees, the Apis mellifera (honeybee) are one of the few bees that A. do not live in the ground 
and B. are not solitary. These two facts combined make them a target of misinformation. 
 
Apis mellifera, or the common honeybee, are not native to North America, but have become a 
key part of agriculture (as was sited earlier). Their populations hit a low point with a 
phenomenon called Colony Collapse Disorder, which “occurs when the majority of worker 
bees in a colony disappear and leave behind a queen, plenty of food and a few nurse bees to 
care for the remaining immature bees and the queen” (epa.gov). During the winter of 2006-
2007 beekeepers reported unusually high losses of 30-90 percent of their hives. A few of the 
contributing factors of CCD are pesticides, pathogens, poor nutrition and lack of food (pollen). 
 
There are ways to come back from these sudden losses. Smaller and more dispersed bee hives 
are being set up as hobbies in urban areas. It is staff’s opinion that these hobby bee keepers 
are a benefit to the community. The more pollinator gardens a community sees being

installed is a benefit, as are the pollinators that are attracted to those gardens. 
Honey bees are defensive but not aggressive, meaning they will sting if provoked or when 
defending the hive. An evergreen hedge should provide the necessary buffer to keep any 
intrusion from neighbors away from the bees. The average hive in early spring contains 
roughly 10 – 15,000 bees. At the height of summer these number can swell to 60 – 80,000 
bees. Bees’ forage radius is roughly 1 – 2 miles from the hive, while some fly 3 to five miles, 
meaning that these bees have the potential to pollinate half of the City of Duluth.
