HB 581 Summary and 
Guidance
ACCG & GMA Joint Trainings
October 3rd, 2024
Ryan Bowersox
Assistant General Counsel, GMA
Dante Handel
Associate Director of Governmental Affairs, ACCG

Background: Where Did This Come 
From?
• Legislature entered 2024 session concerned about 
rising property value assessments and in turn 
property tax
• Senate leaders wanted measures to control rapid 
increases in property assessments
• House leaders looked to expand sales tax options
• Various proposals ultimately resulted in HB 581 (& 
HR 1022)

HB 581: Overview 
Signed into law April 18, 2024 (Act 379).
Contingent upon November Statewide Referendum 
(HR 1022)
Major Components:
1.Statewide Floating Homestead Exemption (Part 2)
2.New Local Option Sales Tax (Part 3)
3.Property Tax Procedural Changes​ (Part 1)

Presentation Outline
• When does this bill take effect?
• Who gets a floating homestead exemption?
• What is a floating homestead exemption?
• What is the procedure to opt out and what is the timeline?
• What is the new sales tax?
• Other sales tax revisions
• Other property tax changes
• Policy considerations for local governments
• Other local government considerations

When Does this Bill Take Effect?
• HB 581 is contingent upon the passage of the constitutional 
amendment from HR 1022 on November 5, 2024 which allows 
local governments the ability to opt out of the floating homestead 
exemption. 
• A simple majority is required for passage. 
• If the constitutional amendment fails, all of HB 581 is 
repealed. 
• If the constitutional amendment passes, then the bill takes 
effect January 1, 2025. 

HB 581
Part 1: Statewide Floating Homestead 
Exemption
•
If approved, HB 581 implements a statewide floating homestead exemption for all local 
governments:
•
Counties
•
Cities
•
School Boards
•
A floating homestead is a special type of homestead exemption designed to offset or 
reduce increases in taxable value to the property. 
•
It is also referred to as a base-year or value offset exemption. 
•
Freezes are a type of floating homestead exemption, but do not have an annual 
inflationary adjustment. 

How Does a Floating Homestead Exemption 
Work?
• It works by increasing the value of the exemption to 
offset inflation. 
• For example, if a property had a taxable value of 
$100,000 and the taxable value increased the 
following year due to market changes to 
$110,000, then the exemption ‘floats’ to be worth 
$10,000 of taxable value so the taxpayer still 
pays on the original base year value of 
$100,000. 

How Does HB 581’s Floating Homestead 
Exemption Work?
• The HB 581 floating homestead exemption is unique because the base 
year value is adjusted and will increase by a rate of inflation determined 
by the State Revenue Commissioner – likely CPI. 
• If we take the same property with a $100,000 taxable base year value 
and CPI is 2% the following year, then the base value of $100,000 
may be increased by up to 2% to give an adjusted base year value of 
$102,000. The exemption ‘floats’ to be worth $8,000 of assessed 
value so the taxpayer would pay on a taxable value of $102,000 in 
year 2. 

How Does HB 581’s Floating Homestead 
Exemption Work?
• For homes first receiving this exemption in taxable year 2025, the 
base year assessed value will be the 2024 assessed value. 
• For homes first receiving the exemption in later years, the base year 
assessed value will be the assessed value for the immediately 
preceding year.
• Similar to other homestead exemptions, the value will be reset when 
the home is sold and is adjusted with “substantial property change.”
• Homeowners can not transfer exemption to new property.

How Does HB 581’s Floating Homestead 
Exemption Work?
• The effect of HB 581’s homestead exemption:
• The taxable value of a home may only increase at a 
rate of inflation each year.
• Essentially controlling this will control how much the 
“value” of a home can increase annually.
• Homeowners already granted a homestead will receive 
this exemption automatically.
• Non-homesteaded property (i.e. Commercial) will 
continue to be valued at fair market.

How Does this New Homestead Exemption 
Impact Existing Homestead Exemptions?
• This new floating homestead exemption is in addition to and not in 
lieu of all non-floating homestead exemptions. This will not 
repeal/replace existing homestead exemptions!
• If there is an existing local floating homestead exemption, the 
taxpayer will receive whichever of the two exemptions is more 
beneficial. This is also true if a local floating homestead 
exemption is added in the future. 
• Existing local exemptions, such as the $2,000 of assessed value, 
are added after the floating homestead exemption is calculated. 

How Can a Local Government “Opt Out” of 
the Homestead Exemption?
• Any governing authority may elect to opt out of the floating homestead 
exemption created by HB 581 by following a procedure like the “public 
notification of tax increase” when a full rollback is not taken. 
• The local government must advertise and conduct three public 
hearings of intent to opt out and later adopt a resolution. 
• Must file resolution to Secretary of State by March 1, 2025!
• If procedures are not met, opt out is not effective.

How Can a Local Government “Opt Out” of 
the Homestead Exemption?
• This process may not begin until the bill 
takes effect on January 1, 2025, and must 
be completed by March 1, 2025. 
• A governing authority may not opt-out of 
the statewide floating homestead 
exemption after this deadline. 
• However, the local delegation may pass a 
local Act of the General Assembly to 
implement a local floating homestead 
exemption at any time. 

How Can a Local Government “Opt Out” of 
the Homestead Exemption?
• Important to note: The decision to opt out is 
independent among local governments.
• A county, the cities, and the school board 
may each decide whether to opt out.
• The decision of whether or not to opt out 
will not impact the other local government’s 
homestead exemption.
• This may result in homes having different 
taxable values.

Is the Decision to “Opt Out” or “Stay In” 
Permanent?
• Yes
• No action is needed by the local government to have the homestead 
exemption apply if it is approved in November.
• Once the opt out period has passed, currently there is no future method 
to opt out.
• If a local government opts out, there is no future method to opt in to the HB 
581 exemption.
• Of course, a similar homestead exemption can still be done in 
traditional manner.

HB 581 Timeline
November 5, 2024: Statewide Question on Constitutional Amendment 
January 1, 2025: HB 581 takes effect, if approved
March 1, 2025: Deadline for local governments to “opt out” of homestead 
exemption

HB 581
Part 2: Sales Tax Revisions and FLOST
• HB 581 makes two major changes to 
local sales tax:
• Revises the provisions of O.C.G.A. 48-8-6 
which limits the percentage of local sales 
tax a jurisdiction​ may levy. 
• Creates new local option sales 
tax contingent upon jurisdictions having a 
base year value homestead exemption.

Revised Local Sales Tax Limitation
•
This legislation revises the existing two percent local sales tax cap; exemptions now include:
•
ESPLOST 
•
Up to one percent of the transportation sales taxes, which include:
•
Regional TSPLOST 
•
Single-County TSPLOST
•
Transit SPLOST
•
MARTA
•
One of the specialty pennies, including:
•
The new sales tax for property tax relief created by HB 581
•
Columbus-Muscogee and Macon-Bibb OLOST
•
Augusta-Richmond Coliseum SPLOST
•
MOST for Atlanta and cities connected to its water system (East Point, College Park, 
and Hapeville)

What is the New Sales Tax?
• A new sales tax is created for the limited purpose of property tax relief – 
it may be levied in 0.05 percent increments up to one percent. 
• To be eligible to levy the tax, both the county and all cities within the 
county that levy a property tax must have in effect a floating 
homestead exemption: either the one created by this bill or a local 
floating homestead exemption. 
• It does not matter if the school boards opt out or not since they are 
ineligible to share in the proceeds of the tax without a separate 
constitutional amendment. 

How is the New Sales Tax Implemented?
• The county and city/cities representing at least 
fifty percent of the municipal population of cities 
that levy a property tax must enter into an 
intergovernmental agreement (IGA) calling for 
the tax.
• The IGA shall specify the rate, duration (not to 
exceed five years), and the distribution between 
the county and cities. It will also set the ballot 
question.

How is the New Sales Tax Implemented?
• Following the adoption of the IGA, the 
tax must be approved through local 
referendum.
• Approval by the voters will be required 
to levy the sales tax.
• This is a different vote than the one that 
occurs in November approving the 
constitutional amendment!

How are Cities Not on the IGA Treated? 
• The IGA must also specify a portion of the 
proceeds that the cities not on the IGA will receive.
• Must not be less than the proportion the absent 
municipality’s population bears to the total 
population of all cities within the county that levy a 
property tax. 
• Modelled after LOST absent municipality 
provisions.

How are MOST Cities Treated?
• Cities levying a MOST (Municipal Option Sales Tax 
for Water and Sewer Projects) are excluded. 
• Will not be considered for eligibility and are not 
included in these calculations.
• Tax will not be collected within the city and city can 
not receive the proceeds of this tax. 
• Currently Atlanta, East Point, College Park, & 
Hapeville.

How is the New Tax Collected and 
Distributed?
• Collection of the tax will begin at the start of the next calendar quarter beginning 
more than 50 days after that date (as opposed to eighty days for other local sales 
taxes).
• The Georgia Department of Revenue (DOR) sends the money to the county and 
the county will be responsible for distributing the money to the cities in 
accordance with the IGA. 

How Can the Tax Be Renewed?
• The tax can run up to 5 years.
• Prior to the expiration, if the local governments want to renew, 
it requires:
• Passage of a local Act calling for the reimposition of the 
tax.
• A new IGA between the county and eligible number of 
cities.
• A new referendum to approve the tax by the voters.
• Talk to your local delegation!

How are Funds From the New Sales Tax 
Used?
• Funds must be used exclusively for property tax relief.
• Each taxpayer’s property tax bill shall state the amount by which property tax 
has been reduced because of the imposition of this tax.
• The roll-back rate shall be reduced annually by the millage equivalent of the 
net proceeds of this new tax received by the political subdivision during the 
prior taxable year. 
• If any political subdivision is not in compliance with the use of the proceeds 
from this tax, then the State Revenue Commissioner shall not certify the tax 
digest of that political subdivision until it comes into compliance. 

HB 581
Part 3: Procedural Property Tax Changes
• Created an “estimated roll-back rate” which is 
certified to the tax commissioner/collector by the 
local governments. 
• The estimated roll-back rate is required to be 
included on the assessment notice, replacing 
the previous year’s millage rate.
• Designed to attempt to allow local 
government to give more accurate estimate 
of what tax liability will be.

HB 581
Part 3: Procedural Property Tax Changes
• This gives local governments broad flexibility to set this rate wherever 
they deem appropriate.
• This does not need to be the same millage rate as the rollback rate for 
taxpayer bill of rights.
• If the adopted millage rate exceeds the estimated roll-back rate, then a 
disclaimer is included on the tax bill stating the name of the governing 
authority that exceeded the estimated roll-back rate and that this will 
result in an increase of taxes owed. 

HB 581
Part 3: Procedural Property Tax Changes
• Removed the provision that the sale price is the maximum allowable fair 
market value in the next taxable year. 
• This provision caused the Department of Audits and Accounts (DOAA) to 
change their sales ratio study methodology when it was originally passed 
in 2010, so this change will improve the sales ratio study and prevent 
penalties on local governments and their taxpayers. 
• This legislation also allows the Board of Assessors to appeal the sales ratio 
study directly instead of requiring a local government to appeal on their 
behalf. 

HB 581
Part 3: Procedural Property Tax Changes
• Modifying the three-year lock for appeals so the taxpayer only receives the lock if 
they receive a value reduction upon appeal. 
• Updating the settlement conference statute so that if neither the taxpayer nor their 
representative participates in good faith, then the taxpayer shall not receive the 
benefit of the temporary 15 percent reduction in taxes owed and shall not be 
awarded attorney’s fees.
• Requiring that the chief appraiser ensure that every parcel in the county be 
appraised at least every three years. 

Policy Considerations for Local Governments
• As with any other local government choice, this is a policy decision with 
pros and cons to be considered. 
• The floating homestead exemption rewards homeowners, especially those 
that reside in the community for a long period of time after this legislation 
takes effect. 
• Taxes do not disappear – they only shift: in this instance, the taxes are 
shifting from homestead properties to all other property types (commercial, 
agricultural, industrial, residential non-homestead). 

Policy Considerations for Local Governments
• Taxation is a formula: taxable value multiplied by the millage rate gives the 
property tax revenue to meet local budgets. 
• Since the floating homestead exemption slows the growth in value for 
residential homestead properties, it will create some upward pressure on 
the millage rate. The effects of a floating homestead increase over time, 
so this will have a smaller impact in the early years and a larger impact in 
the later years. 
• Counties and cities may more easily increase the millage rate if needed than 
schools due to the 20-mill cap, which may only be exceeded after the 
successful passage of a local referendum. 

Other Local Government Considerations
• Each local government (counties, cities, and schools) may independently 
decide whether to opt out.
• This decision does not impact the homestead exemptions but cities and 
counties can impact eligibility for the FLOST.
• Every local government has a unique digest mix of property types. Local 
officials are encouraged to contact their Chief Appraiser for information 
regarding their specific situation. Some communities will better be able to 
support a floating homestead exemption than others. 

Other Local Government Considerations
• The referendum is likely to be very popular and citizens may not understand 
a local government’s decision. 
• Even if your local government decides to opt out of the HB 581 floating 
homestead exemption, nothing precludes your local delegation of the 
General Assembly from passing a local Act putting a local floating 
homestead to referendum in your jurisdiction. 
• If a local government decides to opt out, it may be best practice to explain 
this decision to the public and the local delegation.

Other Local Government Considerations
• Many jurisdictions have existing floating homestead exemptions. These 
typically apply only to M&O millage rates, but not to special service districts 
(SSDs). 
• The HB 581 floating homestead exemption applies to special service 
districts in addition to M&O but does not apply to bond millage. 
• If a local government that has a floating homestead exemption already 
in place does not opt out, then their special service districts will be 
affected by the new floating homestead exemption. 
• A local government may consider opting out to avoid confusion. 

Other Local Government Considerations
• While the decision to opt out of the floating homestead exemption is 
independent, instituting the new sales tax requires collaboration between the 
county and cities.
• The county and all cities in the county that levy a property tax must have a 
base year homestead exemption in place (statewide or through a local Act).
• The county and cities should discuss the option of the sales tax before 
expiration of the opt out period.
• Know the distribution is determined by the IGA, so this should be discussed 
early.
• A local Act is required for renewal, so involve your local delegation.

Next Steps….

(live and recorded).

presentation

released today!

• ACCG Advancing Georgia's 
Counties

1. TAYLOR PARK RESTROOM EXPANSION {A}
City Manager James Riker presented three potential design changes associated with a
restroom expansion at Taylor Park. Option 1 includes men, women’s and family
restrooms. Option 2 does not include the family restroom and has more storage;
Option 3 has limited storage area.
Following discussion, the council agreed to move forward with preparing design, costs
and funding source for Option 2 and to bring back to the council for further discussion
and budgeting.

2. STORMWATER PROGRAM - OFFICIAL STATEMENTS OF PURPOSE _ {B}
Stormwater Coordinator Alyssa Gilhooly came forward to present.
To better position the city for grant applications as the stormwater program grows,
staff has prepared a program description, a mission statement, and a vision statement.
In addition, staff plans to develop a short-term work program from the overall list of
projects, by year, that is fiscally constrained. It will be reviewed and adjusted each year
to reflect new projects, completed projects, and unforeseen/emergency projects, and
will be published for accountability. Staff plans to implement these statements
starting on November 1, 2024.

[page 2]
M&C Work Session Notes
October 28, 2024
Page 2 of 4
To apply for stormwater grants, the city must have a vision and mission statement for
the department. The goals and objectives include Infrastructure Management,
Environmental Sustainability, Pollution Prevention, Regulation Compliance, Public
Education and outreach, and Continuing Education.
The Mission Statement is “to serve the City of Duluth and protect water resources by
safely managing rainwater through efficient storm drainage systems.” The Vision
Statement is “we aspire to strengthen our community through sustainable and
innovative stormwater management that is resilient to environmental challenges.”
Ms. Gilhooly outlined the next steps, beginning with work on the Short-term Work
Program.
Council complimented staff on the formal documentation for the program.

3. HOUSE BILL 581 UPDATE {C}
Assistant City Manager/Finance Ken Sakmar came forward to provide an update on
House Bill 581 which was signed into law April 18, 2024, and is contingent upon passing
of a statewide voter referendum in November. The major components include a
potential statewide Floating Homestead Exemption and new Local Option Sales Tax.
The 2024 valuations would be considered “base” amounts. If the exemption is
approved, those with homestead currently would automatically receive this. It would
not affect any exemptions that are currently in effect. However, cities, counties and
school boards would have the option to “opt out” of the new formula but would have
to do so rather quickly, prior to March 1, 2025.

Mr. Sakmar outlined the sales tax revisions and explained that HB 581 revises the
provisions of O.C.G.A. 48-8-6 which limits the percentage of local sales tax a jurisdiction
may levy, and also creates new local option sales tax contingent upon jurisdictions
having a base year value homestead exemption. He described some of the impacts of
each.
City Manager James Riker noted that the first decision point is whether the council
wishes to opt out. Public hearings would be required with a short timeline. If voter
support is broad, it becomes a political perception to not curb control of assessments,
which are not in check at the moment. Long term spending should be monitored
closely, but inaction does not freeze the city's current millage rate if it becomes an
issue in the future.
Staff was directed to work through a process and timeline whereby the city could opt
out if so desired, present an alternative tax savings plan for homestead citizens, and
present back to council.

4. RED CLAY THEATRE UPDATE {D}

City Manager James Riker presented an update on potential design changes to the
interior and exterior of the Red Clay Theatre. Budget to be determined based on final
designs.

Council directed staff to move forward with obtaining costs for redesign, flexibility for
possible removal of trees (replace with large piece of art), etc.

5. BUFORD HWY - PEDESTRIAN FACILITY BEAUTIFICATION {E}
Community Development/Engineering Development Director Margie Pozin
presented. At their 2024 strategic retreat, council requested upgrades to pedestrian
facilities on Buford Highway on pavement markings for refreshed/decorative
crosswalks. She also noted that the Brock Road intersection should be updated as
well, since all three intersections are “gateways” to downtown.

Ms. Pozin obtained and presented costs for the work, required agreements and
agencies to coordinate with. The weather has to be above 45 degrees, and the vendor
agreed to hold pricing as is until the spring. She also requested that the span wire at
Brock Road be replaced with a mast arm signal. There is no funding set aside at this
point.

Staff was directed to move forward including the Brock Road intersection in the plan,
at the same time as Buford Highway if SPLOST transportation funding is available,
and waiting to consider the mast arm signal until the nearby property is developed.

6. TAX ALLOCATION DISTRICT (TAD)- URA UPDATE {F}

City Manager James Riker gave an update on recent activities, potential projects and a
financial update relating to the Urban Redevelopment Agency (URA) Tax Allocation
District. Of the $27,250,000 there is approximately $3,000,000 remaining.

Mr. Riker outlined the areas of redevelopment and potential uses for each site.

7. STAFFING REQUEST —- POLICE DEPARTMENT PSA
Chief Carruth explained that a command staff position has recently become vacant
due to retirement. The Public Safety Ambassador (PSA) program which has been in
effect since January 2024 has proven to be a very successful program. She did not
intend to backfill the command staff position, and therefore would like to re-classify a
command staff position to a third Ambassador position. This would be a reduction in
salary; however, another dedicated vehicle would be required.

The council supported the request.

1. ORDINANCES TO AMEND DULUTH CODE-BOARDS/COMMISSIONS

work with the City Attorney in preparing amendments to standardize the content 
and language in each of the board/commission ordinances relating to 
appointment of officers, meetings, quorum, compensation, ethics, term limits, 
service/removal clause, attendance, open meetings, oaths, and background

under the Unified Development Code (UDC), the URA and DDA are governed by 
State Law, the TADAC is founded on an intergovernmental agreement with 
Gwinnett County, and currently no changes are being proposed to the Ethics 
ordinance. Approval of this item approves ordinances O2024-38, 47, 48, 49 and 50

presented.

The Garden Club of Duluth has proposed improving and maintaining certain

and the City. DDA will provide funding and guidance. The IGA allows the Garden

4. ORDINANCE TO AMEND BUDGET -$9,400 – VEHICLES 
 
The Police Department sold a police vehicle, drone, and seven (7) bicycles at 
auction. After commission and fees, the city received $9,400. Staff is requesting 
the $9,400 be added to Police Vehicles - Consolidated Vehicle Maintenance - 
Vehicles line item, including associated transfers. Approval of this item authorizes 
ordinance BA-FY25-10 to amend the FY25 budget as presented. 
 
5. ORDINANCE TO AMEND BUDGET -$29,000 – FOX ST EASEMENT 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
For connectivity reasons, staff acquired a permanent sidewalk easement from a 
Fox Street property owner, Mr. Chavez to install a sidewalk. The cost of the 
easement was $29,000 and was paid out of existing budgeted project funds. 
 
These funds need to be replaced to cover a shortfall on existing projects. 
Therefore, staff is requesting $29,000 in unallocated 2023 SPLOST Transportation 
funds be added to Transportation/Infrastructure Improvements - Paved Streets - 
Repairs & Maintenance of Streets/Sidewalks line item, including associated 
transfers. Approval of this item authorizes BA-FY25-12 to amend the FY25 budget. 
 
6. ORDINANCE TO AMEND BUDGET -$9,982 – TEMPORARY EASEMENT 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
To complete the necessary easements for the construction of the sanitary sewer 
line in the Hill community, the city acquired an additional temporary easement 
from Mount Carmel Baptist Church for $15,000. Additional project funding is 
needed to complete the acquisition. Project funding of $5,018.56 was available to 
offset some of the cost; staff is requesting a budget amendment of $9,982 to make 
up the balance. Staff is requesting $9,982 in 2021 American Rescue Plan Act funds 
be added to American Rescue Plan Act 2021 - New Sewer Services - Land line item. 
Approval of this item authorizes ordinance BA-FY25-11 to amend the FY25 budget.

1. AWARD OF BID/AMEND FY25 BUDGET – PUBLIC SAFETY HVAC 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The Mayor and Council to consider awarding a contract for the Public Safety HVAC 
and AHU Replacement. 
 
The HVAC Systems at the Public Safety Building are original to the building and 
circa 2005. Accordingly, staff published a Request for Proposal (RFP) for 
replacement of the systems. Staff received two responses, and following an 
evaluation by an outside consultant it was determined there was only one 
responsive proposer. Accordingly, staff is recommending that the contract be 
awarded to John F. Pennebaker Co in the amount of $ 996,655. Given the 
complexity of the system staff is also recommending that a budget amendment 
in the amount of $996,655 with 20% contingency for a total amount of $ 1,195,986 
be approved. 
 
Additionally, staff is requesting approval of a budget amendment BA-FY25-13 to 
add $1,195,986 in unallocated 2023 SPLOST Public Safety funds to Police Capital 
Projects - Police - Buildings line item, including associated transfers. 
 
2. AUTHORIZATION FOR IGA – DOVER DRIVE SPEED HUMPS 
 
At discussed at the August 26 work session, Gwinnett County has been asked by 
several citizens to install speed humps on Dover Drive. Dover Drive is along the 
edge of the Duluth city limit, and the speed humps would affect city residents in 
the Bromley Rowe neighborhood. Once an intergovernmental agreement (IGA) is 
signed, the County will circulate a petition among the financially affected 
properties. Four Duluth incorporated properties would be required to pay $12/year 
to Gwinnett County for the speed hump installation and maintenance if the 
County's petition for speed humps gets enough support. Those four will have an 
opportunity to review and sign the petition as well. 
 
Approval of the IGA allows Gwinnett County to move forward with their process 
which may or may not result in speed humps on Dover Drive. Denial of the IGA 
prohibits the County from determining level of interest in speed humps and keeps 
them from being able to install them in this location. Staff is requesting Council 
approve the IGA to allow the County to move forward with their process to assist 
the citizens of that area with traffic calming, if the citizens so desire.

committee or task force shall have voting power or authority to obligate funds from the PAAF. The 
mayor or council representative to DPAC or their designee shall chair any committee or task force. 
Sec. 2-272. Performing Arts and Acquisition Fund. 
(a) Accounting. The performing art and acquisition fund ("PAAF") shall be a separate, special revenue 
fund as part of the city's overall fund structure into which public art donations and funding are 
deposited, transferred and used for the acquisition, commissioning, performance, exhibition and 
conservation of public art as recommended by DPAC and approved by the city manager or 
designee. The funds shall be included as part of the city's main operating account for banking 
purposes. 
 
(b) Developer/builder contributions. The planning and development department shall institute a 
process whereby prior to the issuance of any development permit, certificate of completion, or 
certificate of occupancy, the applicant must meet with DPAC representatives. Donations shall not 
be required, nor shall there be any bias for or against any applicant based on their decision to 
participate in the art program. The purpose of the meeting shall be for education and awareness of 
the impact of art on the community and the economy. As part of the development and/or 
construction process, all applicants with projects in excess of one hundred thousand dollars 
($100,000.00) in value shall be referred to DPAC for the purpose of educating the applicant on 
opportunities for contribution to the arts as articulated in the city public arts master plan. 
Developers and builders shall be encouraged by designated members of the DPAC to voluntarily 
contribute an art project or amount of money equal to the value of one (1) percent of new, non-
city initiated, construction or renovation projects, excluding projects that have their own master 
art plan.

INTERGOVERNMENTAL AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE CITY OF 
DULUTH, GEORGIA AND THE DOWNTOWN DEVELOPMENT 
AUTHORITY OF DULUTH, GEORGIA FOR DOWNTOWN 
LANDSCAPING SERVICES 
 
This Agreement is hereby entered into between the City of Duluth (hereinafter referred to as 
"CITY") and the Downtown Development Authority of Duluth, Georgia (hereinafter referred to as 
"DDA"). This agreement is intended to and shall be construed as an intergovernmental agreement 
under the provisions of the Constitution of the State of Georgia. 
WHEREAS, both parties believe that the downtown landscaping is an asset of the public space 
requiring additional tending and care commensurate with its value and importance to the greater 
downtown experience and would beneﬁt from the consistent eﬀorts provided by the local 
community; and 
WHEREAS, the DDA has an interest in improving the appearance of existing landscaping beds 
which consist of the installation of plants, landscaping, and other aesthetic improvements 
(herein referred to as “Landscaping”) in the downtown Duluth area, bounded on the north by 
Hill Street, on the east by the city's right-of-way line for Highway 120, on the west by Hardy 
Street and on the south by the Norfolk Southern railroad tracks; and 
 
WHEREAS, the DDA has an interest in working with local volunteer community groups to carry 
out such Landscaping projects; an 
WHEREAS, the CITY and DDA wish to formalize the relationship between the Parties by setting 
forth a series of mutual expectations with regard to the installation of small scale landscaping 
improvements and stewardship of the downtown landscaping; 
NOW THEREFORE, in consideration of the mutual covenants, promises and commitments herein, 
the parties agree as follows: 
WITNESSETH 
1. The CITY authorizes the DDA to enter into agreements with a list of approved by the City 
Manager of third-party organizations, contractors, and non-proﬁt community groups for the 
installation and care of small-scale landscaping improvements on public properties in 
downtown Duluth. Speciﬁcally, the CITY authorizes the DDA to install landscaping 
improvements in any existing landscaping beds in the publicly owned area bounded on the 
north by Hill Street, on the east by the city's right-of-way line for Highway 120, on the west by 
Hardy Street and on the south by the Norfolk Southern railroad tracks after approval from the 
City Manager; 
2. The small-scale landscaping improvements authorized under this agreement shall not include 
the construction or placement of statues, art, pillars, monuments or any decorative pieces. 

2 
3. The CITY will continue to maintain existing landscaping service contracts for the downtown 
area and will include within such contracts maintenance of the approved small-scale 
landscaping improvements made by the DDA. 
4. DDA will be responsible for the cost of installation of the landscaping improvements installed 
pursuant to this agreement and may from time to time invite volunteers to perform routine 
maintenance to supplement the existing landscaping service contracts provided by the CITY. 
5. Should the CITY in its sole discretion determine that the Landscaping installed by the DDA 
would cause hardship to the CITY, then the DDA will remove the Landscaping that was installed 
by or for the DDA and restore landscaping bed to the standard for all downtown landscaping 
beds.

State of Georgia.

A. How the proposed special use will allow a use that is suitable in view of the use and development of

threshold for requirement of special use permit so will maintain a suitable view of use for patrons of Downtown 
Duluth. With the increase of office tenants in Downtown Duluth, through the addition of CoHatch and Thrive, 
walkable fitness options are in increasing demand. The addition of a pilates studio and yoga studio will also help 
fill a void in fitness options on the Town Green. Furthermore, the addition of retail to 3150-3160 Main St adds 
vibrancy to the Main Street Corridor and further activates the downtown as visitors travel southwest along the 
Town Green.

Literal Interpretation of the Unified Development Code (UDC) 
 
A. Table 2-C of the UDC allows “yoga, pilates and similar studios” in CBD zoning district 
by-right unless the commercial use occupies more than 3,500 square feet in which 
case Special Use approval from the Duluth City Council is required. 
 
B. Section 1101.02 of the UDC states if a proposed use is not allowed by right under the 
existing zoning on a property, a request for an amendment to the Official Zoning Map 
(often called a “rezoning”) must be approved prior to development, construction, or

C. Section 1105 of the UDC establishes the Special Use Considerations. 
 
The Special Use is designed to apply under any one of the following circumstances: 
1. A Special Use listed under the zoning district is desired for development and a 
more intensive zoning district containing that use, as a use by right would not be 
appropriate for the property; or 
 
2. A Special Use listed under the zoning district is desired for development and no 
zoning district contains that use as a use by right; or 
 
3. A unique use not addressed in any zoning district is desired for development and 
is not likely to be duplicated within the City of Duluth; or 
 
4. The density of development may be affected by the height of a building; or 
 
5. The neighboring properties may be affected by the height of any structure; or 
 
6. The Special Use would be consistent with the needs of the neighborhood or the 
community as a whole, be compatible with the neighborhood and would not be 
in conflict with the overall objective of the Comprehensive Plan. 
 
In order to accommodate these particular uses, Special Use approval allows the City Council 
to approve such a use on a particular parcel without changing the general zoning district.

The subject property is located in the Downtown Core. FORWARDuluth envisions this

amenities. The Future Land Use Map (FLUM) envisions the uses to be

IV. 
PLANNING STAFF REVIEW 
 
Section 317 of the UDC states that special use approval is required for commercial services 
businesses that exceed 3,500 square feet in the CBD zoning district. Staff understands that 
historically, this piece of code was to deter commercial services that did not have high levels 
of customer traffic or the potential for high levels of customer traffic, such as a bank, to occupy 
such a large amount of “dead” space. 
 
Although the pilates/yoga use would take up 4,727 square feet, it is split between three suites 
of the building and two different businesses (PowerUp Pilates and Lift Yoga). There were two 
options for the businesses to occupy the spaces in this particular building: 1. In order to avoid 
the special use they would have had to enclose the cased opening between the suites and put 
in a fire rated wall that would separate the two distinct businesses. This would have made it 
a use by-right in downtown since each business would be occupying a space less than 3,500 
square feet but would have been necessary for fire approval. It would have been a high cost 
burden for each business. Or, 2. They ask for a special use so that each business can occupy 
the same space with only a cased opening separating them. 
 
These particular uses will assist in activating downtown during most hours. Businesses in 
downtown may benefit from the added morning and afternoon foot traffic. Both Thrive and 
CoHatch employees may benefit from having pilate and yoga facilities within walking 
distance.

In addition to the general regulations and restrictions applying to all sign classifications, billboard signs

a. All applications for billboards shall be accompanied by written permission of the owner of the 
property on which the proposed sign is to be placed, a site plan showing the proposed location

removed when a Land Disturbance (i.e., Clearing, Grubbing, Grading or Development) Permit is 
issued for development on the property on which a billboard is located. 
c. Location and Spacing. 
1. No billboard shall be placed within 500 feet of a residence, church, school, park or 
cemetery.

the right-of-way of the street or streets on which such billboard is located, and provided 
further that no billboard may be located closer than 500 feet to another billboard in any 
direction.

vegetation shall be cut or removed in locating or erecting a billboard.

one sign face or exceed 45 feet in overall height as measured from undisturbed grade to the top

Advertising Act, O.C.G.A. 32-6-70 et seq.

202.03 Interpretation of Zoning District Boundaries 
The planning Director, or designee, shall interpret any ambiguity in accordance with the following principals: 
Where uncertainty exists with respect to the location and boundaries shown on the Official Zoning Map, the following 
rules shall apply: 
A. Boundaries that Follow Lot Lines 
1. A boundary shown on the Official Zoning Map as following a lot line or parcel boundary shall be 
construed as following the lot line or parcel boundary as it actually existed at the time the zoning 
boundary was established as determined on the basis of the legal descriptions associated with approved 
zoning applications, or, lacking such legal descriptions, on the basis of the location of the boundary as 
depicted on the Official Zoning Map along with any dimensions shown. 
2. If, after the establishment of the zoning boundary, a property line adjustment is made based upon a court 
ruling, the zoning boundary shall be construed to move with the lot line or parcel boundary. 

O2024-44 
B. Boundaries that Do Not Follow Lot Lines 
1. Where the ordinance establishing a zoning boundary identifies the boundary as following a particular 
natural feature such as a ridgeline, contour line, a river, stream, lake or other water course or reflects a 
clear intent that the boundary follow the feature, the boundary shall be construed as following the feature 
as it actually exists and extends to the centerline of that feature. If after the establishment of the boundary, 
such a natural feature should move as a result of natural processes (slippage, subsidence, erosion, 
flooding, sedimentation, etc.), the boundary shall be construed as moving with the natural feature and 
shall extend to that features centerline. 
2. Where a zoning boundary shown on the Official Zoning Map is approximately following a street, county 
road, state highway, an interstate highway or a railroad and/or railroad right-of-way, it shall be construed 
as following and extending to the centerline of the street, county road, state highway, interstate highway 
or railroad and/or railroad right-of-way. If after the establishment of the boundary, the centerline of the 
street, county road, state highway, interstate highway or railroad and/or railroad right-of-way should be 
moved as a result of its widening or a minor realignment (such as at an intersection), the boundary shall 
be construed as moving with and extending to the centerline of said feature. 
3. A boundary shown on the Official Zoning Map as approximately parallel to, or as an apparent extension 
of, a feature described above shall be construed as being actually parallel to, or an extension of, that 
feature. 
4. If a zoning boundary splits an existing lot or parcel, the metes and bounds description, if one was 
submitted at the time the zoning boundary was established, shall be used to establish the boundary. 
5. If the specific location of the boundary cannot be determined from application of the above rules to the 
Official Zoning Map, it shall be determined by scaling the mapped boundary’s distance from other 
features on the map. 
C. Any property that is interpreted to be unzoned shall be construed as being zoned RA-200 (Residential-

and eventually make it to larger streams or rivers. In order for these drainage easements to

I. 
PURPOSE AND DESCRIPTION OF THE REQUEST 
The purpose of the rezoning request (Z2024-003) is to rezone all railroad right-of-way and 
property from what it is currently zoned (which varies throughout the city) to a uniformed 
zoning of M-1 (light Industrial District). 
 
Maps detailing the new zoning of the railroad property and right-of-way is attached hereto 
as Exhibit “A”. 
 
II. 
EXISTING CONDITIONS 
 
The subject property totals roughly 6 miles in length and is developed by Norfolk Southern 
as an active rail line. The subject property bisects the City boundary line at Suwanee Creek 
on the northeaster entryway and runs through the Cty at its terminus running under North 
Berkely Lake Road to the southwest. 
 
 
III. 
ZONING HISTORY 
 
The current zoning of the railroad right-of-way has been interpreted to begin at the center 
line of the track and run generally parallel to the zoning boundary adjacent to it. However, 
the railroad is not considered by all to be just right-of-way, but real property and therefore 
must be properly zoned. Staff is recommending that all railroad property and right-of-way be 
zoned M-1 (light industrial district) and be shown on the official zoning map of the City as 
such. 
 
There are a few spur tracks that exist within the City limits that do not belong to Norfolk 
Southern. These spur tracks that do not belong to Norfolk Southern are already zoned 
appropriately on the parcels on which they exist. 
 
IV. 
REVIEW OF THE REQUEST 
 
1. 
Literal Interpretation of the Unified Development Code (UDC) 
 
 
A. Section 1101.02 of the UDC states if a proposed use is not allowed by right under the 
existing zoning on a property, a request for an amendment to the Official Zoning Map 
(often called a “rezoning”) must be approved prior to development, construction, or 
occupancy. 
 
2. 
Standards Governing the Exercise of Zoning Power 
 
Section 1104.02 of the UDC establishes the standards governing the exercise of zoning 
power. The following standards are relevant in balancing the interest and promoting 

 
 
Z2024-003 
 
 
 
 
3 | P a g e 
 
 
 
 
 
the public health, safety, morality, and general welfare against the right to the 
unrestricted use of property: 
A. 
Whether the zoning proposal will permit a use that is suitable in view of the use 
and development of adjacent and nearby property. 
 
B. 
Whether the zoning proposal will adversely affect the existing use or usability 
of adjacent or nearby property. 
 
C. 
Whether the zoning proposal will result in a use that will or could cause an 
excessive or burdensome use of existing streets, transportation facilities, 
utilities, or schools. 
 
D. 
Whether the zoning proposal is consistent with the Land Use Policy Plan, 
Comprehensive Plan, transportation plans, or other plans adopted for guiding 
development within the City of Duluth. 
 
E. 
Whether there are other existing or changing conditions affecting the use and 
development of property that give supporting grounds for either approval or 
disapproval of the zoning or special use proposal. 
 
 
3. 
Literal Interpretation of FORWARDuluth, Plan 2040 (Comprehensive Plan) 
 
The railroad property runs through the Established Neighborhood Character Area, 
Buford Highway North Corridor Character Area, Core Neighborhood District, Buford 
Highway South Corridor Character Area, North Berkeley Industrial District and along 
the north section of North Berkeley International Village Character Area. Like the 
zoning and the character areas, the FLUM (Future Land Use Map) shows the railroad 
property encompassing multiple categories including Commercial/Retail/Office, 
Industrial, Institutional, Mixed Use and Residential. However, the railroad is already 
developed and has a very low likelihood of being developed into anything other than 
railroad. 
 
 
 
 
V. 
PLANNING STAFF REVIEW 
 
This rezone request is to create a uniformed zoning designation over the entire +/- 6 mile 
stretch of railroad property. No other substantive changes are being requested for the 
railroad property.

single chiller calculated per the method defined by AHRI 550/590 and intended for operating 
conditions other than the AHRI standard rating conditions.

INTERGOVERNMENTAL AGREEMENT BETWEEN GWINNETT COUNTY AND THE CITY 
OF DULUTH REGARDING THE GWINNETT COUNTY SPEED HUMP PROGRAM 
This Agreement (hereinafter referred to as "Agreement") made by and between the City 
of Duluth, a municipal corporation chartered by the State of Georgia and headquartered 
at 3167 Main Street, Duluth, GA 30096 (hereinafter referred to as "CITY") and Gwinnett 
County, Georgia, a political subdivision of the State of Georgia headquartered at 75 
Langley Drive, Lawrenceville, Georgia 30046, (hereinafter referred to as "COUNTY") each 
of whom has been duly authorized to enter into this Agreement. Both COUNTY and CITY 
are collectively referred to as “parties” or individually referred to as “party”. 
WITNESSETH 
WHEREAS, the parties to this Agreement are governmental units located within 
Gwinnett County, Georgia and are authorized by law to enter into intergovernmental 
agreements; and 
WHEREAS, the parties hereto are interested in serving the needs of the citizens of 
Gwinnett County by allowing and administrating the installation of asphaltic speed 
humps to moderate speeds on residential streets; and 
WHEREAS, the COUNTY has provided the CITY a copy of the Gwinnett County 
Speed Hump Program Manual (hereinafter referred to as “Program Manual”); 
NOW, THEREFORE, in consideration of the mutual promises and understandings 
herein made, the parties hereto do consent and agree as follows: 
1. The COUNTY will evaluate the need for speed humps as part of a residential speed 
control district and will plan their placement on the respective streets which are 
located both within the limits of the CITY as well as within the unincorporated 
boundaries of the COUNTY. 
2. No speed hump installation will proceed unless all requirements outlined in the 
Gwinnett County Speed Hump Program Manual are met. 
3. The COUNTY will prepare work orders for the contractor for the installation of speed 
humps. The speed humps will be constructed to the specifications as outlined in the 
Program Manual. The COUNTY will monitor, inspect, and perform a final inspection 
of all speed hump installations, and will hold the contractor responsible for all 
specifications indicated in the speed hump installation contract. 
4. Pursuant to the Program Manual, the COUNTY will collect an annual assessment for 
the costs associated with the maintenance and repair of speed humps from each 
lot, whether developed or not, that is located within a Special Assessment District 
created pursuant to Chapter 86 of the Code of Ordinances of Gwinnett County 

Page 2of 4 
 
entitled “Special Assessment Districts”. The COUNTY will be responsible for all 
revenue collection and payables to contractors regarding speed hump installation. 
The CITY will not be responsible for any revenue collection or disbursement of 
payment in relation to the installation and maintenance of the speed humps, or the 
administration of the speed hump program. 
5. The procedure and requirements for the removal of speed humps are outlined in the 
Program Manual. Once the requirements are met, the COUNTY will prepare work 
orders for the contractor to remove the speed humps. The COUNTY will be 
responsible for all revenue collection and payables to contractors regarding the 
removal of speed humps. 
6. Upon the need to repave the CITY maintained streets that feature speed humps, the 
CITY will follow its normal procedures with road resurfacing and include the removal 
of speed humps. The CITY will cover the cost for the resurfacing of these streets 
and removal of speed humps. The COUNTY will cover the cost for the reinstallation 
of the speed humps and the speed humps will be reinstalled to specifications. 
7. By signing this Agreement, the CITY accepts the speed hump layout(s) as designed 
by the COUNTY, as well as the accompanying signs and striping. The speed humps 
will be constructed to the specifications as outlined in the Program Manual. 
8. To the extent permitted by law, the CITY shall indemnify and hold harmless the

9. Nothing contained within this Agreement shall be construed to in any way waive, 
restrict, or limit any privileges, protections, or immunities which may exist for the

10. This provision shall in no way relieve any contractor performing services of any

Vv. CONSENT AGENDA
1. ORDINANCES TO AMEND DULUTH CODE-BOARDS/COMMISSIONS
{A,B,C,D,E}
As discussed at the July 22 work session, Mayor and Council authorized staff to work with
the City Attorney in preparing amendments to standardize the content and language in
each of the board/commission ordinances relating to appointment of officers, meetings,
quorum, compensation, ethics, term limits, service/removal clause, attendance, open
meetings, oaths, and background checks. The proposed amendments do not include
the Planning Commission, URA, TADAC, ZBA and Ethics. The Planning Commission and
ZBA are governed under the Unified Development Code (UDC), the URA and DDA are
governed by State Law, the TADAC is founded on an intergovernmental agreement with
Gwinnett County, and currently no changes are being proposed to the Ethics ordinance.
Approval of this item approves ordinances O2024-38, 47, 48, 49 and 50 to amend the
Alcohol Board, Public Art Commission, Employee Benefits/Audit Review Committee,
Parks & Recreation Board, and Veterans Marker Committee as presented.

2. AUTHORIZATION FOR CONTRACT — RED CLAY THEATRE {F}
Approval of this item authorizes the City Manager to execute a contract with Solid Rock
Church Furniture and Design for the replacement of carpet and installation of seats at
the Red Clay Theatre.

3. APPROVAL OF IGA - DDA- GARDEN CLUB/LANDSCAPING {G}

The Garden Club of Duluth has proposed improving and maintaining certain planting
beds and planting containers in and around downtown and the Town Green. The
mechanism for implementation is a proposed intergovernmental agreement (IGA)
between the Duluth Downtown Development Authority (DDA) and the City. DDA will
provide funding and guidance. The IGA allows the Garden Club to perform projects on
city-owned property. Approval of this item approves the IGA as presented. Final approval
of all projects will fall under the City Manager.

4. ORDINANCE TO AMEND BUDGET -$9,400 — VEHICLES {H}

The Police Department sold a police vehicle, drone, and seven (7) bicycles at auction.
After commission and fees, the city received $9,400. Staff is requesting the $9,400 be
added to Police Vehicles - Consolidated Vehicle Maintenance - Vehicles line item,
including associated transfers. Approval of this item authorizes ordinance BA-FY25-10 to
amend the FY25 budget as presented.

5. ORDINANCE TO AMEND BUDGET -$29,000 — FOX ST EASEMENT {I}

For connectivity reasons, staff acquired a permanent sidewalk easement from a Fox
Street property owner, Mr. Chavez, to install a sidewalk. The cost of the easement was
$29,000 and was paid out of existing budgeted project funds.

3

[page 4]
Minutes of M&C
October 14, 2024
Page 4 of 12
These funds need to be replaced to cover a shortfall on existing projects. Therefore, staff
is requesting $29,000 in unallocated 2023 SPLOST Transportation funds be added to
Transportation/Infrastructure Improvements - Paved Streets - Repairs & Maintenance of
Streets/Sidewalks line item, including associated transfers. Approval of this item
authorizes BA-FY25-12 to amend the FY25 budget.
6. ORDINANCE TO AMEND BUDGET -$9,982 - TEMPORARY EASEMENT {J}

Mayor Whitlock opened the public hearing to consider an ordinance for text
amendments to the Unified Development Code that will clarify language as it pertains to
plantings in a drainage easement for case number TA2024-015.
Community Development/Engineering Director Margie Pozin presented the
recommended text amendment for Article 9. Project Design and Construction
Standards Section 915.04 Easements. She explained that this past summer, the
Stormwater Department employed two interns to survey drainage easements
throughout the city and found an over-abundance of trees within the easements.
These drainage easements convey stormwater runoff through underground pipes or
over shallow swales and eventually make it to larger streams or rivers. In order for
these drainage easements to properly function, they must be clear of large objects or
debris. Furthermore, trees planted above pipes conveying water will eventually destroy
the pipe as their roots grow and seek water.
Therefore, Staff recommended that trees not be planted within a drainage easement
and that only turf grass, ornamental grasses and/or shrubs and/or shrubbery not to
exceed 2 feet at maturity be allowed to be planted within the drainage easement.

1. PARKS & RECREATION UPDATE 
 
 
 
 
 
Parks & Recreation Director Kathy Marelle will present the annual program report for 
2024. The presentation will highlight the programs offered to all segments of the 
community, how to determine what is essential to our community, what activities are 
most successful, and what activities and trends they anticipate for the future. 
 
2. RED CLAY THEATRE CARPET & SEAT UPDATE 
 
 
 
 
SUMMARY: 
At the last Council meeting, M&M Interior Solutions was awarded the contract to install 
carpet and seats at the Red Clay Theatre. M&M has since informed the city that they 
are not able to fulfill the contract.

Accordingly, Eddie Owen reached out to Solid Rock Furniture to see if they would still 
be interested in providing the carpet and seats. Solid Rock was the only other bidder 
that submitted a combined proposal for carpet and seats. Solid Rock responded with 
an updated price, and as a result staff is recommending a contract be placed on the 
next agenda awarding installation of carpet and seats to them. The contract amount is 
within the budget amendment previously approved by Council. 
 
IMPACT TO BUDGET: N/A 
 
3. HALL CIRCLE TRANSPORTATION UPDATE 
 
 
 
 
SUMMARY: 
Staff has been moving forward with a plan to transition the streets within the Hall 
Circle Community to one-way operation, except for Fox Street, which will remain two-
way. 
 
As developers approach staff with opportunities to redevelop the Hall Circle area, staff 
is alerting them to the change in roadway operations. For the project to be successful 
and comprehensive, it must be done prior to the first redevelopment completion, as 
each redevelopment is based on one-way interaction with the street system and will 
include the appropriate on-street parking to meet their development requirements. 
 
Each developer is required to build their section of curb/gutter, sidewalk, and on-street 
parking, which may require them to add a small section of asphalt width to the street. 
All of this will then be dedicated to the city/public for use and maintenance within the 
public right-of-way. Once a critical mass of infrastructure is in, the city will need to go 
back and install street lighting, as appropriate. 
 
Staff will present the overall future vision for one-way operations and on-street parking 
for the Hall Circle neighborhood. 
 
IMPACT TO BUDGET: N/A 
 
4. HUDGENS PROPERTY – SMALL AREA PLAN 
 
SUMMARY: 
At the June 2024 strategic retreat, Council prioritized the development of an updated 
“small area plan” for the Hudgens property, bounded by Pleasant Hill Road, Peachtree 
Industrial Blvd, Howell Springs Drive, and McClure Bridge Road. 
 
 
Since that time, staff and the mayor have met with representatives from the Hudgens 
Foundation to discuss potential future development and to exchange ideas on how 
that property should be handled at the appropriate time. 
 
Based on those discussions, staff has developed a draft small area plan to present. If 
the updated plan is agreed upon, it will be presented in a hearing to the Planning 
Commission and then back to Council. Upon final approval, the revisions will be

3
incorporated in our Comprehensive Plan with an update sent to the Department of 
Community Affairs. 
 
IMPACT TO BUDGET: N/A 
 
 
5. STRATEGIC WORK SESSION UPDATE 
 
 
Staff will present a summary update of the strategic work session held in June. 
 
6. PLANNING COMMISSION VACANCY - CHAIR 
 
SUMMARY: 
Ray Williams has served as the Chair of the Planning Commission for several years. He 
recently told staff he is retiring and moving away; October will be his last month 
serving on Planning Commission. 
 
The current Vice Chair is Alana Moss. Staff is reaching out to Alana to gauge her 
interest in serving as Chair. Alana is eligible to serve one more year on Planning 
Commission before she times out. In the event Alana is unable or unwilling to serve as 
Chair, staff will request Commissioner Carey Fisher step in to fill the role. 
 
Mayor Whitlock is required to officially appoint the new Planning Commission Chair, 
whose service in that role will begin officially at their November 4th meeting. 
 
IMPACT TO BUDGET: N/A 
 
 
7. POSITION REQUEST – STORMWATER ASSISTANT 
 
SUMMARY: 
With an increase in workload, visibility, and expectation for project completion, 
staff is challenged to keep up with the administrative needs of the program. 
Current staff includes one full-time program/project manager, one full-time 
administrator, one part-time grant writer, and one part-time GIS specialist. 
Engineering staff is on-call to the stormwater group for technical assistance as 
needed. 
 
The stormwater group is requesting Council consider expanding staff by one full- 
time position, for a stormwater assistant. This person will assist the project 
manager and the program administrator with invoices, correspondence, 
regulatory reporting, audits, meetings, public education, billing/collections, various 
stormwater related research, easement and right of entry acquisition, citizen calls 
and inquiries, and general administrative actions. If time permits, this person will 
handle administrative inspections such as Highly Visible Pollutant Source (HVPS) 
and/or Industrial inspections. 
 
IMPACT TO BUDGET: requires budget amendment

8. INTERGOVERNMENTAL AGREEMENT W/DDA – GARDEN CLUB 
 
SUMMARY: 
The Garden Club of Duluth would like to assist in improving and maintaining certain 
planting beds and planting containers in and around downtown and the Town Green. 
The mechanism for implementation is a proposed intergovernmental agreement (IGA) 
between the Downtown Development Authority (DDA) of Duluth and the City of 
Duluth. DDA will provide funding and guidance. The IGA allows the Garden Club to 
perform projects on city-owned property through the DDA. Final approval of all 
projects will fall under the City Manager. 
 
IMPACT TO BUDGET: DDA funded

INTERGOVERNMENTAL AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE CITY OF 
DULUTH, GEORGIA AND THE DOWNTOWN DEVELOPMENT 
AUTHORITY OF DULUTH, GEORGIA FOR DOWNTOWN 
LANDSCAPING SERVICES 
 
This Agreement is hereby entered into between the City of Duluth (hereinafter referred to as 
"CITY") and the Downtown Development Authority of Duluth, Georgia (hereinafter referred to as 
"DDA"). This agreement is intended to and shall be construed as an intergovernmental agreement 
under the provisions of the Constitution of the State of Georgia. 
WHEREAS, both parties believe that the downtown landscaping is an asset of the public space 
requiring additional tending and care commensurate with its value and importance to the greater 
downtown experience and would benefit from the consistent efforts provided by the local 
community; and 
WHEREAS, the DDA has an interest in improving the appearance of existing landscaping beds 
which consist of the installation of plants, landscaping, and other aesthetic improvements 
(herein referred to as “Landscaping”) in the downtown Duluth area, bounded on the north by 
Hill Street, on the east by the city's right-of-way line for Highway 120, on the west by Hardy 
Street and on the south by the Norfolk Southern railroad tracks; and 
 
WHEREAS, the DDA has an interest in working with local volunteer community groups to carry 
out such Landscaping projects; an 
WHEREAS, the CITY and DDA wish to formalize the relationship between the Parties by setting 
forth a series of mutual expectations with regard to the installation of small scale landscaping 
improvements and stewardship of the downtown landscaping; 
NOW THEREFORE, in consideration of the mutual covenants, promises and commitments herein, 
the parties agree as follows: 
WITNESSETH 
1. The CITY authorizes the DDA to enter into agreements with third party organizations, 
contractors, and non-profit community groups for the installation and care of small scale 
landscaping improvements on public properties in downtown Duluth. Specifically, the CITY 
authorizes the DDA to install landscaping improvements in any existing landscaping beds in 
the publicly owned area bounded on the north by Hill Street, on the east by the city's right-of-
way line for Highway 120, on the west by Hardy Street and on the south by the Norfolk 
Southern railroad tracks; 
2. The small scale landscaping improvements authorized under this agreement shall not include 
the construction or placement of large statues, art, pillars, monuments or any decorative 
pieces larger than 2 feet by 2 feet in size. 

2 
3. The CITY will continue to maintain existing landscaping service contracts for the downtown 
area and will include within such contacts maintenance of any small scale landscaping 
improvements made by the DDA. 
4. DDA will be responsible for the cost of installation of the landscaping improvements installed 
pursuant to this agreement and may from time to time invite volunteers to perform routine 
maintenance to supplement the existing landscaping service contracts provided by the CITY. 
5. Should the CITY in its sole discretion determine that the Landscaping installed by the DDA 
would cause hardship to the CITY, then the DDA will remove the Landscaping that was installed 
by or for the DDA and restore landscaping bed to the standard for all downtown landscaping 
beds. 
GOVERNING LAW 
This IGA shall in all respects be governed by, and construed in accordance with, the laws of the 
State of Georgia. 
SIGNATURES 
 IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the City of Duluth, Georgia and the authorized representative of the 
Downtown Development Authority of Duluth, Georgia have executed this Understanding on this 
day of
 2024, the effective date of this Agreement.

Approval if this item authorizes ordinance BA-FY25-05 to amend the FY25 budget. 
Recently, the Police Department sold three (3) vehicles, chairs and a drone at 
auction, after commission and fees the City received $21,501. Staff is requesting 
$21,501 be added to Police Vehicles - Consolidated Vehicle Maintenance - Vehicle 
line item, including associated transfers. 
 
2. ORDINANCE TO AMEND BUDGET - $1,000,000 –STORMWATER 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
At the August 26th council work session, staff updated council on the condition of 
various City maintained detention ponds. The City is responsible for the 
maintenance of 17 detention ponds, with conditions ranging from in compliance 
and only needing annual maintenance, to others requiring minor to significant 
repairs. Staff requested a transfer of $1,000,000 from the General Fund to the 
Stormwater Utility Fund to address both repairs to the overall stormwater system 
in the amount of $850,000 and $150,000 for repairs to the Public Works and Public 
Safety detention pond. Staff will continue to research the cost and funding for the 
repairs to other detention ponds and provide an update to council. Approval of 
this item authorizes ordinance BA-FY25-06 to amend the FY25 budget as 
presented.

new carpet and seats at the Red Clay Theatre. The attached contract with M & M 
Interior Solutions will include replacement of carpet and installation of Sauder 
seats within the theatre. Approval of this item authorizes the Mayor or City 
Manager to execute the contract.

Cultural Facilities to replace the carpet and seating, painting and hiring SOGO 
Studio to redesign the lobby. Approval of this item approves BA-FY25-07 to added 
$10,000 in unallocated 2023 SPLOST Cultural Facilities funds to (CA-10) Red Clay 
Theatre - Special Recreational Facilities - Professional Services line item and 
$100,814 in unallocated 2023 SPLOST Cultural Facilities funds to Red Clay Theatre - 
Special Recreational Facilities - Site Improvements line item, including associated 
transfers.

The Mayor and Council to consider an ordinance to revise section 303 of the 
Unified Development Code. As the Unified Development Code (UDC) is currently 
written, a lot which is comprised of one single-family dwelling is exempt from the 
Outdoor Lighting Standards as set forth in Section 303. 
 
Staff recommended that lots comprised of one single-family dwelling be 
regulated through Section 303. Outdoor Lighting Standards. This includes those 
single-family dwellings within the HRD (Historic Residential District). 
 
Planning Commission recommended approval of these the original text 
amendments on August 5, 2024. A public hearing was held at the August 12th 
Council meeting, and council postponed this item and directed staff to amend 
some of the language, so as not to impede on holiday lights.

1. ORDINANCE TO AMEND FY25 BUDGET - $269,960 – POLICE EQUIPMENT 
 
As part of the upgrades to the real time crime center (RTCC), the Police 
Department would like to upgrade their drone capabilities. They are proposing 
the purchase of two new drones and docking stations that will be housed at the 
public safety facility and dispatched by the RTCC personnel. The new drones are 
specifically designed for police operations and will eliminate the practice of an 
officer on each shift carrying a drone in his vehicle. The start-up cost of the new 
system is $84,000 in year one, with ongoing support in subsequent years, which 
will be offset by the elimination of the support agreement for the Virtual Reality 
Shooting Simulator.

1. PROPOSED TAX MILLAGE RATE – 2024 
 
 
 
 
{D} 
 
Mayor Whitlock opened the public hearing to consider the tax millage rate for 
2024. 
 
Assistant City Manager/Finance Director Ken Sakmar came forward to present. 
He explained that each year, the Gwinnett County Tax Assessor reviews the assessed 
value of taxable property in the County. When the total digest of taxable property is 
prepared, Georgia Law requires calculation of a "rollback" millage rate (RMR) that 
produces the same total revenue on the current year's new digest that last year's 
millage rate would have produced, had no reassessments occurred. The City of Duluth 
is considering maintaining the same millage rate as last year, which is 6.551 mills. 
 
For the 2024 digest, the current millage rate exceeded the rollback millage rate by 
0.415 mills, or stated another way, as a percentage of the rollback millage rate, the 
current millage rate represents a 6.76% "increase." The reassessment revenue is 
approximately $1,029,072. He outlined the value impact to homeowners depending on 
their property value. The two factors that increase the revenue are the growth of the 
city, and reassessments. Growth produced in increase of 7.2% increase and 
reassessments (before appeals) resulted in a 6.65% increase for both residential and 
commercial properties. Mr. Sakmar noted the revenues and expenditures for the 
FY2025 budget, discussed exemptions, and noted that the millage rate history has 
been the same since 2016. 
 
Georgia law requires that the City publish a "Notice of Property Tax Increase" in the 
legal organ when the tentative adopted millage rate exceeds the rollback millage rate. 
In addition, three public hearings must be scheduled to allow the public an 
opportunity to express their opinion on the proposed tax millage. This is the third and 
final public hearing; an ordinance is presented for adoption. 
 
Mayor Whitlock called for discussion from Council and the public. As no 
comments were made, the Mayor closed the public hearing and called for a 
motion. 
 
A motion was made by Councilmember Harkness, seconded by 
Councilmember Holloway, to approve ordinance O2024-35 as presented, 
setting the tax millage rate for 2024 at 6.551 mills. 
 
Voted For: 
Council members Harkness, Thomas, Doss, Graeder, and Holloway 
Motion carried.

1. STORMWATER/DRAINAGE EASEMENT PROJECT – SUMMER 2024 REPORT 
 
Stormwater Coordinator Alyssa Gilhooly came forward to present. 
 
The stormwater department hired interns Graycen Murray and Jared Denman for the 
summer to assist with drainage easement research, field visits, documentation, and 
education. Ms. Gilhooly explained the groundwork for this assignment, the means for 
communication with property owners and how information was gathered. 
 
Mr. Denman came forward to report on the inspection progress, which consisted of 553 
parcels located in one square mile. Of the properties inspected, 460 had partially 
obstructed drainage easements, with issues such as overgrown vegetation, fences, 
debris and identification of other obstructions. Most of the inspections were performed 
in Howell Glen and Riverbrooke, the communities with the highest number of flooding 
complaints. 
 
Ms. Murray came forward to discuss the evaluation/grading process for the issues they 
discovered, in order to rank the severity of the problems and potentially give the Code 
Compliance Division better information to work with. She described the scale ranging 
from 0 (no corrective measures needed) to 3 (completely blocked/does not function). 
She discussed additional work that was completed in the recently annexed Boles Farm 
and Parkway Circle areas. 
 
Ms. Gilhooly referenced the Unified Development Code (UDC) requirements for 
drainage easements and property owner responsibilities. She noted that the program 
is currently for educational purposes only, aimed at helping property owners identify 
their drainage easement(s) and understand how to take care of them. No code 
violations have been issued as a result of these inspections. 
 
Ms. Gilhooly further outlined the challenges and considerations. 
• 
Drainage easements are often shared by two or more properties and therefore 
the maintenance responsibilities are also shared. 
• 
The City does not know for certain what many drainage easements were 
intended to look like when it was designated as part of development. 
• 
Without a survey, it is difficult to know exactly where an easement is in the field, 
especially for drainage ditches and swales.

6. UDC TEXT AMENDMENT – HOME OCCUPATIONS 
 
 
 
 
 
Community Development/Engineering Deputy Director Aron Hall came forward to 
present. Currently, the UDC includes only three potential home occupations: "Home 
Office" which is allowed by right in every residential zoning category, "Beauty Parlor or 
Barber Shop" which is allowed by special use permit (SUP) in all residential zoning 
categories except R-TH (Residential - Town Homes), and "Family Day Care" which is 
also allowed by SUP in all residential zoning categories except R-TH (Residential - Town 
Homes). 
 
Recognizing there are some inconsistencies in the code as well as some other home 
based businesses outside of these three categories, staff is contemplating a request for 
Council to consider a text amendment allowing adjustments to the category list and 
their allowable zones, primarily to address small-scale manufacturing. 
 
Smart Growth America states that “small-scale manufacturing” is an umbrella term 
that refers to all types of small businesses that produce tangible goods. This includes 
textiles, hardware, woodworking, metalworking, and 3D-printing.

PROCLAMATION 
 
 
 
 
 
 
GEORGIA READS DAY 
WHEREAS: 
Literacy is not just an education issue but an economic, workforce, and quality of life issue. It is also a 
predictor of future educational achievement, economic status, and lifelong health and well-being. 
 
WHEREAS: 
In 2023, 61% of Georgia rising fourth graders did not read proficiently, and research shows that 
children who are proficient readers by the end of third grade are four times more likely to graduate 
from high school than their peers who are not reading on grade level. 
 
WHEREAS: 
The General Assembly recognized the importance of literacy skills with the passage of two bills in 
2023: SB 211, that created the Georgia Council on Literacy, and HB 538, that requires comprehensive 
education reforms for reading instruction in the science of reading. 
 
WHEREAS: 
Understanding that collaborative efforts and strategic partnerships must be undertaken to effectively 
address literacy issues, the Georgia Municipal Association (GMA) and its nonprofit organization, 
Georgia City Solutions, members of the Georgia General Assembly, and football champion now turned 
children’s author, Malcolm Mitchell, partnered with the Georgia Council on Literacy to launch “Georgia 
Reads” at the 2024 GMA Annual Convention. 
 
WHEREAS: 
Community involvement is essential to literacy improvements and “Georgia Reads” will include 
recognizing 10 community partnerships that have increased literacy in the past three to five years as 
Georgia Reads Communities. 
 
WHEREAS: 
September 30, 2024, marks a date when all Georgians are encouraged to create awareness about 
the importance of reading and encourage community partnerships to promote future literacy 
improvements. 
 
WHEREAS: 
Together we can improve Georgia’s economic vitality one book at a time. 
 
THEREFORE: 
I, Mayor Greg Whitlock, do hereby proclaim September 30, 2024 as the CITY OF DULUTH READS 
DAY and encourage all residents, businesses, and community partners to help promote and elevate 
literacy as a community priority.

A RESOLUTION TO INCLUDE MUNICIPAL BOUNDARIES 
AS PART OF THE GWINNETT COUNTY MULTI-JURISDICTIONAL 
HAZARD MITIGATION PLAN 
 
 
WHEREAS, the City of Duluth, Georgia, understands the need to develop a multi-
jurisdictional hazard mitigation plan in order for the City to comprehend its 
vulnerability to natural and man-made hazards, and the actions needed to reduce or 
eliminate those risks. 
 
WHEREAS, the City of Duluth, Georgia, realizes the development of such a plan is 
vital to the protection, health, safety and welfare of its citizens as well as its visitors. 
 
WHEREAS, the City of Duluth, Georgia, understands that in order for the City to 
receive mitigation funding from the Federal Emergency Management Agency 
(FEMA), it must have a mitigation plan in place at the time of submitting a proposal. 
 
NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the City of Duluth will work with 
Gwinnett County to include its municipal boundaries as part of the Gwinnett County 
multi-jurisdictional hazard mitigation plan.

Sec. 7-25.11. - Occupations and professions subject to regulatory fees and occupation taxes.
